title: Alpine stitch baby blanket
subtitle: Front post trebles worked in rows make a raised mountain-like texture.
excerpt: Alpine stitch alternates plain dc rows with rows of front post trebles worked into the dc 2 rows below. The front post trebles raise forward to make a sharp textured ridge.
sourceNotes: Front post treble stitch from Weldon's Practical Crochet (series 3, 1880s). Alpine stitch structure (alternating dc and FPtr rows) is a modern application. Internet Archive.

content.text: An alpine stitch baby blanket is 75 x 90 cm. Odd rows are plain dc. Even rows alternate dc and
stitches, with each FPtr worked into the post of a dc 2 rows below. The front post trebles pull forward to make ridges.

DK cotton shows the raised ridges clearly. The texture is regular and geometric. Total yardage is around 400 g. Alpine stitch uses slightly more yarn than plain dc because the FPtr stitches wrap around the post below.
16 sts x 14 rows = 10 x 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook, working alpine stitch. At this gauge a foundation chain of 121 gives 75 cm width.
FPtr: front post treble (worked into post 2 rows below)
Chain 121. Work one plain row of 120 dc. Turn.
Ch 1. Dc into every stitch. Turn.
Ch 1. Dc into first stitch. *FPtr into the dc 2 rows below the next stitch (skip the dc on the current row). Dc into the next stitch*. Repeat. Turn.
pattern: work Row 2 (plain dc) then Row 3 (alpine) alternately until piece measures 90 cm (approximately 126 rows). Fasten off.
Work one round of dc (UK) around the perimeter. Work 3 dc into each corner. Secure tails with
Machine wash 30 degrees gentle. Dry flat.

content.text: This Easter egg works up quickly in a single oval piece. The shaping is all in the
increases and decreases; the decoration comes entirely from surface embroidery after stuffing.
Pastel DK yarn in two or three colours, approx. 15 g total
, increasing to 30 dc over five rounds. Work even for 6 rounds. Add a
stripe at the widest point if desired. Then decrease with
back to 6 dc. Stuff firmly before the opening closes.

Thread a contrasting pastel yarn onto the tapestry needle. Embroider horizontal running-stitch stripes around the egg body. Add French knot dots between stripes. Finish with a zigzag line in a third pastel shade around the middle.
Make a set of three in different pastel shades for a spring display. The Easter bunny amigurumi is the natural companion piece.

along both short ends. The leaves are worked separately and then joined to the body with a

In the main colour, chain 61. Work in a simple V-stitch repeat (as given for the Lace Neck Wrap) until the body measures 155 cm. Fasten off.
Row 1 (spine): dc into the 2nd ch from hook. Dc across to the last ch. Work 3 dc into the last ch (tip). Rotate work, dc back along the other side of the foundation chain to the start. Do not turn.

Block all 10 leaves. Lay five leaves along one short end of the body, aligning their bases with the scarf edge. With the tapestry needle and main colour yarn, slip-stitch the base of each leaf to the scarf edge. Repeat at the other short end. Weave in all ends.

title: Basket weave door mat
subtitle: Front and back post trebles in chunky cotton, 40 × 60 cm
excerpt: A 40 × 60 cm door mat in chunky cotton worked in basket weave: alternating columns of front and back post trebles create a raised woven texture. Intermediate skill for the post stitch technique.
sourceNotes: Original pattern. Basket weave crochet using front and back post trebles is a well-established technique.

content.text: A basket weave door mat is a 40 × 60 cm mat in chunky cotton worked in alternating columns of front and back
. The raised woven texture is firm and durable. Intermediate skill is needed to position the hook correctly around the post: once the technique is clear it works up quickly.
400 m chunky cotton. Two 200 m balls.
12 post sts × 10 rows = 10 × 10 cm in chunky cotton with a 6 mm hook. The basket weave pattern pulls in slightly: check width after the first two pattern rows.
Treble (tr). UK term; US equivalent is double crochet (dc)
Front post treble (fptr): yarn over, insert hook from front to back to front around the post of the stitch 2 rows below, draw up a loop, complete as tr.
Back post treble (bptr): yarn over, insert hook from back to front to back around the post of the stitch 2 rows below, draw up a loop, complete as tr.
The pattern repeat is 4 sts wide. Foundation: ch 51.
Row 1 (base row): ch 3 (counts as tr), tr in each ch across (48 tr). Turn.
Row 2 (basket pattern): ch 3 (counts as tr), *fptr around each of next 4 sts, bptr around each of next 4 sts; repeat from * across (48 sts). Turn.
Row 3: same as row 2: continue the same fptr/bptr columns as the previous row (48 sts). Turn.
Row 4 (switch): ch 3, *bptr around each of next 4 sts, fptr around each of next 4 sts; repeat from * across (48 sts). Turn. This swaps the raised and recessed columns.
Row 5: same as row 4 (48 sts). Turn.
Repeat rows 2, 5 until mat measures 60 cm (approx. 60 rows). Fasten off.
Weave in both ends. The basket weave fabric is naturally dense and lies flat without blocking.
Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle. Lay flat to dry. The cotton softens with use.

title: Bobble dot table runner
subtitle: Raised bobbles on a plain double crochet ground, 30 × 90 cm
excerpt: A textured table runner with raised bobble stitches scattered every four rows across a plain double crochet background. 30 × 90 cm in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook.
sourceNotes: Original pattern. Bobble-textured flat fabric is a well-established crochet convention; no single primary source.

content.text: A bobble dot table runner is a 30 × 90 cm cotton runner with raised

scattered across a plain double crochet ground every four rows. The bobbles sit on the right side of the fabric; the pattern repeats every 8 stitches across and every 4 rows up. Intermediate skill is needed to keep even tension between the bobble rows and the plain rows.
200 m DK cotton (100% cotton or cotton blend). Two 100 m balls.
16 dc × 20 rows = 10 × 10 cm in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook, lightly blocked. Bobble rows pull in slightly. The tension evens out after blocking.
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
Bobble (bob): insert hook, draw up loop, yarn over, draw through 2 loops. Do this 4 more times in the same stitch. Yarn over and draw through all 6 loops on hook.
Foundation: ch 51. Row 1 (WS): ch 1 (t-ch, does not count as st), 1 dc in 2nd ch from hook, 1 dc in each ch to end (48 dc). Turn.
Rows 1, 3 (plain rows, RS or WS): ch 1, 1 dc in each st across (48 dc). Turn.
Row 4 (bobble row, RS): ch 1, 3 dc, *1 bob, 7 dc; repeat from * 4 more times, 1 bob, 4 dc (48 sts, with 6 bobbles at sts 4, 12, 20, 28, 36, 44). Turn.
Rows 5, 7 (plain): ch 1, 1 dc in each st (48 dc). Turn.
Row 8 (bobble row, offset): ch 1, 7 dc, *1 bob, 7 dc; repeat from * 3 more times, 1 bob, 8 dc (48 sts, bobbles at sts 8, 16, 24, 32, 40). Turn.
Repeat rows 1, 8 until the runner measures 90 cm from the foundation chain (approx. 90 rows). Fasten off.
Weave in ends. Wet-block on a flat surface: pin the long edges straight and the short ends square. The bobble rows relax to match the plain rows after blocking.
Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle. Lay flat to dry.

title: Butterfly lace shawl
subtitle: A triangular shawl with a butterfly stitch repeat border in fingering weight.
excerpt: The butterfly stitch clusters open and close like wings across the border of this triangular shawl. The body is simple mesh; the border is where the stitch really shines, worked in rows of gathered loop clusters.
sourceNotes: Butterfly stitch construction draws on gathered-loop techniques present in mid-20th-century American crochet pattern booklets (public domain, pre-1928 editions held at Internet Archive). Triangular shaping and border placement are original to Homemade.

content.text: A butterfly lace shawl is a triangle worked from the top down. The body uses a simple
ground of chains and trebles; the border is six rows of
clusters that give the lower edge its character. The finished piece is 150 cm across and 70 cm deep at centre back, blocked.
The butterfly stitch works by first making long loops across four mesh rows, then using a

to pull them into the wing shape. The gathered point sits at the centre of what becomes the butterfly body. The technique looks complicated but has only two moves: long yarn-overs and one pull-through.

items.name: Fingering weight yarn
items.substitutions: A smooth fingering in wool or cotton shows the butterfly cluster shapes clearly.

content.text: 18 sts x 12 rows = 10 x 10 cm in fingering weight mesh with a 3.5 mm hook, blocked. The butterfly border is deeper than the mesh gauge suggests; work a 6-row butterfly swatch to check the border depth before committing to the full shawl.
: five long loops dropped across four rows, gathered at row 4 with one pulling sl st
Foundation: ch 5. Work (2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr) into 5th ch from hook (centre spine set). Turn.

Increase row: Ch 4 (counts as tr, ch 1). 1 tr into first tr. Work across in tr-ch-1 mesh to spine space. Work (2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr) into spine. Continue in mesh to end. Work (1 tr, ch 1, 1 tr) into turning chain. Turn.
Repeat the increase row until the shawl is 60 cm deep from the spine, measured straight down. At this point there are approximately 200 stitches across the bottom edge.

Row 1 (right side): Work in tr-ch-1 mesh across, increasing at spine as usual. On every 8th stitch position, pull up a long loop (10 cm) instead of completing the tr. Leave the loop on the hook. Continue across. Turn. (The long loops sit loose on the hook; do not work them yet.)
Rows 2 and 3: Work in plain mesh across, letting the long loops hang at the front of the fabric. Do not work into them.
Row 4 (gathering row): Work in mesh to the first long-loop position. Insert hook through all five long loops from rows 1-3. Pull yarn through all loops in one movement (
made, butterfly body formed). Continue in mesh to next long-loop position. Repeat across. Turn.
Rows 5 and 6: Work two plain mesh rows to anchor the butterfly bases.
After Row 6, work one final row of dc (UK) along the bottom edge only, placing 1 dc into each stitch and 2 dc into each chain space. Fasten off.
Soak, pin wingspan corners to 150 cm apart and centre back to 70 cm deep. Ease the
pins between each butterfly cluster so the wings spread open. Leave to dry completely.

items.fix: Place a removable stitch marker through each long loop at the base to hold its position until the gathering row.
items.cause: Not anchoring the loop base before rows 2-3

items.fix: Before gathering, fold the five loops so their midpoints align, then insert the hook and pull through all at once.
items.cause: Gathering stitch pulled off-centre

items.fix: Work the butterfly rows on a hook one size larger than the body rows and return to the smaller hook for the dc border.
items.cause: Border worked too tightly

title: Corner-to-corner baby blanket
subtitle: Diagonal squares built from one corner to the other.
excerpt: The corner-to-corner (c2c) method works a diagonal grid of small treble-cluster squares from one corner of a baby blanket to the opposite. No seams.
sourceNotes: C2c construction is a modern derivation of the Victorian diagonal square method. No direct public-domain source; synthetic from contemporary technique documentation.

content.text: A corner-to-corner baby blanket is 75 x 90 cm. The fabric is made from a diagonal grid of small treble-cluster
. Work starts at one corner and grows with
until the piece is at its widest. Then the rows shrink back down to the opposite corner.

Each square takes about 30 seconds on a 4 mm hook in DK cotton. The grid runs at 45 degrees to the finished edge, giving the fabric a subtle diagonal texture. DK cotton at this gauge makes 30 squares across the widest row and 36 rows down the length, for a total of 1,080 squares. Total yardage is around 400 g.

One c2c square = 2.5 x 2.5 cm with a 4 mm hook in DK cotton. Make 4 squares in a row and measure: the strip should be 10 cm. This is more accurate than a traditional swatch for c2c because the square size is the gauge unit.
sl st: slip stitch (to connect squares in a row)
c2c square: ch 6, work 3 tr into the 4th ch from hook (a miniature cluster)
Ch 6. Work 3 tr into the 4th chain from hook. This is one c2c square: one arch and three trebles.
Row 1: Make 1 c2c square. (1 square wide.)

Row 2: Sl st up the side of the square just made to reach the top. Ch 6, work 3 tr into 4th ch from hook (new square made). Sl st down into the ch-6 arch of Row 1. Ch 6, work 3 tr into 4th ch from hook (second new square). (2 squares wide.)
Each increase row: add one square at the start and one at the end. Continue until Row 30 (30 squares across the diagonal). This is the widest row.

From Row 31 onward, do not add a new square at the start of each row. Sl st across the top of the edge square instead of chaining a new one. Continue adding one at the end of alternate rows until Row 60 (one square, the opposite corner).
Join a new colour at the start of any row. Cut the old colour, leaving a 15 cm tail. Colour changes show on the diagonal, producing diagonal stripe effects.
Work one round of dc (UK) around the outer edge: 2 dc into each tr on open edges, 1 dc into each sl st point. This smooths the stepped diagonal edge. Fasten off. Secure all tails with
Machine wash 30 degrees, gentle. Dry flat. Pin to the stated dimensions while damp if the edges shift.
For a pixel design, use two colours per row and swap mid-row to make a picture in the diagonal grid. Or try the corner-to-corner adult throw in aran-weight yarn for a much faster version.

title: Corner-to-corner placemat
subtitle: A 30 × 40 cm placemat in the corner-to-corner technique
excerpt: A 30 × 40 cm placemat in the corner-to-corner (C2C) technique: diagonal pixel-block construction in DK cotton. Intermediate skill for managing the increase and decrease sections.
sourceNotes: Original pattern. Corner-to-corner (C2C) crochet construction is a well-established technique with no single primary source.

content.text: A corner-to-corner placemat is a 30 × 40 cm rectangle in

construction: diagonal ch-4 blocks of three trebles that increase to the midpoint then decrease back to a single block. The diagonal lines are visible on the finished mat as a herringbone-like grid. Intermediate skill is needed to manage the increase and decrease turns correctly.
100 m DK cotton. One 100 m ball per placemat. Works well in a single colour or in two alternating colours (switch colour at the start of the decrease section for a split diagonal effect).
Each C2C block (ch 4 + 3 tr) = approx. 2 cm square in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook. A 15 × 20-block mat gives approx. 30 × 40 cm.
Treble (tr). UK term; US equivalent is double crochet (dc)
C2C block: ch 4, 3 tr into the 4th ch from hook. One block.
Row 1 (1 block): ch 6 (counts as 4 + first tr), 2 tr in 4th ch from hook (1 block made). Turn.

Increase row: ch 6, 3 tr into the 4th ch from hook (new block), sl st down into the ch-4 sp of the previous row's last block, ch 3, 3 tr into the same sp (block continued). Continue sl st and ch 3 + 3 tr into each ch-4 sp across the previous row. Each increase row adds one block at the start. Repeat until the row is 20 blocks wide (row 20).

Decrease row: sl st across the top of the first block (do not work into it), sl st into the ch-4 sp of the second block. Ch 3, 3 tr into the same sp. Continue sl st and ch 3 + 3 tr into each remaining block across the row. Each decrease row drops one block at the start. Repeat until the row is 1 block wide (row 35). Fasten off.
Weave in ends. Wet-block flat to 30 × 40 cm, pinning the diagonal corner points out if needed.
Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle. Lay flat to dry. Re-block after washing if the corner points pull in.

title: Chainless foundation blanket
subtitle: The foundation chain and first row worked in one step using chainless foundation trebles.
excerpt: The chainless foundation treble combines the foundation chain and first treble row into one step. The edge is stretchier and neater than a chain-based start.
sourceNotes: Chainless foundation stitch is a modern technique. No direct Weldon source; synthetic from contemporary technique documentation.

content.text: blanket is 75 x 90 cm. The first row is worked as chainless foundation stitches, each one simultaneously creating a treble and its own foundation chain below. After the foundation row the blanket continues in plain treble.
The chainless foundation gives a stretchier, neater bottom edge than a chain start. DK cotton shows the edge difference clearly. Total yardage is around 360 g.
How to work chainless foundation treble

Ch 4 (counts as setup). Yarn over. Insert hook into the 4th ch from hook. Pull up loop. Yarn over, draw through 1 loop (this makes the foundation chain stitch below). Yarn over, draw through 2. Yarn over, draw through 2. One foundation treble made and one chain base created. For each subsequent ftr: yarn over, insert hook into the chain base of the last stitch (the bottom loop), pull up loop, and complete the treble.
16 tr x 8 rows = 10 x 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook. The foundation row gauge matches the body row gauge when the foundation stitches are worked at the same tension.
Work 120 chainless foundation trebles in a chain from the setup ch-4. The bottom edge should measure 75 cm.
of ch 3. Work 1 tr into every stitch. Tr into top of turning chain. Turn. (120 tr.)
Repeat Row 2 until piece measures 90 cm (approximately 72 rows). Fasten off.
. Block lightly with steam. The chainless foundation edge and the final row edge should look identical in weight and stretch.
Machine wash 30 degrees gentle. Dry flat.
Any of the other blanket patterns can use a chainless foundation row instead of a chain start. Try the shell stitch blanket with a chainless foundation for a particularly neat shell edge.

subtitle: Super-chunky cotton rope, one large pot
excerpt: A bold single-tier plant hanger in super-chunky cotton rope or T-shirt yarn, sized for a 15, 20 cm pot. Works up quickly on a 10 mm hook with an open-mesh cup and thick hanging cords.
sourceNotes: Original pattern. Super-chunky plant hangers are a contemporary development. No pre-1928 sources apply.

content.text: A chunky rope plant hanger holds a large 15, 20 cm pot in a thick open-mesh cup worked from a

. Super-chunky cotton rope or T-shirt yarn works on a 10 mm hook. The whole hanger takes under two hours to complete. The thick cords hold heavy pots without strain, and the open cup lets the terracotta breathe.
60 m super-chunky cotton rope or T-shirt yarn (3 mm rope diameter works well). One ball of 100 m is enough for two hangers.
1 wooden ring, 4 cm diameter, for the hanging loop, or use a sturdy metal ring.
7 dc × 9 rows = 10 × 10 cm in super-chunky cotton rope with a 10 mm hook, unblocked. Gauge is approximate: adjust cup size by adding or removing rounds.
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
MR: ch 3, 11 tr into the ring, sl st to top of ch 3 to join (12 sts).
Round 2: ch 1, 2 dc in each st around, sl st to join (24 sts).
Round 3: ch 1, *1 dc in next st, 2 dc in next st; repeat from * around, sl st to join (36 sts).
Rounds 4, 5: ch 1, 1 dc in each st, sl st to join (36 sts). This builds the cup sides.
Hanging cords (work 4, one at each quarter-point)
Mark 4 evenly-spaced points on the cup rim (stitch 1, 10, 19, 28 on the 36-st round).
Attach yarn at a marker. Ch 60 (approx. 45 cm). Sl st back along the chain to the cup rim to form a thick cord. Fasten off leaving a 30 cm tail.
Repeat for the other 3 marked points.
Thread all 4 cord tails through the wooden ring. Pull even and knot securely. Trim tails to 3 cm and weave in with the tapestry needle.
Weave in all ends. The thick cotton rope does not need blocking: it holds its shape under the weight of the pot.

Handwash or machine-wash on a 30°C gentle cycle. Hang to dry with the pot removed. Cotton rope yellows slightly with age in direct sun: position away from a south-facing window if colour-retention matters.

excerpt: Double crochet in chunky-weight yarn on an 8 mm hook builds a thick, warm throw in an afternoon. Tight dc fabric in chunky yarn is heavier and warmer than the same size in DK.
sourceNotes: Plain double crochet blanket. Chunky yarn application is modern; the stitch is documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet (1st series, 1880s). Internet Archive.

content.text: A chunky throw is a 90 x 110 cm piece of plain double crochet worked back and forth in chunky-weight yarn on an 8 mm hook. The thick yarn builds height quickly: the full throw takes around 110 rows, which is a few hours of steady work rather than a multi-day project. The dense dc fabric in chunky yarn is noticeably heavier and warmer than a treble blanket in DK.

Chunky wool or wool-blend gives the best drape and warmth; chunky acrylic is lighter and machine washable. Total yardage is about 500 g chunky. The dc stitch in chunky produces a very tight fabric with few gaps, so it keeps draughts out.

title: Coiled rope rug
subtitle: Thick cotton rope coiled and joined in double crochet
excerpt: A 50 cm round rug made from thick cotton rope coiled in a flat spiral and joined with double crochet stitches through the rope. No yarn: works with 5 mm cotton macramé rope. Advanced due to the tension needed to keep the coil flat.
sourceNotes: Original pattern. Coiled rope rugs crocheted through thick cord are a domestic tradition that predates standardised crochet; this version uses readily available cotton macramé cord.

content.text: A coiled rope rug is a 50 cm disc worked by

, 5 mm cotton macramé rope is coiled in a flat spiral, and each new coil is joined to the previous one with double crochet stitches worked through both strands. No yarn is needed, only the rope itself. The 10 mm hook is the right size for piercing through two strands of 5 mm rope. The result is firm, washable, and reversible.

items.label: Large-eye tapestry needle (for burying rope ends)

content.text: Approx. 60 m of 5 mm single-twist or braided cotton macramé rope. One 100 m spool with some left over.
Work with 5 mm cotton macramé rope on a 10 mm hook. Each coil round adds approx. 4, 5 cm to the diameter. 6 rounds gives approx. 50, 55 cm.
Slip stitch (sl st). Used to join the start of each coil round
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc). Worked through both the new coil and the previous coil simultaneously.

Centre ring: coil the rope end into a tight circle about 5 cm across (approximately 3, 4 wraps). Using the hook, work dc stitches through both layers of the coil all the way around, pulling firmly to close the centre. Sl st to join (approx. 8, 10 dc).

Coil round 2: continue the rope spiral, laying the new coil against the outside of round 1. Work dc stitches through both the new coil and the previous round, spacing them approx. Every 2, 3 cm. Work 2 dc into the same spot approx. Every 5th join to keep the coil lying flat. Sl st at end of round to join.

Rounds 3, 6: continue the spiral, joining the new coil to the previous one with evenly-spaced dc stitches. Add extra dc joins at any point where the coil starts to cup upward (every 4th join rather than every 5th). After 6 rounds, the rug should be approx. 50 cm diameter.
Finishing the end: cut the rope at a point that completes the round evenly. Thread the cut end through a large tapestry needle and bury it back through the previous coil for at least 5 cm to secure.

Work on a hard flat surface and regularly press the rug down as you go: gravity and a firm surface are your main flatness tools here. If the rug cups, undo back to the previous round and add more dc joins on the outside edge.

Bury the rope tail through the last coil using the tapestry needle. No weaving-in. The tail is hidden inside the rope structure. Wet the rug lightly and press flat under heavy books for 30 minutes if it needs final shaping.
Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle. Lay flat to dry. Cotton macramé rope can loosen slightly with washing: press flat again after the first few washes.

is three dc into a chain loop. The cloth grows by one block per row until reaching the widest point, then decreases. The diagonal seams make a naturally dense fabric.

content.text: A cotton bottle bag is a 25 cm circumference cylindrical carrier worked in double crochet from a circular base via a

. The sides are worked straight for 23 cm, then a drawstring channel closes the top around the bottle neck. Fits a standard 750 ml water bottle or wine bottle. One 100 m ball of DK cotton makes one bag with yarn left over.

16 dc × 20 rows = 10 × 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook. Body circumference: 40 dc = approx. 25 cm.
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
Round 2: 2 dc in each st (12 dc).
Round 3: *1 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (18 dc).
Round 4: *2 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (24 dc).
Round 5: *3 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (30 dc).
Round 6: *4 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (36 dc).
Round 7: *5 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (40 dc). Sl st to join.
Round 8: ch 1, 1 dc in each st through back loop only (40 dc). Sl st. This creates a clean base/side transition ridge.
Rounds 9, 47: ch 1, 1 dc in each st through both loops (40 dc). Sl st each round. 40 rounds = approx. 20 cm of straight sides.
Round 48: ch 1, *1 dc, ch 2, skip 1; repeat from * around (20 ch-2 spaces). Sl st.
Round 49: ch 1, 1 dc in each dc, 2 dc in each ch-2 sp (40 dc). Sl st. Fasten off.
Weave in ends. Thread 50 cm cotton cord through the ch-2 drawstring channel, entering and exiting at the same gap. Knot cord ends. Pull to cinch around the bottle neck.
Remove the bottle. Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle. Hang to dry.

title: Single-tier cotton plant hanger
subtitle: A gathered cord hanger for one pot, 10, 15 cm diameter
excerpt: A single-tier cotton plant hanger worked in DK cotton cord, sized for a standard 10, 15 cm terracotta pot. Worked flat and gathered rather than crocheted, but all joining and knotting details are here.
sourceNotes: Original pattern derived from traditional macramé-crochet hybrid hanger techniques documented in general craft references from the 1970s onward. No single primary source.

content.text: A single-tier cotton plant hanger holds one pot. The standard 10, 15 cm terracotta or plastic pot that sits on a windowsill. The cup is worked in double crochet in the round from a
, then the hanging cords extend upward and gather at the top loop. DK cotton gives a clean, non-stretchy cup that holds the pot weight without distorting.

The cup is worked flat in the round to a diameter that fits around the base of your chosen pot. The four hanging cords are then crocheted up from the cup rim and joined at a gathered loop 40, 50 cm above. Total cotton: roughly 80 m of DK cotton.
80 m DK cotton (100% cotton or cotton-linen blend). One ball of 100 m DK cotton is enough for one hanger with off-cuts.
1 small metal ring, 2, 3 cm diameter, for the hanging loop (a curtain ring works well).

16 dc × 20 rows = 10 × 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook, unblocked. Gauge is not critical for plant hangers. The cup size adjusts by changing chain count. Work a quick swatch and see how your fabric drapes; a looser tension suits this project.
Slip stitch (sl st). UK and US
Double crochet (dc). UK; this is single crochet (sc) in US terminology
Treble (tr). UK; this is double crochet (dc) in US terminology
. Work all rounds in a continuous spiral: place a stitch marker on the first stitch of each round and move it up as you work.
Round 1: 6 dc into the magic ring (6 sts).
Round 2: 2 dc in each st (12 sts).
Round 3: *1 dc in next st, 2 dc in next st; repeat from * around (18 sts).
Round 4: *1 dc in each of next 2 sts, 2 dc in next st; repeat from * around (24 sts).
Round 5: *1 dc in each of next 3 sts, 2 dc in next st; repeat from * around (30 sts).
Round 6: *1 dc in each of next 4 sts, 2 dc in next st; repeat from * around (36 sts).
Round 7: *1 dc in each of next 5 sts, 2 dc in next st; repeat from * around (42 sts).

Check that the base fits under your pot. The base should be slightly smaller than the base of the pot. The cup walls will grip the pot. For a 10 cm pot, rounds 1, 5 (30 sts) are usually enough. For a 13 cm pot, rounds 1, 6 (36 sts). For a 15 cm pot, work rounds 1, 7 (42 sts).
From the last base round, work straight (no increases) for 4 rounds of dc. This creates the cup wall that holds the pot. Close the final round with a
into the first st, ch 1, turn.
Divide the cup rim into 4 equal sections. Mark the quarter points with stitch markers. On each marked section, work a hanging cord as follows:
Join yarn at the first marker with a sl st.
Ch 3 (counts as first tr), work 2 tr into the next 2 sts at the marker point (3 tr total).
Turn. Ch 3 (counts as first tr), 2 tr into the top of the previous tr group.
Repeat step 3 for a total of 13 rows (or until the cord measures 40 cm from the cup rim). Each group of 3 tr makes the cord body.
Fasten off, leaving a 30 cm tail for gathering.
Thread the 4 tail ends through the small metal ring.
Pull all 4 tails even and tie a square knot directly against the ring.
Trim to 2 cm below the knot and weave the ends back through the cord with the tapestry needle.

Weave in the starting tail from the magic ring tightly. Give the cup a light steam with a steam iron held 5 cm above the fabric. This tightens the cotton and firms up the cup shape. Do not press the iron down onto the crochet.

Handwash in cool water with a drop of washing-up liquid. Rinse and squeeze gently. Do not wring. Hang to dry naturally. Cotton plant hangers can go in a 30°C machine wash on a gentle cycle if needed; reshape while damp.

title: African flower, four colours
subtitle: A four-colour 15 cm hexagonal motif with an extended treble border
excerpt: A fourth colour adds an outer border round to the three-colour African flower, taking the motif to 15 cm and giving a second frame around the petal ring. The extra border creates a wider flat joining edge for blankets and makes the colour palette more complex without requiring any new stitches.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from the established African flower construction, extended to four-colour working. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 4 (1889), for multi-colour in-the-round motif conventions (Internet Archive).

content.text: The four-colour African flower adds one border round in a fourth colour to the three-colour version. Rounds 1 through 3 are identical. Round 4 mirrors the inner border with a wider three-treble cluster group at each side and an extended ch-2 corner. The result is a 15 cm hexagon with four distinct colour bands and a flatter join edge.

Colour placement matters: the petal round reads best when it contrasts both the centre and the inner border. The outer border does most of the frame work and looks good in either a neutral or a bold contrast.

title: African flower hexagon variant
subtitle: Pointed hexagonal corners replace the standard rounded border, 13 cm
excerpt: The hexagon variant of the African flower changes the border construction so that each of the six corners forms a pointed tip rather than a rounded ch-2 space. The result is a true geometric hexagon that tiles without gaps in a flat grid, making it the joining-friendly choice for throws where the motifs sit edge to edge.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from the African flower construction with hexagonal border modification. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 6 (1891), hexagonal motif section (Internet Archive).

content.text: The hexagon variant of the African flower keeps the puff-stitch petal construction of rounds 1 and 2 but changes the border chain at each corner from ch-2 to ch-3. The single extra chain at each of the six corners produces the pointed tip of a regular hexagon. When these motifs sit edge to edge in a grid the pointed corners interlock. Leaving a very narrow gap, much smaller than the gap between rounded-corner versions.
Three colours give the clearest read: centre, petals, and border. Two colours also work, omitting the colour change before round 3.

title: African flower, three colours
subtitle: A nine-petal hexagonal motif worked in three colours, 12 cm
excerpt: The African flower builds nine puff-stitch petals outward from a tight centre ring, then frames them with a single-colour hexagonal border. Three colours, centre, petals, and border, give the classic high-contrast graphic that tiles into throws, bags, and cushion covers without seams visible from the front.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from widely-documented African flower construction in DK-weight cotton. Weldon's Practical Crochet (1886, Internet Archive) for puff-stitch motif principles. The three-colour arrangement follows the standard published palette convention.

content.text: The African flower builds nine puff-stitch petals in the second round. Then closes them inside a hexagonal treble border. Three distinct yarn colours give the petals maximum contrast against both the centre and the border. Which is why the classic three-colour version tiles so legibly in throws and bags.

A puff stitch is looser and rounder than a bobble: you draw up several elongated half-treble loops from the same stitch before pulling through them all at once. The height of the loops sets the petal height. So tension here affects the finished look more than any other round. Too tight and the petals lie flat; too loose and the motif cups. A 4 mm hook in DK cotton at normal tension gives petals that stand slightly above the border.

title: Bee motif
subtitle: A striped oval body with two oval wing panels and chain antennae, 8 cm
excerpt: The bee motif is a small striped oval body in yellow and black DK cotton with two translucent-style oval wing panels in white or cream and a pair of ch-6 antennae. At 8 cm long it is compact enough for greetings card embellishment and works at full scale as an applique on children's blankets and summer cushions.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from striped oval and wing construction. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 7 (1892), small animal applique chapter (Internet Archive).

content.text: The bee body is a small oval worked from a chain foundation with three stripe colour changes. Two rows yellow, one row black, to give the characteristic three black stripes. The wings are even smaller ovals in cream or white. Worked in the same way as the body but without colour changes. The antennae are simple chain lengths with a small slip-stitch curl at the tip.

title: Butterfly motif
subtitle: Four wing panels with a chain-wrapped body, 12 cm wingspan
excerpt: The butterfly motif consists of two large upper wing panels and two smaller lower wing panels, each worked as a separate dc shape and joined at a central chain-wrapped body. At 12 cm wingspan in DK cotton it is bold enough for cushion centrepieces and works equally well in 4-ply at 8 cm for finer applique.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 6 (1891), butterfly and flower applique chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet applique butterfly.

content.text: The butterfly builds four separate wing panels, two large upper and two smaller lower. And joins them with a chain-wrap body. Each wing is a small oval: dc rows that increase from the inner edge to the widest point. Then decrease back to the outer tip. Working all four wings in the same colour gives a symmetrical silhouette. Using a second colour for the wing centres adds an eyespot effect.

title: Fish motif
subtitle: A flat applique fish with a fan tail and scale texture, 10 cm
excerpt: The fish motif builds an oval body in dc rows with a five-treble fan tail at the wide end and a small embroidered eye. The body is worked in the round in a single oval, giving a clean edge for applique. At 10 cm long in DK cotton it is suitable for children's blankets, beach bag decoration, and bathroom textiles.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from flat oval applique and fan construction. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 8 (1893), flat animal applique chapter (Internet Archive).

content.text: The fish uses an oval foundation for the body: a chain worked along both sides in the round. With 3-dc increases at each rounded end to keep the oval flat. Two rounds give a solid body. The fan tail is added as five trebles into the same space at the wider end. Then a second fan ch-1 apart to form a two-lobe tail. An embroidered eye and a chain line for the pectoral fin complete the fish.

title: Fox motif
subtitle: A flat applique fox face with pointed ears and white muzzle, 9 cm
excerpt: The fox motif builds a round orange dc head with two sharply pointed ear triangles worked from the top edge, a white oval muzzle sewn in place, and a black nose. The angular ear construction and the muzzle overlay together identify the piece as a fox rather than the rounder cat or rabbit. At 9 cm in DK cotton it is a strong applique centrepiece for cushions, book bags, and autumn-theme blankets.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from flat applique animal face construction. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 9 (1894), animal applique chapter (Internet Archive).

content.text: The fox face shares the same round head construction as the cat and rabbit. From a magic ring outward to 24 dc. The ears are sharper triangles than the cat (they reach full treble height in a single stitch rather than rounding over) and are worked directly from the border. The muzzle is a small white oval chain-worked in the round and sewn over the lower centre of the face. A black French knot sits at the top of the muzzle for the nose.

title: Hedgehog motif
subtitle: A flat applique hedgehog with a bobble-spine back, 9 cm
excerpt: The hedgehog motif is a semicircular body with a pointed nose, worked in two parts: a smooth dc belly in a light colour and a dark spine-back with bobble stitches packed across it. The bobbles read as individual spines at 9 cm in DK cotton, and the whole motif sits flat for applique on blankets, pouches, and cushions.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from bobble-texture applique construction. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 10 (1895), texture stitch applique chapter (Internet Archive).

content.text: The hedgehog builds a flat semicircular body in cream dc rows from a chain foundation. Tapering toward a pointed nose. The spine back is a second panel worked in dark brown with bobble stitches every alternate stitch across each row. Then sewn onto the upper curve of the body. The contrast of smooth belly and raised spine back reads clearly even at 9 cm.
The bobbles push outward on the wrong side of the spine panel. So work the spine panel with the wrong side facing. When sewn onto the body, the bobbles stand proud from the surface.

title: Asymmetric Wedge Shawl
subtitle: Garter-effect double crochet rows with a single edge increase for a wedge silhouette
excerpt: A wedge-shaped shawl worked in rows of double crochet with one increase at a single edge on every row. The asymmetric shape and garter-effect ridging come entirely from the dc stitch worked into the back loop only, without any complex shaping.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. Asymmetric one-sided-increase construction is a well-established technique with no single originating source.

content.text: This shawl is a wedge shape measuring approximately 130cm along the long straight edge and 65cm at the widest point. It is worked from the narrow point outward in rows of double crochet worked into the back loop only. A single increase at one edge on every row creates the asymmetric angle: one edge of the shawl stays straight while the other curves outward, producing the characteristic wedge silhouette. Working into the back loop only leaves the front loops exposed as horizontal ridges across the fabric, giving a texture often described as garter-effect. DK weight on a 4mm hook produces firm, substantial fabric with good structure.

Yarn: approximately 450g of DK weight yarn. A smooth, tightly plied yarn makes the ridged texture clear. Hook: 4mm. You will also need a tapestry needle, scissors, and a tape measure. A stitch marker for the increase stitch is helpful. A foam blocking mat and rust-proof pins are useful for the final shaping.

18 dc and 20 rows to 10cm over dc worked into the back loop only, using a 4mm hook. This gauge is critical for the wedge to reach the correct dimensions. Work a 10cm swatch in dc-BLO and measure before starting the full piece.
dc-BLO: double crochet into back loop only
inc: 2 dc in the same stitch

The shawl starts at the point with a foundation chain of 3. The increase always happens at the end of the row (the widening edge). The ch 1 turning chain at the start of each row does not count as a stitch. Work all stitches into the back loop only unless stated otherwise.
Ch 1 (does not count as st), dc in 2nd ch from hook, dc in next ch, 2 dc in last ch (increase), turn. (4 sts)
Ch 1 (does not count as st), dc-BLO in each st to last st, 2 dc-BLO in last st (increase), turn. (5 sts)
Ch 1 (does not count as st), dc-BLO in each st to last st, 2 dc-BLO in last st (increase), turn.

Each row adds exactly 1 stitch. The row count equals the number of stitches in that row. Continue until the long (straight) edge measures approximately 130cm. At the stated gauge this is approximately 260 rows, ending with approximately 263 sts in the final row.
Work one row of dc through both loops evenly along the long straight edge for a neat finish. Do not increase at the corners; keep the edge flat.

Weave in all ends on the wrong side. Block by soaking in cool water and pressing out excess moisture. Pin the long straight edge to 130cm on a foam mat and ease the widest point to 65cm. Allow to dry completely. Blocking straightens the long edge and softens the fabric.
Hand wash in cool water with a gentle detergent. Reshape while damp and dry flat. Check the yarn label: wool-content yarns need cool water to avoid felting. Do not tumble dry.

The back-loop-only technique transfers well to scarves and cowls: a long dc-BLO rectangle in a finer yarn produces a stripy ribbed effect. For a triangle with increases on both sides and a more complex stitch pattern, try the ripple chevron shawl. If you want to explore the wedge shape in a lace yarn, the mohair lace shawl uses a similar one-edge-increase structure in lace weight.

title: Baby Christening Shawl in Openwork Lace
subtitle: Lace weight dc mesh with shell border, 100cm square, adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet
excerpt: A 100cm square christening shawl worked in fine lace weight yarn on a 2.5mm hook. The body is an open dc mesh worked in rows; the border is a deep shell lace edging. Construction follows a traditional pattern from Weldon's Practical Crochet, now in the public domain.
sourceNotes: Construction and border adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet (published 1886-1897), now in the public domain. Pattern updated to modern UK crochet terminology and metric sizing.

content.text: This shawl is a 100cm square worked in lace weight yarn on a 2.5mm hook. The body is a flat dc mesh: alternating double crochets and chain-1 spaces worked in rows, producing a fine open net. A four-round shell lace border is then worked around all four sides in joined rounds. The pattern is adapted from a christening shawl construction documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet, a late nineteenth-century needlework series now in the public domain. The project is rated advanced because of the fine gauge, the long row count, and the precision needed during blocking to achieve a square finish. The stitches themselves are all foundational: if you are confident with dc and treble in DK weight, the techniques are the same here but with a much finer yarn.

A word on blocking: lace weight crochet changes dramatically when blocked. The mesh opens up, the border shells spread into fans, and the square settles flat. Budget time for a proper wet-block before assessing the finished size. Rust-proof pins and a foam mat are essential, not optional, for this pattern.

Yarn: approximately 400g of lace weight yarn (a 2-ply cotton or wool-silk blend is traditional for christening shawls; cotton holds its shape well after blocking). Hook: 2.5mm. You will also need a tapestry needle, scissors, tape measure, a foam blocking mat, and rust-proof pins. At least 50 pins are recommended for blocking the full border.

One dc mesh repeat (1 dc, ch 1) measures approximately 0.6cm wide and 0.6cm tall on a 2.5mm hook. The body mesh square is approximately 85cm x 85cm before the border, which adds approximately 7.5cm on each side. Work a swatch of at least 30 mesh repeats and measure carefully: a difference of even 0.1cm per repeat becomes 16cm over a full 167-repeat row.
dc mesh: dc, ch 1, skip 1, repeat
Shell border: 5 tr in ch sp for the body of each fan
Picot: ch 3, sl st in base st
Ch 337. This gives 168 mesh repeats (ch 2 per repeat = 336 chs, plus 1 turning ch). The foundation chain should measure approximately 85cm laid flat.
Ch 4 (counts as dc + ch 1), skip 1 ch, dc in next ch, [ch 1, skip 1 ch, dc in next ch] to end, turn. (168 dc, 168 ch-1 sps)
Ch 4 (counts as dc + ch 1), skip first ch-1 sp, dc in next dc, [ch 1, skip ch-1 sp, dc in next dc] to end, working final dc into 3rd ch of turning ch, turn. (168 dc, 168 ch-1 sps)
Repeat this row until the mesh square measures approximately 85cm x 85cm, approximately 142 rows at stated gauge. Fasten off.

Join yarn in any corner ch-1 sp. Ch 1 (does not count as st), dc evenly along each side: 1 dc per ch-1 sp along row ends, 1 dc per ch-1 sp along foundation and final row. Work 3 dc into each corner. Sl st to join. (approximately 680 dc total: 168 per side plus 4 corner groups of 3)

Ch 3 (counts as first tr), skip next dc, [5 tr in next dc, skip 2 dc, dc in next dc, skip 2 dc] across each side, placing a 7-tr corner shell into each corner centre dc. Sl st to join. (approximately 45 shells per side plus 4 corner shells)
Sl st to centre tr of first shell, ch 1, dc in same tr, picot (ch 3, sl st in base dc), [dc in centre tr of next shell, picot] across each side and at each corner. Sl st to join. (1 picot per shell)
Work a final round of dc between each picot with a further picot at each dc. This gives a double-picot border edge. Fasten off.

Weave in all ends on the wrong side. Wet-block the shawl by soaking in cool water for 20 minutes, removing excess moisture in a towel, and laying flat on a foam mat. Pin the four corners to 100cm square, then pin along each side edge at approximately 5cm intervals. Pin each border shell open so it fans fully. Leave to dry completely, which may take 24 hours or more depending on the fibre. Do not remove pins until the fabric is entirely dry.
Hand wash in cool water with a gentle detergent suitable for the fibre. Rinse well. Dry flat, reshaping as needed. Re-block if the square loses its shape after washing. Do not tumble dry.

The dc mesh technique in this pattern is the foundation for all filet crochet: a dc-and-chain grid where filled squares form images and open squares form the background. For a simpler lace shawl using the same yarn weight but a larger hook for a more open mesh, see the mohair lace shawl. The shell border worked in rounds here is the same technique used in the baby shell stitch shawl, but at a much finer scale.

title: Baby Shawl in Shell Stitch
subtitle: DK weight shell stitch squares worked in the round for a 80cm x 80cm baby shawl
excerpt: A square baby shawl for a 0 to 6 month old, worked from the centre outward in shell stitch. Each shell is 5 trebles in a single chain space. DK weight on a 4mm hook produces a fabric soft enough for a newborn but structured enough to hold its shape.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. Centre-out square construction with shell edging is a well-established baby shawl technique with no single originating source.

content.text: This baby shawl is an 80cm square worked from the centre outward in rounds using shell stitch. It is sized for a 0 to 6 month old infant. Each shell is 5 trebles worked into a single chain space. You begin with a magic ring, work an initial set of shells in the first round, then increase by adding corner shells on every subsequent round. The technique is the same throughout: shell into each chain space from the previous round, plus an extra shell at each corner. DK weight on a 4mm hook produces fabric that is soft against newborn skin and firm enough to wrap securely. The square shape is practical: it can be folded on the diagonal as a triangle or laid flat as a swaddle.

Yarn: approximately 350g of DK weight yarn. For a baby item, use a machine-washable yarn with a soft finish. Pure cotton, bamboo-cotton, or superwash merino work well. Hook: 4mm. You will also need a tapestry needle, scissors, a tape measure, and optional stitch markers and blocking mat.

One shell (5 tr) measures approximately 3.5cm wide on a 4mm hook over shell stitch. Tension is not critical for a baby shawl, but if your tension is tighter than stated the finished piece will be smaller than 80cm square. Work a small swatch in shell stitch to check.
Shell: 5 tr in same ch sp

The shawl is worked in joined rounds from the centre. A corner is formed by working ch 2 between two shells into the same chain space. Each corner chain space appears at the same position every round. Use stitch markers on the corner chain spaces if helpful.
Ch 4 (counts as tr + ch 1), [shell in ring, ch 2] 4 times, sl st to 3rd ch of starting ch-4 to join. Pull magic ring tail to close centre. (4 shells, 4 corner ch-2 sps)

Sl st into first ch-2 corner sp, ch 4 (counts as tr + ch 1), shell in same corner sp, ch 1, [shell in corner ch-2 sp, ch 2, shell in same corner ch-2 sp, ch 1] 3 times, sl st to 3rd ch of starting ch-4. (8 shells)

Sl st into corner sp, ch 4, shell in same corner sp, ch 1, shell in side ch-1 sp, ch 1, [shell in corner sp, ch 2, shell in same corner sp, ch 1, shell in side ch-1 sp, ch 1] 3 times, sl st to join. (12 shells)

Each round adds 4 shells (one extra side shell per side). Work [shell in corner sp, ch 2, shell in same corner sp, ch 1] at every corner, and [shell in each ch-1 sp along each side, ch 1] between corners. Continue until the square measures approximately 80cm on each side. End with a sl st join. Fasten off.
Work one round of dc evenly around all four sides, placing 3 dc into each corner ch-2 sp. Sl st to join, fasten off.

Weave in all ends on the wrong side using the tapestry needle. Block by soaking in cool water, pressing out excess moisture in a towel, then pinning the four corners and sides square on a foam mat. Allow to dry completely. Make sure there are no loose tails that could unravel and be dangerous for a baby.
Machine wash on a gentle cool cycle if you have used a superwash or cotton yarn. Check the yarn label for the specific fibre. Dry flat to maintain the square shape. Do not tumble dry.

Once the centre-out square technique feels comfortable, try a baby blanket using the same method with a larger hook and bulkier yarn. For a more formal baby shawl, the baby christening shawl uses lace weight on a 2.5mm hook with a dc mesh body and shell border. For an adult garment using the same shell-over-chain-space principle, see the classic prayer shawl.

title: Basketweave Rectangle Wrap
subtitle: Textured front-and-back post treble stitch in a classic woven pattern
excerpt: A chunky rectangular wrap worked in alternating panels of front-post and back-post trebles to create a raised basketweave effect. Aran weight yarn on a 5mm hook gives firm, structured fabric with satisfying depth.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. Basketweave post-stitch construction is a widely established crochet technique with no single source.

content.text: This rectangular wrap measures approximately 170cm wide by 50cm deep and is worked from side to side in rows using alternating panels of front-post and back-post trebles. The raised squares interlock to produce the characteristic woven look of basketweave. You work entirely in one piece with no seaming. Aran weight yarn on a 5mm hook produces firm, structured fabric with good drape at the finished dimensions. Post stitches require a firm and even tension: the raised effect depends on wrapping around the post of the stitch in the row below rather than working into the top loops. Practise on a swatch of at least 20 stitches before casting on for the full wrap.

Yarn: approximately 600g of aran weight yarn (100% wool or wool-acrylic blend works well for stitch definition). Hook: 5mm. You will also need a tapestry needle for weaving in ends, scissors, a tape measure, and optional blocking mat and rust-proof pins.

14 stitches and 10 rows to 10cm over basketweave pattern using a 5mm hook. Check your tension against this measurement after working your swatch. A tighter tension will produce a narrower, shorter wrap; a looser tension will produce a wider, longer one.

The wrap is worked from one short end to the other. The foundation chain is the width of the wrap (the 50cm measurement). Each basketweave square is 4 stitches wide and 4 rows tall. title: Bavarian crochet square
subtitle: Concentric colour rings with front-post treble ridges worked in the round
excerpt: The Bavarian square builds outward from the centre in colour-ringed rounds, each ring locked to the previous with front-post trebles that create a raised ridge at every colour change. The post stitches pull the round inward slightly, producing a slightly domed, textured motif that photographs beautifully from above.
sourceNotes: The Bavarian stitch construction is documented in German needlework manuals from the late 19th century. The crochet adaptation appears in English in Weldon's Practical Needlework, Volume 6 (1891).

content.text: The Bavarian square locks each colour ring to the previous with front post trebles worked around the tops of the previous round. The post stitches pull the fabric slightly toward the centre on each ring. Creating the characteristic slight dome and raised ridges at every colour boundary.

Two colours in alternating rounds give the clearest result. Three or more colours work but require more ends to weave in. Colour A starts the magic ring. Colour B works the first post-ridge round; colours continue alternating through as many rounds as needed.

Rounds 3 to 4 (colour A, then colour B)
Continue alternating colours, working fptr around ALL previous-round side stitches. Corner clusters grow by 0, only the sides grow with each round. Fasten off after round 4.

title: Bobble wrap shawl
subtitle: A rectangle of double crochet studded with five-treble bobbles in aran-weight yarn
excerpt: This rectangular wrap uses a dc background with bobbles on every fourth stitch and every fourth row, creating an all-over raised spot texture. The yarn is aran weight on a 5 mm hook. Finished size is approximately 160 cm wide by 55 cm deep. The bobbles form on wrong-side rows so they push outward on the right side.

content.text: This wrap is a rectangle of double crochet with a five-treble bobble worked on every fourth stitch of every fourth row. The bobbles are made on wrong-side rows, so they push toward the right side as a raised spot when the work is turned. At 160 cm by 55 cm the finished piece is a full wrap with enough depth to fold across the shoulders. Aran weight on a 5 mm hook gives a dense, warm fabric.
is five trebles worked into the same stitch, each left unfinished until the final pull-through. The result is a firm rounded bump. Because the bobbles are
, each bobble-row is a wrong-side row.

attrs.body: Approximately 550 g aran-weight yarn. A 5 mm crochet hook (US H/8). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Tape measure. Stitch markers (optional, to track bobble positions).
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 14 dc x 16 rows = 10 x 10 cm in aran-weight yarn with a 5 mm hook, measured unstretched. Bobble rows pull the fabric in slightly; swatch at least 20 rows including two bobble rows to get an accurate row gauge.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
double crochet (dc): UK; the same move as US "single crochet" (sc).
bobble (5-tr cluster into one stitch, described above).

The wrap is worked flat along its length; the foundation chain is the 55 cm depth and the rows build the 160 cm width. Bobble rows occur on row 3, then every fourth row after that (rows 7, 11, 15, etc.), all of which are wrong-side rows. On bobble rows, work one bobble on every fourth stitch starting at stitch 4, with dc between each bobble.
Ch 78. (This gives 77 working stitches across the 55 cm depth.)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch throughout). 1 dc in each ch across. Turn. (77 sts)
Ch 1 (does not count as stitch). 1 dc in each st across. Turn. (77 sts)

Ch 1 (does not count as stitch). 1 dc in each of first 3 sts. *Bobble in next st, 1 dc in each of next 3 sts*; repeat from * to * to last 2 sts. 1 dc in each of last 2 sts. Turn. (58 dc, 19 bobbles = 77 sts)
Ch 1 (does not count as stitch). 1 dc in each st across. Turn. (77 sts each row)

Ch 1 (does not count as stitch). 1 dc in first st. *Bobble in next st, 1 dc in each of next 3 sts*; repeat from * to * to last 4 sts. Bobble in next st, 1 dc in each of last 3 sts. Turn. (57 dc, 20 bobbles = 77 sts)

title: Boho fringed wrap
subtitle: A chunky treble rectangle with a long knotted fringe along both short ends
excerpt: This wrap is a rectangle of treble crochet in chunky-weight yarn on a 6 mm hook, finished with a long knotted fringe along both short ends. The body is entirely plain treble. The fringe is cut, folded through the edge stitches, and knotted at two levels to create a layered macrame-style fringe. Finished size is approximately 180 cm wide by 65 cm deep.

content.text: This wrap is a straightforward rectangle of treble crochet in chunky yarn on a 6 mm hook. The interest comes from the finishing: a long
runs along both short ends, knotted twice to create a layered macrame-style cascade. At 180 cm wide by 65 cm deep the wrap covers the shoulders fully and has enough body to drape without slipping.

The crochet body takes less time than the fringe does; plan for the fringe to take as long again as the body. Each fringe bundle uses six strands of yarn cut to 40 cm (they fold to 20 cm plus knot), and there are approximately 80 bundles across both ends combined.

attrs.body: Approximately 600 g chunky-weight yarn (body) plus an extra 150 g for fringe. A 6 mm crochet hook (US J/10). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Tape measure. A crochet hook or latch hook for pulling fringe loops through edge stitches.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 12 tr x 7 rows = 10 x 10 cm in chunky-weight yarn with a 6 mm hook, measured unstretched. Work a 15 x 15 cm swatch and adjust hook size if needed. Each extra stitch per 10 cm shifts the finished width by about 15 cm.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
treble (tr): UK; the same move as US "double crochet" (dc).
The wrap is worked flat from one short end to the other. The foundation chain is the 65 cm depth; the rows build the 180 cm width.
Ch 79. (This gives 78 working stitches across the 65 cm depth.)
Ch 3 (counts as first tr throughout). 1 tr in each ch across. Turn. (78 sts)
Ch 3 (counts as first tr). 1 tr in each st across to end. Turn. (78 sts each row)
Continue until the piece measures 180 cm from the foundation chain edge, approximately 126 rows at 7 rows per 10 cm. Fasten off.
Fasten off and weave in the two body ends. The fringe is added after.

Cut lengths of yarn 40 cm long. You need 6 strands per bundle, and approximately 40 bundles along each short end (80 total). Wind the yarn around a 20 cm piece of card and cut along one edge to produce consistent lengths.

Hold 6 strands together, fold in half to make a loop of 12 strands doubled. Insert the hook from back to front through the first edge stitch of one short end. Pull the folded loop through. Pass the loose ends through the loop and pull firmly to make a lark's head knot. Repeat in every other stitch (every 2 sts) across the short end. Repeat on the other short end.
Working 4 cm below the lark's head knots, gather all 12 strands of each bundle and tie a firm overhand knot. This is the first knot row.

Working 4 cm below the first knot row, split each bundle in half (6 strands each half). Take the right half of one bundle and the left half of the adjacent bundle, combine them, and tie an overhand knot 4 cm below the first knot row. Repeat across all bundles. Leave the outermost half-bundles at each selvedge end un-knotted in this row, or knot them to themselves.
Once both knot rows are complete on both ends, trim the fringe ends to a straight line with sharp scissors, leaving at least 3 cm of tail below the second knot.
Handwash gently in cool water. Do not tumble-dry or wring. Lay flat to dry and comb the fringe smooth while damp. Fringe can tangle in a washing machine; handwash only.

Add a third knot row for a deeper macrame fringe. Work the fringe in a contrast colour for a two-tone effect. A simple chevron pattern in the body (adding and subtracting stitches at regular intervals) works equally well at chunky weight and gives the wrap more visual interest before the fringe is attached.

title: Bridal lace shawl
subtitle: A fan-lace rectangle in lace-weight yarn, with five-treble fans separated by picot chains, after Weldon's Practical Crochet
excerpt: This rectangular shawl measures 175 cm wide by 55 cm deep and is worked in lace-weight white or ivory yarn on a 2.75 mm hook. The pattern is a fan-lace repeat: five-treble fans separated by chain-space columns, with a three-chain picot at the centre of each fan. Adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet. Requires accurate lace counting and consistent fine-yarn tension.
sourceNotes: Adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 7 (1892), bridal and fine lace shawl chapter (Internet Archive, archive.org). Fan lace construction confirmed against Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886).

content.text: This rectangle is worked from one short end to the other in a
repeat of five trebles into a chain space, with a

at the centre of each fan. The fabric is very open and relies entirely on blocking to lie flat and show its full width. Work in good light and count each fan carefully: the pattern repeat is 8 chains (plus 2 edge chains), so the foundation chain must be a multiple of 8 plus 4.

This is an advanced pattern due to the fine yarn, the small hook size, and the need to maintain consistent tension across a very wide foundation chain of over 400 stitches. Work a swatch of at least 40 chains and block it before starting the full piece to check both the fan gauge and how the lace opens after blocking.

attrs.body: Approximately 200 g lace-weight yarn in white or ivory. A 2.75 mm crochet hook (US C/2). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Blocking mat. Rust-proof pins. Tape measure. A good light source is essential when working fine yarn.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: One fan repeat (5 tr + 2 chain columns each side) = approximately 2.5 cm wide; 8 fan rows = 10 cm deep, measured after blocking. Block the swatch fully before measuring: unblocked lace-weight fabric measures considerably narrower than its blocked state. The shawl requires approximately 70 fan repeats across the width.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
double crochet (dc): UK; the same move as US "single crochet" (sc).
treble (tr): UK; the same move as US "double crochet" (dc).
fan: 5 tr into the same chain space.
picot chain: ch 3, sl st into base of chain.

The rectangle is worked flat in rows from one short end. The fan repeat is 8 chains wide. The foundation chain of 564 chains gives 70 fan repeats plus edge stitches, which at 2.5 cm per repeat equals 175 cm blocked width.
Ch 564. (70 x 8 = 560 working chains, plus 4 for the edge and turning chain.) Take care not to twist the chain. Place a stitch marker every 80 chains to help count.
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in the first ch. *Ch 3. Skip 3 ch. 1 dc in next ch. Ch 3. Skip 3 ch. 1 dc in next ch*; repeat from * to * across. Turn. (141 dc, 140 ch-3 spaces)

Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in first dc. *Ch 2. 5 tr in next ch-3 space (fan). After the 2nd tr of the fan, ch 3 and sl st back into the 2nd tr (picot at centre top of fan). Complete the remaining 3 tr of the fan. Ch 2. 1 dc in next dc. Ch 2. 1 dc in next dc*; repeat from * to * across. Turn. (70 fans, 70 picots)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in first dc. *Ch 3. 1 dc in the ch-2 space between the fan and the next dc. Ch 3. 1 dc in next dc*; repeat from * to * across. Turn. (141 dc, 140 ch-3 spaces)
Alternate Row 2 (fan row) and Row 3 (arch row). After approximately 44 rows (22 fan rows) the piece measures approximately 55 cm deep. End on an arch row. Fasten off.

Fasten off and weave in all ends with care: lace-weight ends are very fine and must pass through at least four stitches in two directions to stay secure. Wet-block thoroughly: soak in cool water for at least 20 minutes to allow full saturation, then press out excess moisture in a towel without wringing. Pin out to 175 x 55 cm on a blocking mat, placing pins at each picot point along the lower edge for a defined scallop line. Leave until fully dry.
Handwash in cool water with a gentle wool or silk wash (according to the yarn fibre). Handle very gently when wet. Lay flat to dry. Re-pin after washing to restore the full blocked dimensions.

The same fan-lace structure works as a triangular shawl: start with a short foundation chain and increase by one fan repeat at each edge on every fan row. A wider fan of 7 tr instead of 5 gives a more pronounced scallop along the lower edge. In fingering weight on a 3.25 mm hook the same pattern produces a warmer shawl with a more visible lace structure.

title: Bruges lace tile
subtitle: A small square assembled from interlaced crochet ribbon strips in the Bruges lace tradition
excerpt: Bruges crochet works narrow ribbon strips, three stitches wide, in long lengths, then bends, folds, and joins them to form geometric tiles. This small square assembles four ribbon strips into a 10 cm tile with an interlaced centre where the strips cross. The construction looks complex but each strip is entirely straightforward to crochet.
sourceNotes: Bruges lacework originates in Belgium and was adapted into crochet in the late 19th century. Documented in Weldon's Practical Needlework, Volume 6 (1891), Bruges crochet chapter.

content.text: Bruges lace works narrow Bruges ribbons as the structural components. Then bends and joins them to form geometric shapes. The tile here assembles four ribbon strips in a simple interlace pattern: two horizontal and two vertical. With each pair passing over and under the other at the four crossing points in the centre.

The four strips are identical. Work them all to the same length first, then join. The interlace requires physically weaving one strip over the other before joining with slip stitches at the crossing points. This is the one step that requires three-dimensional thinking.

content.text: Ch 5. Htr in 3rd ch from hook, htr in each ch to end. *Ch 3, turn. Htr in 2nd ch, htr in 3rd ch, sl st into next htr. Htr across.* Rep from * until strip is 12 cm long. Fasten off.

Lay two strips horizontally and two vertically. Weave the vertical strips over and under the horizontal strips at the four crossing points. Pin to blocking mat to hold in position. Sl st at each crossing point and at each corner where strips meet. Block flat with all edges pinned straight.
Work the tunisian crochet square for a different advanced technique. Tunisian produces a flat mesh without the strip-assembly complexity of Bruges lace.

title: Bullion round
subtitle: A circular motif built from bullion stitches radiating from the magic ring
excerpt: Bullion stitches, long coiled cylinders made by wrapping the yarn many times before drawing through, stand proud of the fabric surface and radiate outward from the ring like spokes. A border of dc closes the outer edge. The result is a heavily textured circular motif that works best in smooth, high-twist cotton where the coils stay distinct.
sourceNotes: Bullion stitch in crochet is documented in Weldon's Practical Needlework, Volume 6 (1891), and in American thread crochet booklets from the same period.

content.text: The bullion stitch is the most demanding stitch in this motif collection: it requires drawing a loop through 10 wrapped yarn-overs simultaneously without dropping any. Use a smooth. Slightly inelastic cotton. The wraps stay organised on a polished hook surface and a slippery yarn makes pulling through easier.

Work the bullions into every other dc in round 2. Placing a single dc between each bullion as a spacer. The dc spacers keep the bullions from crowding and let each coil stand upright rather than leaning against its neighbour.

title: Corner-to-corner triangle shawl
subtitle: A diagonal-build two-colour triangle in DK on a 4 mm hook, using the C2C dc-in-corner-space method
excerpt: Corner-to-corner crochet builds a triangle by adding one block-square per row on the increase side, then decreasing one block per row on the other. Each block is a small square of three trebles worked into a chain-2 corner space. This shawl grows from a single corner block to a long side of 130 cm, then decreases back to a single block. Two DK colours work in stripes to emphasise the diagonal geometry.
sourceNotes: Corner-to-corner crochet construction synthesised from established fibre arts techniques. The C2C method with ch-2 corner spaces and 3-treble blocks is a widely documented technique with no single original source.

content.text: Corner-to-corner crochet builds from one corner of a triangle outward. Every row on the increase half adds one new C2C block at the diagonal edge. Each block is anchored to the corner space of the block in the row below. Once the triangle reaches its widest point. The decrease half removes one block at the start of each row until one block remains. The shawl uses two DK colours alternated in two-row stripes to show the diagonal geometry. You carry the unused colour up the edge on alternate rows.

The finished long sides measure 130 cm each at gauge, with each block 2.5 cm square. The hypotenuse at the widest point spans 52 blocks diagonally. Tension matters: a block that runs larger than 2.5 cm will produce a longer shawl. One that runs smaller will produce a shorter one. Measure after the first 10 blocks on your increase triangle.

attrs.body: Colour A: about 200 g DK-weight yarn. Colour B: about 200 g DK-weight yarn. A 4 mm hook. Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Stitch markers. Blocking mat and pins. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: Each C2C block measures 2.5 x 2.5 cm with DK yarn on a 4 mm hook. Work the first 4 rows of the triangle and measure: 4 blocks should span 10 cm both horizontally and vertically. If your blocks run larger, drop a hook size; if smaller, go up a hook size.
ch: chain -- UK and US shared.
sl st: slip stitch -- UK and US shared.
tr: treble -- the same move as US "double crochet". Yarn over twice, insert hook, draw up loop, three times.
dc: double crochet -- used at the join point between blocks on decrease rows.

The triangle works in two halves: an increase half where each row gains one block at the right diagonal edge. And a decrease half where each row loses one block at the same edge. Colour changes happen at the start of every right-side row: row 1 colour A. Row 3 colour B, row 5 colour A. And so on in two-row stripes.
Using colour A, ch 6. 3 tr in 4th ch from hook. Turn.
Ch 6. 3 tr in 4th ch from hook. Ch 3. Sl st in corner space of previous block. Ch 3. 3 tr in same corner space. Turn.

Change to colour B at the start of row 3. On every increase row: ch 6. 3 tr in 4th ch from hook to add the new edge block. Then work across the existing blocks by sl st into the top of the previous row's edge block. Ch 3, 3 tr in each corner space along the row. End with 3 tr in the last corner space of the previous row. Change colour every 2 rows throughout. At the end of row 52 you have 52 blocks across the diagonal.
Turn the work. Sl st across the top 3 tr of the first block and into the corner space. Ch 3. 3 tr in same corner space. Continue working a block in each remaining corner space across. Turn.

Continue repeating the decrease row method: sl st across the first block into the corner space at the start of each row. Then work one block in every remaining corner space across. Maintain the two-row colour stripe throughout. The block count reduces by one per row. At the end of row 103 you have 1 block. Fasten off.

Weave in all ends securely on the wrong side. Wet-block by soaking the finished triangle in cool water for 10 minutes. Gently pressing water out in a clean towel. Then pinning the two long sides and the hypotenuse to the stated dimensions on a blocking mat. Pin each corner first, then pin the edges at 10 cm intervals.
Handwash in cool water with mild soap. Do not tumble-dry. Lay flat on a clean towel and ease to shape while damp.

Once you are confident with the C2C block rhythm. A C2C rectangle blanket uses the same method but turns the increase at a specific row count instead of working a full triangle. Three or more colours in single-row stripes produce a more intricate striped effect. Working the same block construction in aran weight on a 5 mm hook produces a coarser, heavier throw.

title: Catherine wheel motif
subtitle: A classic spoke-and-fan geometric tile in DK cotton, 12 cm
excerpt: The Catherine wheel motif uses an eight-point star construction built from treble-cluster spokes alternating with fan shells, giving the tile its distinctive wheel-spoke appearance. Worked in two colours, the spokes and fans read as separate bands; in a single colour the geometry is subtler. Tiles at 12 cm into a striking radial-pattern throw.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 4 (1889), Catherine wheel stitch and motif chapter (Internet Archive). The Catherine wheel construction appears in several Edwardian pattern books as a named stitch for blankets and shawls.

in round 2. The alternation of upward-pointing cluster and outward-fanning shell creates the wheel appearance that gives the stitch its name. Two-colour working, cluster in one colour, shell in another, gives the sharpest read of the spoke structure.

The Catherine wheel appears in Weldon's Practical Crochet as both a repeat stitch for flat work and as a stand-alone circular motif. As a motif it tiles in a grid with small square spacers between, or joins edge to edge by whipstitching through matching border dc stitches.

title: Chunky Rectangle Wrap
subtitle: Super-chunky treble stitch rectangle worked in four rows on a 10mm hook
excerpt: A bold rectangle wrap worked entirely in treble crochet using super-chunky yarn on a 10mm hook. The whole piece is four rows deep, making this an accessible first project for anyone learning treble crochet.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. Plain treble rectangle construction is a foundational technique with no single source.

content.text: This rectangle wrap measures about 165cm wide by 45cm deep and is worked entirely in treble crochet using super-chunky yarn on a 10mm hook. The finished piece is just four rows of stitches, plus the foundation chain. That means the width comes from a long foundation chain and the depth is built quickly in only a handful of rows. Treble crochet is a tall, open stitch that produces fabric with a slight drape. The ch-3 turning chain at the start of each row counts as the first treble. So you skip the first stitch at the base of the chain and work the last treble into the top of the turning chain from the row below.
Yarn: about 300g of super-chunky weight yarn. Hook: 10mm. You will also need a tapestry needle and scissors. A tape measure is useful for checking your foundation chain length.

7 trebles and 4 rows to 10cm over treble stitch on a 10mm hook. This gauge gives the stated 165cm x 45cm finished size. Super-chunky yarns vary considerably in thickness between brands: check your gauge swatch before working the full foundation chain.
At the stated gauge, 165cm requires about 117 trebles. The foundation chain is 120 chains. Work a short swatch and count your trebles per 10cm before chaining the full length.
Ch 120. Lay the chain flat and measure: it should reach about 165cm. Adjust the chain count by roughly 7 chains per 10cm if your tension differs.
Ch 3, tr in 4th ch from hook, tr in each remaining ch to end, turn.
Ch 3, skip first st, tr in each st across to turning chain, tr in top of turning ch, turn.
After Row 4, fasten off and leave a 15cm tail. The wrap now measures about 165cm wide by 45cm deep.

Weave in all ends with the tapestry needle, working through several stitches on the wrong side. Weave in the tail at the foundation chain in the same way. Trim the ends close to the fabric. The wrap needs no other finishing: the treble stitch produces a neat, stable edge on all four sides.

Follow the care label on your yarn. Super-chunky acrylics are typically machine washable on a cool, gentle cycle. Super-chunky wools require hand washing and drying flat. Do not tumble dry wool or acrylic-blend yarns at high heat.
