title: Chunky throw shawl
subtitle: A top-down triangle in super-chunky treble stitch, worked in a single colour on a 10 mm hook
excerpt: This top-down triangular shawl grows from a four-chain foundation to 140 cm wide and 65 cm deep in super-chunky yarn on a 10 mm hook. Each row adds two trebles, one on each side of the central spine. The resulting fabric is thick and cosy. Suitable for crocheters who know the treble stitch.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. Top-down triangular shawl construction from a central spine is a widely documented technique with no single source.

content.text: This triangular shawl starts at the top centre and grows downward on a 10 mm hook in super-chunky yarn. The construction is straightforward: each row begins with a ch-3 turning chain, works trebles to the central spine stitch, places one treble on each side of the spine to create the increase, and continues to the end of the row. After roughly 33 rows the triangle reaches the finished dimensions.
sits at the exact centre of every row. Mark it with a stitch marker and move the marker up on each row so you can always find the centre without counting across. The
of ch-3 counts as the first treble on every row.

attrs.body: Approximately 500 g super-chunky weight yarn. A 10 mm crochet hook (US N/P 15). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Stitch marker. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 8 tr x 5 rows = 10 x 10 cm in super-chunky yarn with a 10 mm hook, measured unstretched. Work a swatch of 12 stitches and 7 rows and measure the central 10 x 10 cm. At this scale, one stitch per 10 cm changes the finished width by about 18 cm, so it is worth checking before beginning.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
treble (tr): UK; the same move as US "double crochet" (dc).
The shawl is worked flat. The ch-3 turning chain counts as the first treble on every row. Place a stitch marker in the centre spine stitch and move it up on every row.
Ch 4. Place a stitch marker in the 2nd ch from the hook. This is the centre spine chain.
Ch 3 (counts as first tr). 1 tr in the 4th ch from hook. 2 tr in the marked spine ch. 1 tr in the last ch. Turn. (5 sts)

Ch 3 (counts as first tr). 1 tr in each st to 1 st before the spine st. 2 tr in the st before the spine. 1 tr in the marked spine st (move marker to this st). 2 tr in the st after the spine. 1 tr in each st to end, working the final tr into the top of the turning ch. Turn. (7 sts)

Repeat Row 2 on every row. Two stitches are added on each row (one on each side of the spine). After Row 33 you have 69 sts, the shawl is approximately 140 cm wide and 65 cm deep. Move the marker up each row to keep track of the spine.

attrs.body: Each additional row adds approximately 2.5 cm to the width (1 tr each side at the stated gauge). Work more rows for a larger shawl or fewer for a smaller one.
attrs.title: Adjusting the size

content.text: After the final row, do not turn. Work 1 dc (UK) along the top straight edge to neaten: join with sl st at the top left corner, work 1 dc in each stitch along the foundation chain edge, sl st to the starting corner. Fasten off.

Fasten off and weave in all ends. Thread each tail through the tapestry needle and pass it through the backs of several stitches. Super-chunky yarn does not need aggressive blocking. Lay the shawl flat, ease gently to the stated dimensions, cover with a damp cloth, and allow to dry.
Handwash in cool water with a gentle wool wash. Press out excess water gently and lay flat to dry. Do not tumble-dry or hang while wet, as the weight of chunky yarn will distort the shape.

Work the same top-down triangle construction in DK on a 4 mm hook for a finer, lighter shawl with more rows. Add a simple shell-stitch border along both diagonal edges after the last row. A striped version using two contrasting super-chunky colours changes shade every four rows for a bold block effect.

title: Circular base motif
subtitle: A solid flat circle used as a base for bags, hats, and amigurumi, worked in dc increases
excerpt: The circular base motif is the foundational flat-circle construction that underlies bags, bowls, berets, and amigurumi. It works 6 increases per round distributed evenly, giving a flat circle without any spiral distortion. The same increase formula works in any yarn weight, the number of stitches and the hook change; the geometry stays the same.
sourceNotes: Flat-circle construction by even increases is described in Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 1 (1885), circular foundation chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), circular crochet section.

content.text: The circular base motif applies the flat circle formula. 6 increases per round. Position shifted by 1 stitch each round. To produce a smooth circle without spiral ridges or visible increase lines. Six rounds give a 12 cm circle; nine rounds give 18 cm.
This pattern is the foundation for bags, berets, amigurumi bodies, and flat trivets. The same formula works in any weight yarn with any hook, only the finished size changes.

attrs.body: About 10 g of DK-weight cotton for a 12 cm circle. A 4 mm hook. Tapestry needle and scissors.
attrs.title: Materials for one motif

content.text: Magic ring. 6 dc into ring. Sl st to join. Pull ring closed.
2 dc into every dc around. Sl st to join.
*2 dc into next dc. 1 dc into next dc.* Rep from * around. Sl st to join.
Rnd 4: *2dc, 1dc, 1dc* × 6. Rnd 5: *2dc, 1dc, 1dc, 1dc* × 6. Rnd 6: *2dc, 1dc, 1dc, 1dc, 1dc* × 6. Sl st and fasten off.
To continue into a bag or bowl, work 1 dc into every dc around from round 7 onward. The sides grow straight upward from the flat base.
For a decorative circular motif. Use this base and continue with the five-petal flower round or the vintage fan round to add pattern on top of the solid circle.

excerpt: This rectangular wrap measures 180 cm wide by 55 cm deep in aran weight yarn. title: Compass rose round
subtitle: An eight-section circular motif with alternating long and short points in two colours
excerpt: Eight sections alternate between four long treble-spike cardinal points and four shorter htr intercardinal points, giving the compass rose its distinctive asymmetric star outline. Worked in two colours, one per point type, the motif reads clearly from across a room.
sourceNotes: Compass rose and directional motifs appear in Victorian needlework collections from the 1880s. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 4 (1889).

content.text: The compass rose alternates four tall

in colour A with four shorter intercardinal points in colour B. The cardinal points use stitch stepping up to a chain-2 tip; the intercardinal points reach only to htr height. This difference in length gives the compass rose its distinctive uneven star outline.

The finished motif requires blocking with all 8 points pinned open. Navy and cream is the classic colourway; any high-contrast pair works. Avoid similar tones, the motif reads by colour contrast as much as by stitch height.

attrs.body: About 7 g colour A and 5 g colour B in DK-weight cotton. A 4 mm hook. Blocking mat and 8 pins.
attrs.title: Materials for one motif

content.text: Round 1: magic ring, 16 dc into ring, sl st join. (Sets 16 base positions, 2 per point section.)

The compass rose alternates four tall

in colour A with four shorter intercardinal points in colour B. The cardinal points use stitch stepping up to a chain-2 tip; the intercardinal points reach only to htr height. This difference in length gives the compass rose its distinctive uneven star outline.

The finished motif requires blocking with all 8 points pinned open. Navy and cream is the classic colourway; any high-contrast pair works. Avoid similar tones — the motif reads by colour contrast as much as by stitch height.

title: Corner-to-corner diamond motif
subtitle: A two-colour diamond worked diagonally using the corner-to-corner technique
excerpt: The corner-to-corner technique builds a diamond by increasing on both diagonal axes, placing one colour in the centre and another in the four outer quadrants. No colour changes mid-row, each dc-block tile is fully one colour, making the technique straightforward once the diagonal increase and decrease logic is clear.
sourceNotes: Corner-to-corner construction appears in American craft manuals from the 1880s and is documented in British needlework publications from the same period. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 4 (1889).

content.text: Corner-to-corner crochet works from one corner of a square to the opposite corner, building a grid of

. Each diagonal row increases by one tile until the midpoint, then decreases symmetrically. The diamond pattern places the contrast colour in the centre tiles of the grid, with the background colour filling the outer tiles.

Each tile is complete in one colour before moving to the next, so colour changes are clean. Use a grid chart, the pattern below gives a 13-diagonal-row square with the diamond spanning the middle 7 rows. Adjust the diamond placement by shifting the contrast colour start row.

attrs.body: About 10 g colour A and 6 g colour B in DK-weight cotton. A 4 mm hook. A printed grid chart helps track tile placement.
attrs.title: Materials for one motif

content.text: Row 1: ch 6 in colour A. 3 dc into 4th ch from hook. (1 tile.) Row 2: ch 6, turn. 3 dc into ch-3 sp of row 1 tile. Ch 3, 3 dc into same sp. (2 tiles.) Continue adding 1 tile per row until row 7 (7 tiles per row). From row 4, change the centre tiles to colour B for the diamond.
Row 8: sl st across first tile to the second ch-3 sp. Begin working tiles from the second sp. (6 tiles.) Continue reducing by 1 tile per row through row 13 (1 tile). Fasten off.

title: Crescent shawl in treble
subtitle: A curved crescent shape worked in rows of treble with short-row shaping at each edge
excerpt: A crescent shawl sits close to the neck and drapes across the shoulders in a gentle curve. This version is worked in treble on a 4 mm hook with DK yarn, using simple edge increases to build the crescent shape over roughly 40 rows. Finished width is about 160 cm along the curved lower edge; depth is about 35 cm at the centre point.
sourceNotes: Crescent shaping technique synthesised from Weldon's Practical Crochet Volume 3 (1887), which describes increasing at the selvedge of rectangular shawls to create curved lower edges (Internet Archive). General treble-stitch construction from de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886).

content.text: A crescent shawl hugs the neck and fans across both shoulders in a curved arc. This pattern works in rows of treble (UK tr, the same move US patterns call double crochet) on a 4 mm hook, with increases at both ends of every row plus three increase points across the centre of alternate rows. The result of this
is a curved lower edge about 160 cm wide.

attrs.body: Approximately 350 g DK-weight yarn, merino or merino-blend is warm and holds the block well. A 4 mm hook (US G/6). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Stitch markers (3). Blocking mat and pins. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 18 tr × 10 rows = 10 × 10 cm in DK yarn with a 4 mm hook, measured unstretched. Swatch before beginning and adjust hook size if needed: one stitch per 10 cm off changes the finished width by about 9 cm at the final row count.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
treble (tr): UK; the same move as US "double crochet" (dc).

The shawl is worked flat, turning at the end of each row. On increase rows (rows 2, 4, 6 etc.) three internal increase points sit at roughly one-quarter, one-half, and three-quarters of the row width. Mark these with stitch markers and move them up on each row.
Ch 41. (This is the starting top edge, measuring approximately 22 cm.)
Ch 3 (counts as first tr). 1 tr in each ch across. Turn. (40 tr)

Ch 3 (counts as first tr). 2 tr in the first st (edge increase). 1 tr in each of next 8 sts. Place marker. 2 tr in the next st (centre-left increase). 1 tr in each of next 18 sts. Place marker. 2 tr in the next st (centre increase). 1 tr in each of next 8 sts. Place marker. 2 tr in the next st (centre-right increase). 1 tr in the last st. 2 tr in the last st (edge increase). Turn. (46 tr)
Ch 3 (counts as first tr). 1 tr in each st across. Turn. (46 tr)

Continue alternating increase rows (row 2 pattern, working the increases at the same marked positions plus at both ends) and plain rows (row 3 pattern). On each increase row, work 2 tr at the beginning, 2 tr at each of the three internal markers (moving markers after each increase row), and 2 tr at the end. By row 40 you have approximately 160 sts.

attrs.body: The three internal increase points must stay evenly spaced as the row count grows. On every increase row, the middle marker should sit at the centre of the row count; if it drifts more than 2 stitches from centre, move it back before working the increase.
attrs.title: Keeping the crescent curve

content.text: Fasten off and weave in all ends. Wet-block by soaking in cool water for 10 minutes, pressing water out gently, then pinning to shape on a blocking mat. Pin the two top corners first to hold the straight upper edge, then pin the curved lower edge at 10 cm intervals, easing the crescent shape gently.
Handwash in cool water with mild wool wash. Lay flat to dry. Do not tumble-dry or hang. Wet treble fabric will stretch under its own weight.

Work the same crescent construction in a shell stitch pattern on every row instead of plain treble for a lighter, more open fabric. A lace-weight single crochet version on a 2.5 mm hook makes a finer shawlette suitable for summer wear.

title: Crossed treble square
subtitle: A square motif with a woven X-pattern built from crossed treble pairs
excerpt: Crossed trebles work the second stitch of each pair in front of the first, locking the yarn into an X on the surface. Working these pairs in sequence across each round of a square gives a woven-looking fabric with diagonal lines running in both directions across the motif.
sourceNotes: Crossed treble construction documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 3 (1888), crossed-stitch chapter (Internet Archive).

content.text: pairs along the sides of each round, replacing the plain trebles or cluster groups of the standard granny structure. The crossing stitches pull toward each other slightly, giving a compact, dense side panel with a visible diagonal.

Work a plain 3-treble corner cluster at each corner as usual. Between corners, work crossed treble pairs: skip 1, tr in next, tr back into skipped st passing in front. Side stitches must be worked in pairs, so the stitch count per side must be even.

title: Daisy motif, basic
subtitle: Eight double-crochet petals around a tight chain-ring centre, 9 cm
excerpt: Eight simple petals worked on chain loops from a centre ring give this 9 cm daisy its clean, flat shape. The petals are rows of double crochet worked back and forth on individual chain foundations, so the motif needs no specialist stitches and lies flat without blocking. It joins into wreaths, garlands, and grid throws.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 2 (1886), flower motif section (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet daisy chapter.

content.text: The basic daisy works eight flat petals outward from a chain ring centre. Each petal is a separate back-and-forth rectangle of double crochet on a 10-chain foundation. Attached at the base to the ring. No specialist stitches are needed, this is double crochet and chain only, and it lies flat without blocking. Two colours give the clearest daisy read.

The petals can be worked all in one go around the ring. Attaching each to the next with a single slip stitch at the centre ring before beginning the chain foundation of the next petal. Keep the chain foundation even. Pulling the chain tighter on the first petal and looser on the eighth produces petals of different widths. Which throws the symmetry.

attrs.body: About 5 g of DK-weight cotton in white or cream. Plus a small amount of a contrast colour for the centre ring. A 4 mm crochet hook. Tapestry needle. Scissors.
attrs.title: Materials for one motif

content.text: Each finished basic daisy measures 9 cm across in DK-weight cotton with a 4 mm hook. No blocking required; the petals lie flat naturally.
slip stitch, UK and US shared.
In contrast colour: Ch 6. Sl st to first ch to form a ring. Ch 1. Work 12dc into the ring. Sl st to first dc to join. Do not fasten off; drop contrast colour and join petal colour.
Work 8 petals as follows. Spacing them evenly around the centre ring by anchoring each at the next dc of the ring:.
Ch 10. Turn. Sk first ch, dc across next 8 ch. Turn. Ch 1. Dc across all 8 sts. Turn. Ch 1. Dc across all 8 sts. Sl st back to the next dc of the centre ring to anchor this petal and start the next.
Repeat this petal sequence 7 more times, anchoring each to the next dc of the centre ring. After the 8th petal, sl st to the dc of the ring adjacent to where you started. Fasten off.

definition.title: Daisy motif, basic
definition.caption: Centre ring with eight petal foundations. Each petal is three rows of 8dc worked back and forth on a 10-chain foundation, anchored to the ring at base.

content.text: Fasten off petal colour. Pick up the dropped contrast colour and weave it in through the back of the ring stitches. Trim all tails to 1 cm. The motif lies flat without pinning; a light steam-press can neaten any uneven edges.

For a garland, join daisies through a corner stitch of adjacent petals with a length of chain. For a flat throw, whipstitch through the outermost row of each petal edge to neighbour. The layered daisy adds a second ring of petals between the first eight.
Handwash in cool water with mild soap, or machine-wash on a wool cycle. Lay flat on a clean towel and ease to shape while damp.

The layered daisy adds a second ring of petals in a shorter length. Creating a double-layer flower with more depth. The bobble-centre daisy replaces the flat chain ring with a cluster of bobble stitches for a raised three-dimensional centre.
The basic daisy works eight flat petals outward from a

centre. Each petal is a separate back-and-forth rectangle of double crochet on a 10-chain foundation, attached at the base to the ring. No specialist stitches are needed — this is double crochet and chain only, and it lies flat without blocking. Two colours (centre ring in a contrast colour, petals in white or cream) give the clearest daisy read.

The petals can be worked all in one go around the ring, attaching each to the next with a single slip stitch at the centre ring before beginning the chain foundation of the next petal. Keep the chain foundation even — pulling the chain tighter on the first petal and looser on the eighth produces petals of different widths, which throws the symmetry.

title: Daisy motif, bobble centre

sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 4 (1889), raised-centre flower motif chapter (Internet Archive). Beeton's Book of Needlework (1870), flower crochet patterns.

content.text: The bobble-centre daisy builds five bobble stitches into a tight magic ring. Then anchors eight flat petal rectangles around the outside of the ring. The bobbles push to the right side of the work and stand 1 to 2 cm proud of the petal surface. The centre can be worked in a contrasting colour. Yellow or orange against cream petals gives the classic daisy read.

A bobble in this context is five trebles worked into the same magic ring. Each left with its final two loops on the hook. Until the last yarn-over pulls through all six loops together. The more hooks held, the higher the bobble. A four-treble bobble gives a smaller centre; a six-treble gives a higher one.

title: Daisy motif, layered petals
subtitle: Two rings of petals in contrasting lengths give depth and a fuller flower, 11 cm
excerpt: A second inner ring of shorter petals sits between and behind the eight outer petals, giving the flower depth without any three-dimensional techniques. The inner petals peek out between the outer ones, producing a layered effect visible from the front. At 11 cm it works as an applique flower on cushion covers, bags, and garment panels.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 3 (1888), layered flower motif chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), flower crochet section.

content.text: The layered daisy works an inner ring of eight shorter petals before the outer ring. So they sit behind and between the outer petals. The inner petals use a 6-chain foundation and two dc rows. The outer petals use a 10-chain foundation and three dc rows. The centre chain ring has 16 dc to give both petal rings enough anchor points without crowding.

Work the inner petals first, in the contrast colour. So they are covered from the front by the outer petals when both are flat. If you work the outer ring first and try to add the inner ring behind. The inner petals tend to push forward.

title: Double treble lace wrap
subtitle: Vertical columns of double treble with ch-1 gaps for a high-drape lace rectangle in lace weight on a 3 mm hook
excerpt: Double treble (UK dtr) produces a tall, open stitch that sets naturally into vertical columns with chain-1 gaps between. Worked in lace-weight yarn on a 3 mm hook, the fabric is light, drapey, and translucent. This rectangle wrap measures 190 cm wide by 55 cm deep and is worked from one short end to the other in a simple column repeat adapted from Therese de Dillmont's Encyclopedia of Needlework.
sourceNotes: Double treble column lace construction adapted from Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), chapter on crochet lace stitches describing tall-stitch open column patterns. Internet Archive: archive.org/details/encyclopaediaofn00dill.

content.text: This lace wrap uses a simple two-row repeat of
columns separated by single chain spaces. The stitch structure comes from a Victorian needlework encyclopaedia. A

fabric in lace weight is light on the hook. The stitch count per row stays the same throughout. The two skills to manage are consistent tension on the dtr post and accurate placement into each ch-1 space below.

Lace weight yarn on a 3 mm hook requires careful tension management. The ch-4 turning chain that substitutes for the first dtr must match the height of the dtr columns; if your chain is consistently looser or tighter than your stitch posts, try adjusting to a 3.5 mm hook for the turning chains only. Blocking is not optional for lace weight: it sets the column lines and opens the ch-1 gaps to their full width.

attrs.body: Approximately 300 g lace-weight yarn (merino-silk or merino-cashmere blends give drape and strength; pure mohair is not recommended as it is difficult to rip back and re-work). A 3 mm hook (US D/3). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Blocking mat and rust-proof pins. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 1 dtr + 1 ch-1 space = 1.2 cm wide; 2 rows (1 dtr row + 1 return row) = 2 cm tall. Work a swatch of 10 column repeats across for 6 rows, block it fully by soaking, pinning, and drying, then measure the central area. At gauge, 10 repeats should span 12 cm. Lace gauge shifts significantly during blocking; always block the swatch before measuring.
ch: chain -- UK and US shared.
sl st: slip stitch -- UK and US shared.
dc: double crochet (UK) -- used at both edges of each row. The same move as US single crochet (sc).
tr: treble (UK) -- used in the foundation row to set column width. The same move as US double crochet (dc).
-- yarn over 3 times, insert hook, draw up loop, (yarn over, draw through 2 loops) 4 times. The same move as US triple crochet (trc).

The wrap is worked from one short end to the other. The long measurement (190 cm) is set by the foundation chain; the depth (55 cm) builds up over rows. The ch-4 turning chain at the start of each dtr row counts as the first dtr.
Ch 320. (This gives 159 dtr + 158 ch-1 spaces + 2 edge stitches = 319 working positions, plus 1 turning chain.)
Ch 4 (counts as first dtr). *Ch 1. Skip 1 ch. 1 dtr in next ch.* Repeat from * to * across to last ch. 1 dtr in last ch. Turn. (160 dtr including turning ch, 158 ch-1 spaces)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in first dtr. *Ch 1. 1 dc in next ch-1 space.* Repeat from * to * to last dtr. Ch 1. 1 dc in top of turning ch. Turn. (160 dc, 159 ch-1 spaces)
Ch 4 (counts as first dtr). *1 dtr in next ch-1 space. Ch 1.* Repeat from * to * to last dc. 1 dtr in last dc. Turn. (160 dtr including turning ch, 158 ch-1 spaces)

repeat. Continue repeating rows 2 and 3 until the work measures 55 cm from the foundation chain. At 2 cm per two-row repeat the depth reaches 55 cm after approximately 55 rows total (including the foundation row). End with a completed return row (row 2 pattern). Fasten off, leaving a 20 cm tail.

Weave in all ends using a fine tapestry needle, drawing the tail through the backs of several stitches and reversing direction to secure without a knot. Blocking is essential for lace weight: soak the finished wrap in cool water for 15 minutes, roll gently in a towel, then pin to the stated dimensions on a blocking mat. Pin the long edges first at 5 cm intervals, then pin the short ends. Leave until completely dry before unpinning.

Handwash in cool water with a gentle lace or delicate wash. Do not wring or tumble-dry. Roll in a clean towel, then block flat to restore shape. Store folded away from direct light; lace-weight fibres fade if left in strong sunlight.

Replacing the ch-1 gaps with ch-2 opens the column structure further and produces a more open mesh. Working the same column repeat in DK weight on a 4.5 mm hook gives a much faster, denser fabric that reads as textured stripes rather than lace. -- yarn over 3 times, insert hook, draw up loop, (yarn over, draw through 2 loops) 4 times. The same move as US triple crochet (trc).

The wrap is worked from one short end to the other. The long measurement (190 cm) is set by the foundation chain; the depth (55 cm) builds up over rows. The ch-4 turning chain at the start of each dtr row counts as the first dtr.
Ch 320. (This gives 159 dtr + 158 ch-1 spaces + 2 edge stitches = 319 working positions, plus 1 turning chain.)
Ch 4 (counts as first dtr). *Ch 1. Skip 1 ch. 1 dtr in next ch.* Repeat from * to * across to last ch. 1 dtr in last ch. Turn. (160 dtr including turning ch, 158 ch-1 spaces)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in first dtr. *Ch 1. 1 dc in next ch-1 space.* Repeat from * to * to last dtr. Ch 1. 1 dc in top of turning ch. Turn. (160 dc, 159 ch-1 spaces)
Ch 4 (counts as first dtr). *1 dtr in next ch-1 space. Ch 1.* Repeat from * to * to last dc. 1 dtr in last dc. Turn. (160 dtr including turning ch, 158 ch-1 spaces)

repeat. Continue repeating rows 2 and 3 until the work measures 55 cm from the foundation chain. At 2 cm per two-row repeat the depth reaches 55 cm after approximately 55 rows total (including the foundation row). End with a completed return row (row 2 pattern). Fasten off, leaving a 20 cm tail.

Weave in all ends using a fine tapestry needle, drawing the tail through the backs of several stitches and reversing direction to secure without a knot. Blocking is essential for lace weight: soak the finished wrap in cool water for 15 minutes, roll gently in a towel, then pin to the stated dimensions on a blocking mat. Pin the long edges first at 5 cm intervals, then pin the short ends. Leave until completely dry before unpinning.

Handwash in cool water with a gentle lace or delicate wash. Do not wring or tumble-dry. Roll in a clean towel, then block flat to restore shape. Store folded away from direct light; lace-weight fibres fade if left in strong sunlight.

Replacing the ch-1 gaps with ch-2 opens the column structure further and produces a more open mesh. Working the same column repeat in DK weight on a 4.5 mm hook gives a much faster, denser fabric that reads as textured stripes rather than lace. A ch-3 space between every third column pair produces a grouped-column variation found in Victorian needlework references of the same period.

title: Evening lace shawl
subtitle: A triangle in lace-weight yarn with a repeating five-treble fan separated by chain spaces
excerpt: This triangular shawl uses a fan-and-shell lace pattern worked from the top down in lace-weight yarn on a 2.5 mm hook. Each fan is five trebles fanned into a ch-2 space, separated by chain arches from the previous row. Finished size is approximately 145 cm wide by 65 cm deep. The pattern is adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet (1886).
sourceNotes: Fan-and-shell lace triangle adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 2 (1886), 'A Shawl in Crochet Lace', Internet Archive scan. Stitch proportions updated for lace-weight yarn; original used 3-ply wool.

content.text: This triangular shawl uses a fan-and-shell lace pattern adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet. The construction is top-down, starting from a short chain at the neck point. Each lace row builds five-treble fans into the chain arches of the row below, with chain spaces between each fan forming the arches for the next row. The work is advanced because the lace repeat must remain aligned across increasing row widths, and because lace-weight yarn on a small hook requires attention to tension throughout.
here is five trebles all worked into the same ch-2 space. The fans sit above
from the row below, and new arches form in the spaces between the fans on each row. The shawl finishes with a
along the two diagonal sides. Blocking is essential: unblocked lace-weight crochet reads as a crumpled mesh; pinned and dried to the full dimensions it opens into clean lace.

attrs.body: Approximately 350 g lace-weight yarn (approximately 800 m per 100 g). A 2.5 mm crochet hook (US B/1 or C/2). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Stitch markers (2). Blocking mat. Blocking pins (at least 60). Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: One fan repeat (5 tr + 2 ch-2 spaces) = approximately 3 cm wide; 6 fan rows = 5 cm deep in lace-weight yarn with a 2.5 mm hook, measured after light blocking. Gauge matters most for finished width: each fan repeat is 3 cm, and the final row has 48 fan repeats.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
double crochet (dc): UK; the same move as US "single crochet" (sc).
treble (tr): UK; the same move as US "double crochet" (dc).
fan stitch (5 tr into the same space).
picot (ch 3, sl st into base of chain).

The shawl grows top-down. Each lace row adds one fan repeat on each side of the central spine, increasing the width by two fans per row. The spine is marked on every row. Work the pattern rows until the desired depth, then work the picot border along both diagonal edges.
Ch 8. Sl st to first ch to form a small ring.
Ch 5 (counts as 1 tr + ch 2). [5 tr, ch 2, 5 tr] into ring (centre fan group). Ch 2, 1 tr into ring. Turn. (2 fans, 1 spine tr)

Ch 3 (does not count as stitch). 1 dc into the first ch-2 space. Ch 5, 1 dc into the ch-2 spine space. Ch 5, 1 dc into the last ch-2 space. Ch 3, sl st to base tr to close. Turn. (2 ch-5 arches, 2 ch-3 edge arches)

Ch 5 (counts as 1 tr + ch 2). 5 tr into first ch-3 edge arch. Ch 2, 5 tr into first ch-5 arch (fan A). Ch 2, [5 tr, ch 2, 5 tr] into spine arch (centre fan group, spine). Ch 2, 5 tr into second ch-5 arch (fan B). Ch 2, 5 tr into last ch-3 edge arch. Ch 2, 1 tr into sl st. Turn. (4 fans + 1 centre fan group = 6 fans)
Rows 4 to 48: continue fan and arch alternation

Continue alternating arch rows (even rows) and fan rows (odd rows). On each fan row, add one new fan on each side of the centre spine fan group by working a fan into each edge arch and each new ch-5 arch. On each arch row, work ch 5 between every adjacent fan's ch-2 spaces and ch 5 on each side of the spine ch-2 space. By row 48, the lower edge has 48 fans. The total stitch count in the final fan row is approximately 288 trebles within fans, plus chain spaces.

Join yarn at the top right corner. Work along the right diagonal edge as follows: *1 dc into the ch-2 space of the edge tr/fan, ch 3, sl st into the base of the ch-3 just made (picot formed), 1 dc into the next ch-2 space or arch*; repeat from * to * along the full right diagonal edge. At the bottom point, work [1 dc, ch 3, sl st, 1 dc] into the lowest spine space. Continue the picot repeat up the left diagonal edge to the top left corner. Fasten off.

Weave in all ends carefully through the backs of solid parts of the lace (not through chain spaces). Wet-block by soaking in cool water with a small amount of wool wash or fabric conditioner, gently squeezing to saturate without twisting. Press excess water out in a clean towel. Pin to 145 x 65 cm on a blocking mat: pin the two top corners first, then the bottom point, then the two diagonal edges at 5 cm intervals, easing each fan point outward. Leave until completely dry before unpinning.
Handwash in cool water with mild wool wash. Do not rub, wring, or tumble-dry. Press gently in a towel and lay flat to dry. Re-pin lightly if the lace loses shape after washing.

Work the same fan-and-arch structure in fingering-weight yarn on a 3 mm hook for a slightly more robust lace fabric with a similar drape. Add a second picot row for a more elaborate border. The same fan repeat works as a rectangular stole if you cast on for the full width and work straight rows without spine increases.

title: Filet crochet motif
subtitle: A lace grid motif worked from a chart of filled and open squares
excerpt: Filet crochet builds a grid of open chain squares with treble posts, filling selected squares with extra trebles to form a pattern from the contrast between filled and empty cells. Any image that reads as a pixel grid, letters, simple animals, geometric shapes, can be translated to a filet chart and crocheted.
sourceNotes: Filet crochet is one of the oldest documented crochet techniques; it appears extensively in Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886) and Weldon's Practical Crochet from Volume 1 (1885) onward.

content.text: Filet crochet builds patterns by alternating open and filled

in a regular grid. An open cell is two trebles with a chain-2 gap; a filled cell is four trebles with no gap. The chart reads like a pixel grid, shaded squares are filled cells, white squares are open. Any pattern that works as a pixel image translates directly to filet.

This motif uses a simple 9 × 9 heart chart. Block the finished piece firmly, wet-blocking opens the chain spaces and gives the grid its characteristic crisp lace appearance. Without blocking, the chain spaces collapse and the pattern is hard to read.

attrs.body: About 8 g of 4-ply cotton thread. A 2.5 mm hook. Blocking mat and pins.
attrs.title: Materials for one motif

content.text: Foundation chain: ch 29. (9 cells × 3 ch per cell + 2 turning ch.)
Row 1: tr in 4th ch from hook. *Ch 2, skip 2 ch, tr in next ch.* Rep across. Turn. (9 open cells.)

Row 2 onward: ch 5 (counts as tr + ch 2). *For open cell: tr in next tr, ch 2. For filled cell: tr in each of the 2 skipped ch, tr in next tr (4 tr total, no ch 2).* Work per heart chart rows 1 to 9. Fasten off.
Work the bruges lace tile for a different lace construction using strip-based rather than grid-based assembly.

Use a contrast colour for the centre to make the raised dc rounds stand out. Work the centre in yellow or orange for a classic daisy look. Match the petals to the project for applique integration.

title: Dahlia motif
subtitle: A multi-layer petal flower with three concentric rings, 13 cm
excerpt: The dahlia builds three concentric petal rings outward from a small treble-cluster centre, each ring with more petals than the last. The inner petals stand upright, the middle petals angle outward, and the outer petals lie flat, replicating the layered ball-dahlia profile. At 13 cm in DK cotton it is the largest flower motif in this set.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 8 (1893), large composite flower motif chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), dahlia and multi-layer crochet flower.

content.text: The dahlia uses the same layered petal trick as the freestanding rose: the inner and outer petal rings are both worked into the centre dc ring. But into different loops. The inner petals use treble cluster spokes around a magic ring. With htr arches for the first petal ring. Tr arches into the front loops of the cluster tops for the middle ring. And dtr arches into the back loops for the outermost ring. The three petal rings are automatically positioned at different radii, producing the dahlia's characteristic concentric depth.

title: Lotus motif

excerpt: The lotus motif uses eight shell-stitch petals worked outward from a puff-stitch centre, giving the characteristic cupped lotus outline. title: Folk striped shawl
subtitle: A rectangle in horizontal treble stripes across three DK colours, changing colour every four rows
excerpt: This rectangular shawl works in horizontal treble stripes across three colours of DK yarn, with a colour change every four rows. The finished piece measures approximately 190 cm wide by 60 cm deep. The stripe sequence builds a bold folk-textile look that works in any combination of three coordinating shades.

content.text: This rectangular shawl is worked flat from end to end in rows of treble, with the colour changing every four rows across three shades of DK yarn. The stripe sequence repeats throughout: four rows in colour A, four rows in colour B, four rows in colour C, then back to colour A. At 190 cm wide and 60 cm deep the finished piece wraps across the shoulders with plenty of length to drape, knot, or tuck.
The construction is rectangular. There is no shaping at any point. The only technique to manage is the
at the end of every fourth row. The unused colours are carried up the selvedge using
. This means you do not need to cut and rejoin at every stripe.

attrs.body: Approximately 200 g each of three colours of DK-weight yarn (600 g total). A 4 mm crochet hook (US G/6). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Blocking mat and pins. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 17 tr x 9 rows = 10 x 10 cm in DK yarn with a 4 mm hook, measured unstretched. Work a 15 x 15 cm swatch in treble, measure the central 10 x 10 cm area, and adjust hook size before beginning the shawl. Each extra stitch per 10 cm shifts the finished width by about 11 cm, so accurate tension here matters.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
treble (tr): UK; the same move as US "double crochet" (dc).

The shawl is worked flat from one short end to the other. Colour A is the first colour, B is the second, C is the third. The stripe sequence is 4 rows A, 4 rows B, 4 rows C, repeated throughout. Do not cut yarn at each colour change; instead carry the unused colours up the right-hand selvedge.
Using colour A, ch 109. (This gives 108 working stitches and measures approximately 64 cm, which becomes the 60 cm depth after the body is worked and blocked.)
Ch 3 (counts as first tr throughout). 1 tr in each ch across. Turn. (108 sts)
Ch 3 (counts as first tr). 1 tr in each st across to end. Turn. (108 sts each row)

At the end of row 4, work the last tr of colour A until 2 loops remain on hook, then draw colour B through both loops to complete the stitch. Drop colour A at the selvedge (do not cut). Continue with colour B.

title: Granny square, eight rounds
subtitle: A 20 cm square with eight cluster rounds, standalone panel size for pot holders and cushion centrepieces
excerpt: Eight rounds from the magic ring give a 20 cm granny square in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook. At this size the square works as a standalone pot holder, a small cushion-cover front on its own, or the centrepiece panel in a granny-stitch blanket with a plain border.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volumes 1-3 (1885-1890) — the square-from-the-centre construction (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet motif chapter.

content.text: The eight-round granny square builds to a 20 cm motif in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook. Large enough to use as a standalone pot holder, a small cushion-cover front. Or the centrepiece panel in a granny-stitch blanket with a plain border surround. The construction follows the same rule as every granny square: each round adds one more cluster group per side. So round 8 carries seven side clusters on each of the four edges.

structure at the corners becomes an important reference point while you work. Placing a stitch marker in each corner ch-2 space at the start of round 4 or 5 helps keep track of corners on the longer rounds.

content.text: This rectangle shawl is built from 100

arranged in a 5-wide by 20-long grid. Each square is worked in three rounds from the centre out on a 4 mm hook, with a colour change between rounds or between squares. The squares are connected during the final joining round of each new square using the
method, so no sewing is needed after the squares are complete.

The pattern uses at least three colours but works with any number. A planned colour layout (drawn out on a grid before you begin) avoids the same colour appearing in adjacent squares. The final round of every square is worked in the same joining colour to give the grid a consistent visual frame.

attrs.body: Approximately 500 g total DK-weight yarn across 3 or more colours. A 4 mm hook (US G/6). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Stitch markers. Blocking mat and pins. Tape measure. Pen and grid paper for a colour plan (optional but helpful with 100 squares).

content.text: Each granny square measures 10 x 10 cm after blocking with DK yarn on a 4 mm hook. Work one square, block it by dampening and pinning to a 10 x 10 cm square, and measure before working all 100. If your square is larger than 10 cm, drop a hook size; if smaller, go up a hook size. The correct square size is what controls the finished shawl dimensions.
ch: chain -- UK and US shared.
sl st: slip stitch -- UK and US shared.
dc: double crochet (UK) -- used in the joining round edging.
tr: treble (UK) -- the main stitch of the granny square body. The same move as US double crochet (dc).
Using colour A, ch 4. Sl st in 1st ch to form a ring.
Round 1: Ch 3 (counts as 1 tr). 2 tr in ring. Ch 2. *3 tr in ring. Ch 2.* Repeat from * to * twice more. Sl st in top of starting ch-3 to close. Fasten off. (4 corner spaces, 12 tr)

Round 2: Join colour B in any corner ch-2 space. Ch 3 (counts as 1 tr). 2 tr in same corner space. Ch 2. 3 tr in same corner space. *Ch 1. 3 tr in next corner space. Ch 2. 3 tr in same corner space.* Repeat from * to * twice more. Ch 1. Sl st in top of starting ch-3 to close. Fasten off. (4 corners each with 2 groups of 3 tr, 4 side spaces)

Round 3 (joining round): Join joining colour in any corner ch-2 space. Ch 3 (counts as 1 tr). 2 tr in same corner space. Ch 2. 3 tr in same corner space. *Ch 1. 3 tr in next side ch-1 space. Ch 1. 3 tr in corner ch-2 space. Ch 2. 3 tr in same corner space.* Repeat from * to * twice more. Ch 1. 3 tr in remaining side ch-1 space. Ch 1. Sl st in top of starting ch-3. Fasten off. (4 corners, 8 side groups, 24 tr)
Join-as-you-go: joining to an existing square

On all squares except the first, modify round 3 along any shared edge. Where the pattern says "ch 2" at a corner shared with an adjacent square: instead of ch 2, work ch 1, then insert hook into the matching corner ch-2 space on the adjacent square and draw up a loop, sl st to join, then ch 1. Where the pattern says "ch 1" at a side space shared with an adjacent square: instead of ch 1, insert hook into the matching ch-1 space on the adjacent square and sl st. Continue in pattern for all other spaces. This produces a flat join visible as a chain ridge on the right side.

Work the grid in columns from left to right, building each column from bottom to top. Square 1 is the bottom-left corner. Squares 2 to 5 complete the first column. Square 6 joins to the right side of square 1 and to no other square. Continue column by column. Squares joining in the middle of the grid will join to one square below and one square to the left simultaneously: work the ch-1 and ch-2 modifications on both the bottom and left edges of round 3 at the same time. (100 squares total)

Weave in all ends through the backs of stitches on the wrong side. Because each square is small and each colour change is short, there are many ends; allow time for this step. Wet-block the completed rectangle by soaking in cool water, pressing out excess water in a towel, then pinning to the stated dimensions on a blocking mat.

Handwash in cool water with mild detergent. Do not tumble-dry. Lay flat and ease to shape while damp. If colours are deep or mixed-fibre, test for colourfastness by wetting a small corner and pressing against a white cloth before the first full wash.

A 6 x 6 grid of the same square makes a cushion cover front. Adding a fourth round to every square before joining produces a coarser, heavier blanket throw from the same grid proportions. Mixing square sizes (some worked to round 2 only) creates a playful patchwork surface where smaller and larger squares fill the same column width.

title: Granny square, six rounds
subtitle: The standard cushion-front size: a 15 cm granny square with six cluster rounds
excerpt: Six rounds from the magic ring give a 15 cm granny square in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook after steam-blocking. At 15 cm this is the go-to size for cushion-cover panels, one square per panel works for small cushions, and a 3 x 3 grid fills a standard 40 x 40 cm front.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volumes 1-3 (1885-1890) — the square-from-the-centre construction (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet motif chapter.

content.text: The six-round granny square lands at 15 cm in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook after steam-blocking. Which makes it the standard cushion-front motif: three squares across three rows fills a 40 x 40 cm cushion panel without gaps. Each round adds one more cluster group per side. So round 6 has five side clusters on each of the four edges and 24 cluster groups in total.

The construction follows the same rules as every granny square: corner chain-space pairs hold a corner group every round. Side chain-1 spaces hold a 3tr side cluster group. The only thing that changes round by round is how many side cluster groups sit between each pair of corners.

title: Granny square, three-colour version
subtitle: Victorian scrap-cotton construction: colour A in round 1, colour B in rounds 2 and 3, colour C in round 4
excerpt: The three-colour granny square puts a different colour in each section of the four-round motif: colour A for the centre round, colour B for the middle two rounds, colour C for the outer border. Each change is a clean fasten-off, no carrying, no floats. The fastest way to use up small yarn remnants.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 1 (1885) — the square-from-the-centre construction (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet motif chapter.

content.text: The three-colour granny square is the Victorian scrap-cotton construction that made the granny square popular in the first place. Colour A works round 1 alone, building the four corner cluster pairs at the centre. Colour B picks up for rounds 2 and 3, then fastens off. Colour C finishes the outer border in round 4. Each colour-change is a clean break rather than a carry. Each colour fastens off at its last round and the new colour joins at the corner chain-space at the start of the next.

This is the fastest way to work through a bag of small yarn remnants: each motif uses as little as 1.5 g of colour A. 3 g of colour B. And 2 g of colour C. No two squares need to match. And a blanket of random three-colour squares with a consistent outer border colour reads as intentional rather than chaotic.

attrs.body: About 1.5 g of colour A, 3 g of colour B. And 2 g of colour C in DK-weight cotton. A 4 mm crochet hook. Tapestry needle. Scissors.

content.text: You will have six tails: the colour A magic ring tail and fasten-off tail. The colour B join tail and fasten-off tail. And the colour C join tail and fasten-off tail. Weave each through 3 to 4 stitches on the wrong side and trim. Steam-block flat.

Join the same way as any four-round granny: whip-stitch through back loops at corner ch-2 spaces and along side ch-1 spaces. Or use a slip-stitch flat join on the wrong side. When colour C is the border colour on every square, the joins effectively disappear into the outer round.

The two-colour version is structurally identical but splits the rounds 2:2 rather than 1:2:1. The five-round version gives more room for colour banding. Try one colour per round for a striped concentric effect. Or keep the outer two rounds in a single joining colour for a consistent blanket border.

title: Granny square, three rounds
subtitle: The smallest useful granny: a compact 7 cm motif that joins quickly into blankets and accessories

title: Granny stripe panel
subtitle: Continuous granny-style rows worked back and forth to build a striped panel without joining separate motifs
excerpt: The granny stripe panel works the cluster-and-chain construction of the granny square continuously back and forth across a row rather than in separate joined squares. Each cluster row produces a stripe, and the turning gives the clusters a chevron offset between rows. No motifs to join, just rows of clusters in sequence.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 2 (1887), continuous cluster stripe chapter (Internet Archive).

content.text: The granny stripe panel takes the cluster row of a granny square and extends it across the full panel width. Turning at each end gives the clusters a half-group offset between rows. Producing a brick-pattern alignment of clusters rather than straight vertical columns.
Change colour at the end of every row to produce a horizontal stripe. Carry the unused colours up the side edge for a two or three-colour stripe sequence without cutting and rejoining every row.

attrs.body: DK-weight cotton in two or three colours. A 4 mm hook. Tapestry needle.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: Ch 34 in colour A. (For a wider panel: foundation chain = number of cluster groups × 3 + 4.).
3 tr into 4th ch from hook. *Ch 1. Skip 2 ch. 3 tr into next ch.* Rep across. Turn.
Ch 3. Skip first cluster. 3 tr into first ch-1 sp. *Ch 1. 3 tr into next ch-1 sp.* Rep across. 1 tr into top of turning ch. Turn.

Continue in stripe sequence, alternating colours every row. Rows 1, 3, 5 work into the foundation and odd-row ch-1 sps. Rows 2, 4, 6 work into the even-row ch-1 sps. The alternating start position produces the brick offset automatically.
Work the circular base motif for a different construction that uses the same cluster structure but in the round to produce a circle rather than a panel.

title: Granny Stripe Shawl
subtitle: DK weight rectangle in granny stripe rows using three colours on a 4mm hook
excerpt: A rectangle shawl worked in the granny stripe: rows of 3-treble clusters with chain-1 gaps, worked in three repeating colours. DK weight on a 4mm hook produces a fabric with the character of a granny square but in a simple rectangular layout.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. Granny stripe construction is a well-established technique with no single originating source.

content.text: This shawl is a rectangle measuring approximately 180cm wide by 55cm deep, worked in the granny stripe stitch using three colours. The granny stripe is a row-by-row version of the granny square: instead of rounds, you work rows of 3-treble clusters with chain-1 spaces between them, and each new row's clusters sit over the chain-1 spaces of the row below. Colour changes happen at the end of every row, cycling through the three colours in order. DK weight on a 4mm hook produces a fabric with firm structure and clear colour stripes. The stitch repeat is consistent throughout: once you have worked the first two rows, the rest of the shawl follows the same sequence.

Yarn: approximately 200g each of three DK weight colours (approximately 600g total). Label these Colour A, Colour B, and Colour C. Hook: 4mm. You will also need a tapestry needle, scissors, and a tape measure. Stitch markers are helpful for checking the repeat at the start.

One granny stripe repeat (3 tr cluster plus ch-1 sp) measures approximately 2.5cm wide on a 4mm hook over granny stripe pattern. 180cm width requires approximately 72 repeats. Work a swatch of at least 20 repeats to check your tension before casting on for the full width.
Granny stripe: 3 tr in ch-1 sp, ch 1, repeat
Colour change at end of row

The foundation chain sets the width of the shawl. The granny stripe repeat is 4 chains (3 tr + 1 ch gap), plus 3 chains for the turning chain at the start of Row 1. For 72 repeats the foundation chain is: 72 x 4 = 288, plus 3 = 291 chains total.
Using Colour A, ch 291. Lay flat and measure: should reach approximately 180cm.

Ch 3 (counts as first tr), 2 tr in 4th ch from hook, [ch 1, skip 3 ch, 3 tr in next ch] across to last 4 ch, ch 1, skip 3 ch, 3 tr in last ch. Change to Colour B on final yarn-over of last cluster, turn. (72 clusters, 71 ch-1 sps)
Ch 3 (counts as first tr), 2 tr in first ch-1 sp, [ch 1, 3 tr in next ch-1 sp] across. Change to Colour C on final yarn-over, turn. (72 clusters, 71 ch-1 sps)
Ch 3 (counts as first tr), 2 tr in first ch-1 sp, [ch 1, 3 tr in next ch-1 sp] across. Change to Colour A on final yarn-over, turn. (72 clusters, 71 ch-1 sps)

Repeat Rows 2 and 3, cycling A, B, C in order. Each row is identical in structure: ch 3, 2 tr in first ch-1 sp, [ch 1, 3 tr in next ch-1 sp] across, change colour on final yarn-over. Continue until the work measures approximately 55cm from the foundation chain edge. At the stated gauge this is approximately 22 rows. End with a complete set of all three colours if possible, finishing after a Row C. Fasten off.

Join Colour A at any corner. Work one round of dc evenly around all four sides, placing 3 dc in each corner. Sl st to join, fasten off. This stabilises the edges and tidies the colour-change selvedge.

Weave in all colour-change tails on the wrong side. There will be two tails per row end (one from the finished colour and one from the new colour). Weave each tail along a row of stitches in a matching colour direction so it does not show from the front. Block by soaking briefly in cool water, pressing out moisture in a towel, and pinning to the stated dimensions on a foam mat.
Hand wash or machine wash on a gentle cool cycle depending on the yarn fibre. Check the label. Reshape and dry flat. Do not tumble dry at high heat.

The granny stripe translates directly into a blanket: use a longer foundation chain and the same three-colour rotation. For a shaped version using the same stitch, a granny stripe triangle shawl adds increases at the edges in the same way the V-stitch triangle shawl does. If you want to use the granny stripe structure in the round rather than in rows, a granny square sampler blanket is the natural progression.

title: Granny triangle
subtitle: A three-corner granny motif for diagonal layouts and edge filling
excerpt: The granny triangle uses three corner positions instead of four, giving an equilateral triangle that fills the gaps when granny squares are set on-point in a diagonal layout. Three rounds in DK cotton produce a tile that fits exactly into the corner gap between four squares arranged in a diamond.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 2 (1887), triangular motif chapter (Internet Archive).

content.text: The granny triangle works the same cluster-and-corner structure as the granny square but with three corners instead of four. It was designed for
, where granny squares set at 45 degrees leave triangular gaps at the edges that need filling.

Work three rounds from the magic ring. Round 1 sets three corner spaces with one cluster pair per corner. Rounds 2 and 3 add side clusters between corners. The triangle joins along any side at the cluster chain spaces.

title: Hairpin lace stole
subtitle: Hairpin lace strips joined with slip stitch to make a 190 cm x 50 cm stole in DK on a 4 mm hook
excerpt: Hairpin lace is worked on a U-shaped frame tool, not a standard crochet hook alone. The frame holds two prongs a set distance apart; you wind yarn around the prongs and work a central crochet spine to produce a strip of looped lace. This stole joins five strips side by side with slip stitch joins to reach 190 cm long by 50 cm wide.
sourceNotes: Hairpin lace construction documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 5 (1889-1890), which describes the use of a staple or fork frame to produce looped braid strips. Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), also describes fork crochet (Internet Archive).

content.text: in addition to a standard 4 mm crochet hook. The frame is a separate specialist tool that holds two prongs 50 mm apart; without it, the stitch cannot be worked. Frames are sold by crochet suppliers and haberdashery shops, often as adjustable sets with multiple prong spacings. Set the prong spacing to 50 mm before beginning.
The stole is made from five
, each 190 cm long with 380 loops per side (20 loops per 10 cm). The five strips are joined flat using a
along each shared inner edge. The outer edges of the two border strips are left as open loops, giving the stole its characteristic fringe-like lace finish.

attrs.body: Approximately 350 g DK-weight yarn (a smooth, slightly plied yarn shows the loops clearly; avoid very fuzzy fibres which obscure the lace structure). A 4 mm crochet hook (US G/6). A hairpin lace frame set to 50 mm prong spacing -- sold separately by crochet suppliers. Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Blocking mat and pins. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

attrs.body: Hairpin lace frames are not included in a standard crochet kit. They are available from specialist crochet suppliers and haberdashery shops, typically sold as a set of prong pairs with a connecting bar. Adjustable metal frames (e.g. 25 mm to 100 mm prong spacing) cover the full range of lace widths and are the most practical option. Confirm the 50 mm setting on your specific frame before casting on.
attrs.title: Hairpin frame note

content.text: 20 loops per 10 cm along the length of the strip, with the frame set at 50 mm prong spacing. Work 20 cm of your first strip, count the loops along one edge, and adjust the tension of your central chain spine if the count does not match. A tighter spine produces more loops per 10 cm and a shorter strip; a looser spine produces fewer loops and a longer strip.
ch: chain -- UK and US shared.
sl st: slip stitch -- UK and US shared. Used in the central spine and in the strip joins.
dc: double crochet (UK) -- used in the central spine of each strip and in the edging.
: yarn wound around prong then dc in central spine -- the core move of the frame-based technique.

Make a slip knot and place it on the 4 mm hook. Hold the frame with the two prongs in your non-hook hand. Drape the yarn over the left prong from front to back, then work 1 dc into the loop on the hook, drawing the yarn through. Turn the frame 180 degrees from left to right (the right prong now faces left). The yarn wraps around the prong as you turn. Work 1 dc into the two threads of the central loop. Turn the frame again. Continue: each full turn deposits one loop on the outer edge of each prong and each dc forms one link of the central chain spine.

Work until each strip has 380 loops on each side (which gives 190 cm at 20 loops per 10 cm). When the strip fills the frame, slip the loops off carefully onto a spare length of yarn or a long stitch holder, then replace them on the frame and continue. Count loops every 50 turns to track progress. Fasten off each strip when the loop count reaches 380 on each side, leaving a 15 cm tail. Make 5 strips total.
Lay two strips side by side with their inner edges facing. Using the 4 mm hook and the working yarn (or a separate joining length), work the

: *insert hook into 1 loop from the left strip and 1 loop from the right strip, draw the right-strip loop through the left-strip loop, then sl st*; repeat from * to * along the full length, working one pair of loops per sl st. Work all 380 loop pairs. Repeat for each join between the 5 strips. You will have 4 joins total. (5 strips joined)

At each short end of the stole, work a row of dc across the 5 strip ends to neaten: join yarn at one corner, ch 1 (does not count as a stitch), work 1 dc into each central spine end across all 5 strips. Fasten off. Repeat at the other short end.

Weave in all ends through the central spines of the strips. Wet-block by soaking the joined stole in cool water for 10 minutes, pressing water out gently in a towel, then pinning the two long edges and both short edges to the stated dimensions on a blocking mat. Leave the outer loop edges free and pin them lightly at intervals to spread them evenly.

Handwash in cool water with mild wool wash. Lay flat to dry. The open loops are delicate; do not wring or tumble-dry. Check the loop joins after washing and ease any pulled stitches back into place while still damp.

Changing the frame width to 75 mm produces wider strips and a more open lace appearance from the same loop count. Working the central spine in a contrast colour so it reads differently from the loops is a well-established hairpin variation. A shorter version using three strips produces a narrower scarf rather than a full stole.

title: Basic hexagon motif
subtitle: Six corner points, three rounds, 11 cm point-to-point, the tile that fills a surface without gaps
excerpt: The basic hexagon uses six corner chain-2 spaces instead of four to give a flat six-sided motif that tiles without gaps. Three rounds in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook give an 11 cm point-to-point motif, a natural companion to granny squares in mixed-motif blankets.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volumes 1-3 (1885-1890) — the hexagonal motif constructions (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet motif chapter.

content.text: The basic hexagon uses six corner points instead of four. With the same chain-space construction that holds a granny square's corners. A pair at each of the six points on every round. Three rounds in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook give an 11 cm motif that tiles without gaps alongside other hexagons. Or alongside granny squares with small fill-in triangles at the joins.
If you can work a granny square. This motif adds only one thing to learn: counting to six instead of four. The cluster construction is identical, and the magic ring start is the same.

attrs.body: About 5 g of DK-weight cotton in one to three colours. A 4 mm crochet hook. Tapestry needle. Scissors. A blocking mat and pins.
attrs.title: Materials for one motif

content.text: Each finished three-round basic hexagon measures 11 cm point-to-point in DK-weight cotton with a 4 mm hook. After a light steam-block. Swatch one motif before starting a large project. Hexagons that are even 1 cm off will not tile cleanly.
slip stitch, UK and US shared.
treble, UK; called double crochet in US patterns.
magic ring, adjustable starting loop; no centre hole.

Worked in the round, right side facing throughout. Ch 3 at the start of each round counts as the first treble of the first cluster. Do not turn. Place a stitch marker in the first ch-2 corner space of each round to track the start.
Form a magic ring. Ch 3. Work 2 tr into the ring. *Ch 2, 3 tr into the ring*; repeat from * to * four more times. Ch 2, sl st to top of beg ch-3 to join. Pull tail to close ring.

Sl st across next 2 tr and into first ch-2 corner sp. Ch 3. Into same sp work 2 tr, ch 2, 3 tr. *Ch 1, into next ch-2 corner sp work 3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr*; repeat from * to * four more times. Ch 1, sl st to top of beg ch-3 to join.

Sl st into first ch-2 corner sp. Ch 3. Into same sp work 2 tr, ch 2, 3 tr. Ch 1. *Into next ch-1 side sp work 3 tr. Ch 1. Into next ch-2 corner sp work 3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr. Ch 1.* Repeat from * to * four more times. Into next ch-1 side sp work 3 tr. Ch 1. Sl st to top of beg ch-3 to join.
The chart reads outward from the magic ring. Six corner ch-2 spaces are evenly spaced throughout all rounds; side ch-1 spaces appear from round 2.

definition.title: Basic hexagon motif
definition.caption: Three rounds from the magic ring. Six corner ch-2 spaces throughout. Round 3 has one side cluster per edge and 54 trebles total.

content.text: Fasten off, leaving a 15 cm tail. Weave through 3 to 4 stitches on the wrong side and trim. Weave in the magic ring tail. Steam-block on a foam mat: pin all six points to keep the hexagon symmetrical. Then pin the six sides straight between the points.

Hexagons join flat along each of their six sides. For a honeycomb grid. Each hexagon shares one full side with its neighbour. Whip-stitch through the back loops along the side clusters and through the adjacent corner ch-2 spaces. A join-as-you-go method works on round 3: replace the ch-2 at each shared corner with a ch-1. Sl st into the corresponding corner sp of the adjacent hexagon, ch-1, then continue.
Handwash in cool water with mild soap, or machine-wash on a delicates cycle. Lay flat to dry, hexagons hold their shape better if pinned at the six points while damp.

The granny-style hexagon uses the same six-corner construction but adds side clusters in the later rounds to match the aesthetic of a granny square. Useful when mixing hexagons and squares in the same project. The treble cluster hexagon replaces the open ch-2 corner with a bold 5-tr cluster at each point.

title: Granny-style hexagon
subtitle: The hexagonal version of the classic granny motif, cluster groups at six corners, side clusters from round 3
excerpt: The granny-style hexagon works cluster groups of three trebles at all six corners and adds side clusters from round 3 onward, matching the granny square's visual texture. Four rounds give a 12 cm point-to-point motif that sits comfortably alongside granny squares in mixed blankets.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volumes 1-3 (1885-1890) — the hexagonal motif constructions (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet motif chapter.

content.text: The granny-style hexagon applies the granny square's cluster construction to a six-sided motif: the same corner groups at all six chain-space corners. And side cluster groups between the corners from round 3 onward. Four rounds give a 12 cm point-to-point motif with two side clusters per edge. Visually consistent with a four-round granny square and able to join alongside squares in the same blanket with only minor gap-filling at the corners.

The main thing to hold in your head is that the repeat is six instead of four. Every other aspect of the method is the same as a standard granny square. Placing a stitch marker in the first corner ch-2 space at the start of each round makes it easier to count the six repeats correctly.

title: Popcorn hexagon
subtitle: One popcorn at each of the six corner points, a raised dot visible from across the room
excerpt: The popcorn hexagon puts one popcorn stitch at each of its six corner points, surrounded by trebles in each round. The popcorn stands out on the public face, a raised dome at every corner that reads clearly even in a single colour and from a distance.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volumes 1-3 (1885-1890) — raised-stitch hexagonal motifs (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet motif chapter.

content.text: The popcorn hexagon places one popcorn stitch at the centre of each of its six corner points. Flanked by chain-2 spaces and surrounded by flat trebles in each round. The popcorn stands out on the public face as a rounded raised dome. A different texture from a cluster because the individual trebles are visible before they are gathered. Giving a more three-dimensional point.

Each chain-space flanking the popcorn keeps the corners open so the motif lies flat. The popcorn needs a slightly looser tension than average to sit fully rounded. If yours are pulling flat, work the five trebles of the popcorn slightly looser before closing.

attrs.body: About 8 g of DK-weight cotton. A 4 mm crochet hook. Tapestry needle. Scissors. A blocking mat and pins, the popcorn domes need gentle steam rather than heavy pressing to stay rounded.

attrs.title: Materials for one motif

content.text: Each finished four-round treble cluster hexagon measures 12 cm point-to-point in DK-weight cotton with a 4 mm hook, after steam-blocking. Make a test motif before starting a large project — the cluster tips can pull tighter than standard clusters and affect the overall diameter.
slip stitch (sl st) — UK and US shared.
treble (tr) — UK; called double crochet (dc) in US patterns.
5-tr cluster (5tr-cl) — five trebles worked into the same space, loops joined at the top. UK; the same technique as US 5-dc cluster.
magic ring (MR) — adjustable starting loop; no centre hole.

Worked in the round, right side facing throughout. The 5-tr cluster counts as one corner unit. Ch 3 at the start of each round does NOT count as a treble here — it lifts the yarn to the correct height before the first cluster. Do not turn.

Form a magic ring. Ch 3 (does not count as st). Work a 5-tr cluster into the ring: [yarn over, insert hook into ring, pull up loop, yarn over, pull through 2 loops] 5 times into the ring, then yarn over and pull through all 6 loops on hook. *Ch 2, work a 5-tr cluster into the ring*; repeat from * to * four more times. Ch 2, sl st to top of first cluster to join. Pull tail to close ring. (6 cluster points, 6 ch-2 spaces.)

Sl st into first ch-2 corner sp. Ch 3. Work a 5-tr cluster into the same sp. *Ch 2, into same sp work a second 5-tr cluster. Ch 1. Into next ch-2 sp work a 5-tr cluster*; repeat from * to * four more times. Ch 2, into same sp work a second 5-tr cluster. Ch 1. Sl st to top of first cluster to join. (12 clusters, 6 ch-2 spaces, 6 ch-1 side spaces.)

Sl st into first ch-2 corner sp. Ch 3. Work a 5-tr cluster into same sp. Ch 2, work a second 5-tr cluster into same sp. Ch 1. *Into next ch-1 side sp work 3 tr. Ch 1. Into next ch-2 corner sp work (5-tr cluster, ch 2, 5-tr cluster). Ch 1.* Repeat from * to * four more times. Into next ch-1 side sp work 3 tr. Ch 1. Sl st to top of first cluster to join. (12 corner clusters, 6 side clusters, 6 ch-2 corners, 12 ch-1 side spaces.)

Sl st into first ch-2 corner sp. Ch 3. Work a 5-tr cluster into same sp. Ch 2, work a second 5-tr cluster into same sp. Ch 1. *[Into next ch-1 side sp work 3 tr. Ch 1.] twice. Into next ch-2 corner sp work (5-tr cluster, ch 2, 5-tr cluster). Ch 1.* Repeat from * to * four more times. [Into next ch-1 side sp work 3 tr. Ch 1.] twice. Sl st to top of first cluster to join. Fasten off. (12 corner clusters, 12 side clusters, 6 ch-2 corners, 18 ch-1 side spaces.)
The chart reads outward from the magic ring. Corner cluster pairs sit at all six points on every round; standard three-treble side clusters fill the edges from round 3.

definition.title: Treble cluster hexagon
definition.caption: Four rounds from the magic ring. 5-tr clusters mark all six corners throughout. Standard 3-tr clusters fill the side spaces from round 3. Chain-1 spaces between all groups.

content.text: Fasten off, leaving a 15 cm tail. Thread through a tapestry needle and weave through 3 to 4 stitches on the wrong side, reverse direction through 2 to 3 stitches, and trim. Weave in the magic ring tail. Steam-block on a foam mat with all six cluster points pinned — the raised tips benefit from gentle pinning to hold their shape while the yarn relaxes.

Join along each of the six sides through the back loops of the side cluster groups and through the ch-2 spaces at the corner tips. The raised cluster tips sit slightly proud of the seam after joining — this is correct; the tip reading as a defined point is part of the motif's character.
Handwash in cool water with mild soap, or machine-wash on a delicates cycle. The cluster tips may compress in the wash — re-pin them while damp to restore the shape. Lay flat to dry.

The popcorn hexagon uses a different raised stitch at each corner point — a popcorn rather than a cluster, giving an even more prominent raised dot. The lacy hexagon moves in the opposite direction: open chain-3 side spaces instead of solid clusters, for an airy finish.

title: Interlocking crochet square
subtitle: Two independent mesh layers worked simultaneously and locked together by chain-space insertion
excerpt: Interlocking crochet works two separate open-mesh grids in different colours simultaneously, with each round of one grid inserting through the chain spaces of the other. The two grids interlock without any stitch catching or yarn carrying. They are structurally independent but visually inseparable.
sourceNotes: Interlocking crochet is documented in 20th-century craft publications and has precursors in Victorian double-mesh crochet described in Weldon's Practical Needlework, Volume 6 (1891).

by inserting each grid's stitches through the chain spaces of the other. The grids never share yarn. They are structurally separate but physically locked together. Each grid is a simple 1 dc + 2 ch mesh.

Work grid A first across all rows. Then work grid B with the wrong side of grid A facing: each dc of grid B inserts through a chain space of grid A, not on top of it. The two grids sit in different planes of the fabric, visible from their respective right sides.

title: Join-as-you-go square
subtitle: A granny square that attaches to its neighbours on the final round rather than sewing up afterward
excerpt: Join-as-you-go replaces the chain-2 corner spaces on the final round of each new square with a slip-stitch join into the matching corner space of the adjacent finished square. Working the join during crochet rather than sewing eliminates seaming and keeps the wrong side flat with no ridges.
sourceNotes: The join-as-you-go technique is documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 3 (1888) and appears in early American crochet booklets throughout the 1890s as a method for assembling afghan squares without a tapestry needle.

content.text: The JAYG method works all rounds of a new square independently through round 3. Then joins on round 4 by replacing the two chain stitches in each corner space with one chain. One slip stitch into the adjacent square's corner, one chain. Side ch-1 spaces get the same treatment: ch 1, sl st, ch 1.

Work the first square fully through all 4 rounds. For each next square in the layout. Complete rounds 1 to 3 normally, then on round 4 join along each shared edge. Corner joins at the intersection of four squares place the sl st through all four meeting corner spaces.

attrs.body: DK-weight cotton, any quantity. A 4 mm hook. No tapestry needle needed for joining, that is the point of the technique.

content.text: Rounds 1 to 3: standard granny square. Finish round 3 normally. Fasten off if this is the anchor square; do not fasten off for joining squares.
Sl st to corner sp. *3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr into corner. Ch 1, 3 tr into side sp. Ch 1.* Rep from * on free edges as standard.

At each joining corner: work 3 tr. Ch 1. Sl st into the adjacent square's ch-2 corner sp. Ch 1. Work 3 tr into same corner sp on new square. At each joining side: ch 1. Sl st into adjacent square's ch-1 side sp. Ch 1. Work 3 tr into next sp on new square.

title: Lace stole in Solomon's knot
subtitle: A long rectangular stole in Solomon's knot lace, worked in lace-weight cotton
excerpt: Solomon's knot is an elongated chain with a locking single crochet worked into the back loop, the result is an open, spiderweb lace fabric that uses very little yarn. This rectangular stole in lace-weight cotton is worked lengthwise, 200 cm long and 55 cm wide, on a 3 mm hook. The fabric is extremely light and drapes in long, fluid folds.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet chapter, Solomon's knot described as the "elongated loop with a locking stitch" and used for shawl borders and gossamer wraps. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 6 (1890), gives a full stole pattern in the same construction (Internet Archive).

content.text: stole is one of the lightest crochet wraps possible: the open mesh uses less than half the yarn of a solid-fabric stole of the same dimensions. This rectangular version in lace-weight cotton on a 3 mm hook finishes at 200 × 55 cm and folds into a very small bundle.

The stole is worked lengthwise along the 200 cm edge. Which means the foundation row is long but each next row adds depth quickly. The selvedge is neat: each row begins and ends with a standard double crochet into the turning knot.

attrs.body: about 150 g lace-weight cotton yarn. A 3 mm hook. Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Blocking mat and pins. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 4 Solomon's knot pairs × 8 rows = 10 × 10 cm in lace-weight cotton with a 3 mm hook. Blocked flat. The gauge is measured after blocking. Unblocked Solomon's knot lace is denser and does not reflect the finished dimensions.
How to work a Solomon's knot
Draw up the working loop to the height required by the pattern. This is the elongated chain loop.
Identify the single strand running behind the elongated loop.
Insert the hook under this back strand only, yarn over, and draw through a loop.
Yarn over, pull through both loops. This locking double crochet anchors the elongated loop.
double crochet: UK; the same move as US "single crochet".
Solomon's knot: elongated chain with a locking dc into the back loop.

Work a foundation row of Solomon's knots to about 200 cm. The exact count is flexible; work an even number of SK pairs. Join the row by working 1 dc into the back loop of the second-to-last locking dc before the turning knot. This sets the first row of mesh.
Turn. *Work 2 SK. Skip the next locking dc, 1 dc into the next locking dc*; repeat from * to * across. 2 SK at end of row, 1 dc into the last locking dc of the foundation. Turn.
Repeat Row 1 on each row. Continue until the stole measures 55 cm deep from the foundation row. Fasten off.

Fasten off and weave in the two ends. Wet-block by soaking in cool water for 15 minutes. Pressing out gently, then pinning to the full 200 × 55 cm dimensions on a blocking mat. Solomon's knot lace opens much on blocking. Do not skip this step.
Handwash in cool water only. Lay flat to dry on a towel. Do not press with a hot iron directly on cotton lace.
Work the same construction in a silk-cotton blend for a softer drape suitable for evening wear. The same mesh pattern scales up to a beach cover-up in a chunky cotton tape yarn on a 5 mm hook.
