double crochet (dc): UK; the same move as US "single crochet" (sc).
Solomon's knot (SK): elongated chain with a locking dc into the back loop.
Abbreviations: SK = one Solomon's knot (elongated 1 cm loop + locking dc into back strand).

Work a foundation row of Solomon's knots to approximately 200 cm. The exact count is flexible; work an even number of SK pairs. Join the row by working 1 dc into the back loop of the second-to-last locking dc before the turning knot. This sets the first row of mesh.
Turn. *Work 2 SK, skip the next locking dc, 1 dc into the next locking dc*; repeat from * to * across. 2 SK at end of row, 1 dc into the last locking dc of the foundation. Turn.
Repeat Row 1 on each row. Continue until the stole measures 55 cm deep from the foundation row (approximately 44 rows at the given gauge). Fasten off.

Fasten off and weave in the two ends. Wet-block by soaking in cool water for 15 minutes, pressing out gently, then pinning to the full 200 × 55 cm dimensions on a blocking mat. Solomon's knot lace opens significantly on blocking . Do not skip this step.
Handwash in cool water only. Lay flat to dry on a towel. Do not press with a hot iron directly on cotton lace.
Work the same construction in a silk-cotton blend for a softer drape suitable for evening wear. The same mesh pattern scales up to a beach cover-up in a chunky cotton tape yarn on a 5 mm hook.

title: Fern leaf motif
subtitle: A pinnate fern frond with paired side leaflets, 14 cm
excerpt: The fern frond is the most architecturally complex of the leaf motifs: a long centre spine with six to eight pairs of small leaflet branches worked outward at regular intervals. The construction is the same as the oak leaf spine but repeated at a miniature scale for each leaflet. At 14 cm in DK cotton the frond is long enough for a large cushion centrepiece.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 7 (1892), fern and botanical applique chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet fern frond section.

content.text: The fern frond is pinnate, a long centre spine with paired leaflets branching at each side. Each leaflet is a chain arch worked outward from the spine. Stitched along its length, then slip stitched back to the spine chain to continue. The leaflets closest to the base are smallest; the middle leaflets are widest. The tip leaflet is a single spine-end rounded point.

attrs.body: About 10 g of mid-green DK cotton. A 4 mm hook. Tapestry needle. Scissors.
attrs.title: Materials for one frond

content.text: Each finished fern frond measures 14 cm long and 6 cm wide at the widest pair of leaflets in DK-weight cotton with a 4 mm hook.
chain, slip stitch, UK and US shared.
half treble, UK; US "half double crochet".
Ch 30. Sl st into 2nd and 3rd ch from hook. The 28 remaining chains form the spine.
Leaflets, work along spine toward tip

At each leaflet position, work the following for a right leaflet: Ch 6. Dc in 2nd ch from hook. Htr. Htr. Dc. Dc. Sl st back to the starting spine chain. For the left leaflet from the same spine position: Ch 6. Dc. Htr. Htr. Dc. Dc. Sl st back. Sl st along the spine 4 chains toward the tip. Repeat for 5 more pairs of leaflets (6 pairs total. Increasing leaflet length toward the middle by adding 1-2 extra ch on the outer 2 pairs). At the spine tip, work 3dc to round the frond end. Sl st back along the spine underside to the stem. Fasten off.

title: Holly leaf motif
subtitle: A spiky flat holly leaf in dark green with optional red berry French knots, 8 cm
excerpt: The holly leaf is worked around a centre spine with sharp alternating points along each side, three deep indentations with spike-tip trebles between them. At 8 cm in DK cotton the spiky profile is unmistakable. Add three red French-knot berries at the base for the classic Christmas motif, or leave it plain for a year-round botanical applique.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 4 (1889), Christmas botanical motif chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet holiday motif section.

title: Ivy leaf motif
subtitle: A three-lobed ivy leaf with a long stem, 8 cm
excerpt: The ivy leaf has a distinctive three-lobed outline, a large central lobe and two smaller side lobes, with a long stem. Worked around a centre spine chain, the ivy leaf is simpler than the oak but still immediately recognisable. At 8 cm in DK cotton it is effective as a trailing-vine applique, sewn in sequence along a blanket border.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 5 (1890), ivy and vine crochet applique chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet botanical leaf section.

content.text: The ivy leaf has three lobes: a tall central lobe at the leaf tip and two smaller side lobes partway along. The side lobes are small chain arches worked outward from the spine and returned. The central lobe is built into the spine itself using taller stitches at the tip point. A long stem ch extends from the base for use in trailing-vine compositions.

title: Maple leaf motif
subtitle: A five-pointed maple leaf in autumn red or orange, 9 cm
excerpt: The maple leaf motif is worked around a centre spine chain, building the five pointed lobes with increasing stitch heights at the point tips. At 9 cm in DK cotton the recognisable maple silhouette is clear, wider and more starred than the oak. It is used on autumn wreaths, Thanksgiving table runners, and seasonal garments.

Five lobes radiate from the spine chain: the centre lobe at the tip, two mid lobes at approximately 45 degrees, and two lower lobes nearly horizontal. The varying angles of the lobes are achieved by working more or fewer slip stitches between lobe bases on the return pass along the spine underside.

title: Oak leaf motif
subtitle: A flat lobed oak leaf in dk green or rust, 9 cm long
excerpt: The oak leaf works from a centre chain spine outward, building the characteristic lobed edge with dc, htr, and tr stitches of increasing height at each lobe and decreasing back down between lobes. The five-lobed outline at 9 cm is unmistakably oak, and the flat applique can be used singly or grouped in clusters on autumnal throws and garlands.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 6 (1891), crochet leaf motif chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet botanical applique chapter.

content.text: The oak leaf is worked around a

of 18 chains, building the lobed outline by varying stitch height. Each lobe rises from dc at the base, through htr on the lobe sides, to tr at the lobe tip, then decreases back to dc before the next inter-lobe notch. Five lobes per side give the unmistakable oak profile. A ch-2 stem at the base is an optional extension.

Ch 18. Sl st into the 2nd and 3rd ch from hook (stem). This positions the hook at the first lobe base.
First side, from base to leaf tip

Working along the spine chain toward the tip: *Dc in 2 ch. Htr in 1 ch. Tr in 1 ch (lobe tip). Htr in 1 ch. Dc in 1 ch. Sl st in 1 ch (lobe notch). Dc in 1 ch.* Repeat to create 5 lobes along the first side, ending at the chain tip. (5 lobe tips on first side.)
At the chain tip, work 3dc to turn the corner. Continue along the underside of the spine chain toward the stem, working 5 more lobes as above, mirroring the first side.
At the base end, sl st into the 2 remaining stem chains. Sl st to close. Fasten off.

title: Linen summer wrap
subtitle: A light dc mesh rectangle in sport-weight linen blend, worked with a ch-1 skip-1 pattern
excerpt: This wrap measures 190 cm wide by 55 cm deep and is worked in a simple dc mesh: double crochet separated by single chain spaces with one stitch skipped between each double crochet. The result is a breathable, semi-open fabric in sport-weight linen blend on a 3.5 mm hook. Suitable for crocheters who know double crochet.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. DC mesh construction is a widely established technique with no single source.

content.text: throughout: one double crochet (UK), one chain, one skipped stitch, repeated across the row. The stitch produces a lightweight grid fabric that suits sport-weight linen-blend yarns, which block flat and hold their shape without stretching. The wrap lies flat against the body or drapes from the shoulders.

is ch 3 at the start of each row: this stands in for the first dc plus ch-1 space. On every row, the first real dc is worked into the first ch-1 space of the previous row (not into the first skipped stitch or the dc above it). The last dc of each row is worked into the 2nd ch of the turning chain from the row below.

attrs.body: Approximately 300 g sport-weight linen-blend yarn. A 3.5 mm crochet hook (US E/4). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Tape measure. Optional: blocking mat and pins for a crisper finish.

Linen opens up noticeably with wet blocking, so measure the swatch after blocking if you intend to block the finished wrap.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.

title: Log cabin square, basic
subtitle: A square built by crocheting strips around a central rectangle, log-cabin style
excerpt: The log cabin square starts with a small foundation rectangle at the centre and adds a strip along each of its four sides in turn, rotating the work 90 degrees after each strip. Four strips in two alternating colours give a geometric square that measures 12 cm across with no corners to fill or chain spaces to navigate.
sourceNotes: Log cabin construction originates in patchwork quilting (documented from the 1860s); the crochet equivalent is described in Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 4 (1889), strip-built motif chapter (Internet Archive).

content.text: The log cabin square grows outward from a central rectangle by adding a

along each side in rotation. After four strips, the block is a square. After eight, it is larger. The construction never requires working into a chain space or managing a corner cluster. It is just rows.
Two colours alternate so each pair of opposite strips reads the same. The block joins flat at any edge and stacks into blankets without gaps between the motifs.

Join colour B to the right edge of the rectangle. Work 1 dc into each row-end along the right side (4 dc). Turn. Work 1 more row in dc. Fasten off.

Rotate the work 90 degrees after each strip. Strip 2 (colour A): work along the top edge including the new Strip 1 corner. Strip 3 (colour B): work along the left edge. title: Log cabin square, textured
subtitle: Alternating htr and dc strips add a ridge texture to the log cabin construction
excerpt: Alternating half treble and double crochet strips across the log cabin square create a subtle ridge at every colour change. The htr strip sits slightly higher than the dc strip beside it, giving each pair a stepped profile visible from the side and a lined texture from above.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 4 (1889), textured strip motif chapter (Internet Archive).

content.text: Alternating dc and htr strips create a htr ridge at each colour change. The half treble is one step taller than the double crochet. And that height difference is enough to give a stepped profile visible in raking light.

Use two tones of the same colour family to keep the texture prominent without the distraction of a strong colour contrast. Two shades of the same blue or two neutrals work well. High contrast pulls the eye to the colour before the texture.

attrs.title: Materials for one motif

content.text: Work the centre rectangle in dc. For each strip, alternate: one strip in htr, one strip in dc. Keep the strip width to 2 rows per strip. The height difference between stitch types means the outer edge stays level.
For a smoother texture. Try the bavarian crochet square, which builds concentric rings with a post-stitch ridge rather than strip-by-strip construction.

title: Advanced mandala, ten rounds
subtitle: Wall hanging, table centrepiece, or shawl centrepiece in DK cotton
excerpt: Ten rounds from the magic ring build a 40 cm mandala with a flat-circle base, shell and V-stitch body, and double treble picot edge.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886). Weldon's Practical Crochet, multiple volumes.

content.text: A mandala that distorts at round 6 cannot be blocked flat at round 10. Consistent gauge from the centre outward is the one structural requirement that determines whether all ten rounds lie flat. This pattern builds a 40 cm mandala in three distinct sections: rounds 1 to 4 establish the flat-circle base using trebles in open spoke groups. Rounds 5 to 7 introduce shell and V-stitch repeats that open the fabric and add volume. Rounds 8 to 10 work double treble arches and a picot edging. Place a stitch marker at the start of every round and count before joining. Use blocking after round 10 to pull the mandala to full diameter and correct any rippling from the outer rounds.
Yarn: DK cotton, approx 180 m. Hook: 4 mm. Notions: tapestry needle, scissors, stitch markers, blocking mat and pins.

40 cm diameter in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook after blocking. Gauge matters most on this pattern, check your diameter at the end of round 4. If the circle is smaller, go up half a hook size; if larger, go down.
Double crochet, UK: short upright stitch.
Treble, UK: yarn over once before inserting hook.
Double treble, UK: yarn over twice before inserting hook.
Picot: ch3, sl st into first ch.
Make a magic ring. Ch 3. Work 11 tr into the ring. Pull the tail to close the ring. Sl st to top of ch-3 to join.
Ch 3. 1 tr in same st. Ch 1. *2 tr in next st, ch 1; repeat from * 10 more times. Sl st to top of ch-3 to join.
Sl st into ch-1 sp. Ch 3. 2 tr in same ch-1 sp. Ch 1. *3 tr in next ch-1 sp, ch 1; repeat from * 10 more times. Sl st to top of ch-3 to join.
Sl st into ch-1 sp. Ch 3. 1 tr in same sp. Ch 2. * into next ch-1 sp, ch 2; repeat from * 10 more times. 2 tr in first sp. Ch 2. Sl st to top of ch-3 to join. Check diameter: 14 cm target.
Sl st into ch-2 sp. Ch 3. 4 tr in same sp. Ch 1. *5 tr in next ch-2 sp, ch 1; repeat from * 22 more times. Sl st to top of ch-3 to join. =.
Sl st into ch-1 sp. Ch 3. 1 tr, ch 1, 2 tr in same sp. Work: * in next ch-1 sp; repeat from * around. Sl st to top of ch-3 to join.

Sl st into ch-1 sp. Ch 3. Work shell of 5 tr in 12 alternate ch-1 sps and V-stitch of in the remaining 12 ch-1 sps. Alternating shell and V-stitch throughout. Sl st to top of ch-3 to join. = =. Check diameter: 26 cm target.

Sl st to top of first shell's 3rd tr. Ch 4. 1 dtr in same st. Ch 2. *2 dtr into centre tr of next shell or into ch-1 sp of next V-stitch. Ch 2; repeat from * 22 more times. Sl st to top of ch-4 to join.
Sl st into ch-2 sp. Ch 4. 2 dtr in same sp. Ch 2. *3 dtr in next ch-2 sp, ch 2; repeat from * 22 more times. Sl st to top of ch-4 to join. Check diameter: 34 cm target.

Ch 1. 1 dc in first dtr. *Ch 3, sl st into first ch of that ch-3. 1 dc in each of next 2 dtr. Into ch-2 sp: 1 dc, picot, 1 dc. 1 dc in each of next 2 dtr. Picot. 1 dc in next dtr; repeat from * around, ending with sl st to first dc. Fasten off. Weave in end. =.

Weave in both ends using a tapestry needle. Soak the mandala in cool water for 10 minutes, squeeze out gently without wringing. And roll in a towel to remove excess moisture. Pin to a blocking mat at 40 cm diameter. Placing pins every 2 cm around the outer picot edge. Leave until fully dry. The mandala will not lie flat without blocking at this diameter.

As a standalone piece the mandala does not need joining. To use as a shawl centrepiece. Join to surrounding motifs by replacing picots on the final round with slip-stitch joins into corresponding points on adjacent motifs. Work the joining picots as: ch 1. Sl st into corresponding picot on adjacent motif, ch 1, sl st back into the current stitch.

repeats that open the fabric and add volume; rounds 8 to 10 work
at the start of every round and count before joining. Use
after round 10 to pull the mandala to full diameter and correct any rippling from the outer rounds.

title: Mandala, eight rounds
subtitle: A 30 cm wall-hanging mandala, flat-circle base, shells, V-stitches, then a picot edging
excerpt: Eight rounds give a wall-hanging mandala at 30 cm diameter. Rounds 1 to 5 work the flat-circle base; rounds 6 to 8 each introduce a new stitch texture, shells, V-stitches, then a picot edging. Blocking matters on this one: pin to a foam mat while still damp to keep the circle flat and round.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), circular motif chapter. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volumes 1-3 (1885-1890) — the round doily construction.

content.text: The eight-round mandala builds to 30 cm diameter using five rounds of flat-circle double crochet before introducing three distinct stitch textures in the final rounds: shells in round 6. V-stitch groups in round 7. And a picot edging in round 8. This is a wall-hanging piece at 30 cm. Large enough to hang as a circular panel or use as a centrepiece on a table.

Blocking matters on this one more than on the smaller mandalas. Pin to a foam mat while still damp to keep the circle flat and round. A 30 cm circle that dries unblocked will develop a gentle wave that is hard to remove afterwards. A generous steam application, then leaving flat overnight pinned at all six shell points, gives the best result.

title: Lacy mandala, eight rounds
subtitle: Open double-treble fans from round 3, a 32 cm wall piece or table centrepiece that is more air than yarn
excerpt: The lacy mandala replaces the solid double-crochet base rounds with chain-and-double-treble fans that open up the fabric from round 3 onward. By round 8 the mandala is more air than yarn, a fine-gauge wall piece or table centrepiece that photographs better than a solid version at the same diameter.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), circular lace motif chapter. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volumes 1-3 (1885-1890) — the lace doily and fan-round construction.

content.text: The lacy mandala departs from the solid double-crochet base of the standard mandalas at round 3. Switching to fan groups of double-treble stitches separated by chain-3 arches. Each round the fans expand by one or two double trebles. So by round 7 each of the six fan groups carries five double trebles flanked by chain-3 arches. Round 8 adds a picot at each outer point. The finished diameter is 32 cm. Slightly larger than the solid eight-round version because the open fans spread the fabric outward.

Blocking is not optional here. The open lace arches between fans contract as they dry. Pulling the circle in and distorting the fan shape. Pin all six outer fan tips while the piece is still damp. Then pin every chain-3 arch midpoint, apply steam. And leave overnight.

content.text: Each finished eight-round lacy mandala measures 32 cm diameter in DK-weight cotton with a 4 mm hook. After steam-blocking. The pre-block measurement will be 2 to 4 cm smaller, always measure after thorough blocking.
slip stitch, UK and US shared.
double crochet, UK; called single crochet in US patterns. Used in rounds 1 and 2 only.
treble, UK; called double crochet in US patterns. Used as anchor stitches beside fan groups.
double treble, UK; yarn over twice before inserting hook. Called triple crochet in US patterns. The main stitch in the fan rounds.
picot, ch 3, sl st into first ch. Outer edging loop on round 8.
magic ring, adjustable starting loop; no centre hole.
Worked in the round, right side facing throughout. Place a stitch marker in the first stitch of rounds 1 and 2. From round 3 onward the fan groups are their own landmarks.
Form a magic ring. Ch 1. Work 6 dc into the ring. Sl st to first dc to join. Pull tail to close ring.
Ch 1. Work 2 dc into each stitch around. Sl st to first dc to join.

Ch 4. *Ch 3, 3 dtr into next st, ch 3, dtr into next st. Ch 2*; repeat from * to * four more times. Ch 3, 3 dtr into next st, ch 3. Sl st to top of beg ch-4 to join. (6 fan groups of 3 dtr each, 6 single dtr anchor points, 12 ch-3 arches, 6 ch-2 spaces.).

Sl st into first ch-3 sp. Ch 4. 2 dtr into same sp. *Ch 3, dtr into centre of 3-dtr fan, ch 3, 3 dtr into next ch-3 sp. Ch 2. 3 dtr into next ch-3 sp*; repeat from * to * four more times. Ch 3, dtr into centre fan st, ch 3, 3 dtr into next ch-3 sp. Ch 2. Sl st to top of beg ch-4 to join. (6 single dtr points, 12 fan groups of 3 dtr, 12 ch-3 arches, 6 ch-2 spaces.).

Each round continues the fan expansion: sl st to first ch-3 sp of the previous round. Work to begin each fan. Ch 3. Dtr into each dtr of the previous-round fan; ch 3; close the fan into the next ch-3 sp; ch 2 between fan pairs. Fans grow by one dtr per side per round. So round 5 has fans of 5 dtr, round 6 of 7 dtr, round 7 of 9 dtr. (Round 7 total: 6 fans of 9 dtr, 6 anchor dtr, 12 ch-3 arches, 6 ch-2 spaces.).

stitches separated by chain-3 arches. Each round the fans expand by one or two double trebles, so by round 7 each of the six fan groups carries five double trebles flanked by chain-3 arches. Round 8 adds a
at each outer point. The finished diameter is 32 cm — slightly larger than the solid eight-round version because the open fans spread the fabric outward.

title: Mandala, three rounds
subtitle: A flat 14 cm circle with six-stitch increases and a shell finishing round, the entry point for mandala work
excerpt: The three-round mandala is a flat circle built from six-stitch increases per round in double crochet, with a shell round at round 3 that gives the radiating petal effect. At 14 cm diameter in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook, it works as a coaster, a bag base, or the central panel in a larger mandala project.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), circular motif chapter. Weldon's Practical Crochet — the doily and round-mat construction.

content.text: The three-round mandala is a flat-circle built from six-stitch increases per round in double crochet. With a shell round at round 3 that gives the radiating petal effect. This is the entry point for mandala work: the shape stays flat, the increases are consistent. And the shell round establishes the pattern that the more complex versions extend.

At 14 cm diameter in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook. The three-round mandala works as a coaster, a bag base. Or a standalone decorative panel. The shell round reads as six radiating petals. Which is the visual language all the larger mandalas develop from this foundation.

slip stitch, UK and US shared.
double crochet, UK; called single crochet in US patterns.
treble, UK; called double crochet in US patterns.
magic ring, adjustable starting loop; no centre hole.
Worked in the round, right side facing throughout. Place a stitch marker in the first stitch of each round to keep track of the round boundary. Do not turn.

definition.title: Mandala, three rounds
definition.caption: Three rounds from the magic ring. Rounds 1 and 2 flat-circle double crochet with six-stitch increases per round. Round 3: six radiating treble shell groups of 3tr each, separated by ch-2 spaces.

content.text: Fasten off, leaving a 15 cm tail. Thread through a tapestry needle and weave through 3 to 4 stitches on the wrong side of round 3. Reverse direction through 2 to 3 stitches. And trim. Weave in the magic ring tail along round 1. Steam-block flat on a blocking mat. Pin each of the six shell groups to keep the petal shape even.

The three-round mandala does not tile edge-to-edge like a square or hexagon. It is a circle, so joining into a flat fabric requires fill-in motifs or a joining row. As a standalone coaster or bag base, it needs no joining. For a blanket, join through the chain-2 spaces of adjacent shell rounds with a flat slip-stitch seam. And fill gaps with small treble triangles.
Handwash in cool water with mild soap, or machine-wash on a delicates cycle. Lay flat to dry, re-blocking the circle shape if the shell round has shifted during washing.

The five-round mandala continues the same flat-circle base for two more rounds before the shell edging. Giving a 20 cm diameter motif suited to a bag base or small wall piece. The eight-round version reaches 30 cm and introduces V-stitches in the later rounds for extra texture.

title: Meditation comfort shawl
subtitle: A large rectangle in chunky weight with alternating dc and treble columns, designed for sitting meditation
excerpt: This large rectangular shawl measures 170 cm wide by 70 cm deep in chunky weight yarn on a 6 mm hook. The stitch pattern alternates columns of double crochet and treble across each row, producing a textured surface with good body. The generous dimensions make it suitable for wrapping fully around the shoulders while seated. Suitable for crocheters who know both double crochet and treble.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. Alternating dc and treble column fabric is a widely used texture technique with no single source.

content.text: pattern throughout: each stitch in a row sits directly above the same stitch type in the row below. The result is a series of vertical raised columns across the fabric, which gives more texture and structure than plain treble alone. The wrap is large at 170 x 70 cm, designed to cover both shoulders and the lap when seated.
Because the rows contain both dc and tr, the

pattern is consistent: the foundation chain sets the width and every subsequent row is identical. The stitch multiple is 2 (one dc plus one tr), so the stitch count must be even. A count of 204 gives 170 cm at the stated gauge.

double crochet (dc): UK; the same move as US "single crochet" (sc).

The wrap is worked flat in rows. Every row follows the same sequence: dc into each dc column, tr into each tr column. The first stitch of every row is always a dc (the dc column is on the left edge when viewed from the right side on odd rows).

Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). *1 dc in the next dc. 1 tr in the next tr*; repeat from * to * across. Turn. (204 sts)
Repeat Row 2 on every row. After Row 56 the wrap measures approximately 170 x 70 cm. Fasten off.

attrs.body: The most common error in this stitch is working a dc into a tr or a tr into a dc, which breaks the column lines. After the first few rows, look down the fabric: each dc should sit directly above a dc and each tr above a tr. If the columns look diagonal, check the last row and correct before continuing.

title: Merino heirloom shawl
subtitle: An openwork treble lace triangle with a picot border in fingering-weight merino, after Weldon's Practical Crochet
excerpt: This triangular shawl uses an openwork treble lace body worked from the top centre to 155 cm wide and 72 cm deep, finishing with a two-round picot border. The fabric is worked in fingering-weight merino on a 3.25 mm hook. The pattern is adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet and requires confidence with counting open-lace rows and maintaining consistent tension.
sourceNotes: Adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 5 (1890), triangular lace shawl with picot border (Internet Archive, archive.org). Openwork lace structure confirmed against Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet lace chapter.

content.text: This shawl is based on a triangular lace construction published in Weldon's Practical Crochet in 1890. The body is an
worked in pairs of trebles separated by ch-2 bars, with ch-2 spaces between each pair. The triangle grows from a central chain ring, adding one
at each edge on every other row. A two-round

This is an advanced pattern. The lace structure requires accurate stitch counting on every row: a missed chain space or an extra treble shifts all subsequent repeats. Work in good light and check the count after every increase row. Fingering-weight merino benefits considerably from wet blocking, which opens the chain bars and sets the lace structure firmly.

attrs.body: Approximately 300 g fingering-weight merino yarn (4-ply). A 3.25 mm crochet hook (US D/3). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Stitch markers (at least 2). Blocking mat. Rust-proof blocking pins. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 24 tr x 12 rows = 10 x 10 cm in fingering-weight merino with a 3.25 mm hook, measured over plain treble fabric after blocking. Lace gauge opens up with blocking, so measure the swatch after a full wet block rather than before. The finished shawl dimensions depend on both pre-block tension and the thoroughness of blocking.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
double crochet (dc): UK; the same move as US "single crochet" (sc).
treble (tr): UK; the same move as US "double crochet" (dc).
picot: ch 3, sl st into base of chain.

The shawl is worked flat in rows. The lace repeat is: 2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr (V-pair), ch 2 between each V-pair. The central spine on odd rows is a ch-4 loop; on even rows it is a (2 tr, ch 4, 2 tr) unit. Place a stitch marker in the central chain on every row and move it up each row.
Ch 8. Sl st to form a ring.
Ch 5 (counts as tr + ch 2). 2 tr in ring. Ch 4 (centre loop, mark it). 2 tr in ring. Ch 2. 1 tr in ring. Turn. (7 tr, 2 ch-2 spaces, 1 ch-4 centre loop)

Ch 5 (counts as tr + ch 2). 2 tr in first ch-2 space. Ch 2. Into the ch-4 centre loop work: 2 tr, ch 4 (move marker), 2 tr. Ch 2. 2 tr in last ch-2 space. Ch 2. 1 tr in 3rd ch of turning ch. Turn. (15 tr, 4 ch-2 spaces, 1 ch-4 centre loop)

Ch 5 (counts as tr + ch 2). *2 tr in next ch-2 space. Ch 2*; repeat from * to * to the ch-4 centre loop. Into the ch-4 loop work: 2 tr, ch 4 (move marker), 2 tr. Ch 2. *2 tr in next ch-2 space. Ch 2*; repeat from * to * to end. 1 tr in 3rd ch of turning ch. Turn. (one V-pair added at each edge)

Repeat Row 3 on every row. Each row adds one V-pair at each edge. After approximately 86 rows the widest row contains approximately 43 V-pairs on each side of the centre loop, giving a width of 155 cm and depth of 72 cm after blocking. Continue down the right diagonal edge and up the left diagonal edge, working 1 dc into each row-end tr and 1 dc into each chain space along the edges. Join with sl st.

Fasten off and weave in all ends. title: Mitred square, basic
subtitle: A flat square built by decreasing from a corner rather than growing from the centre
excerpt: The mitred square starts at a corner cast-on and works inward through a central decrease on every right-side row, landing on a single stitch at the opposite corner. Two triangular halves meet at the diagonal spine, giving a neat seam line that reads as a design detail in stripe colourwork.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 2 (1887), mitred and diagonal squares chapter (Internet Archive). Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938) documents the mitred construction; the crochet equivalent follows the same geometry.

content.text: The mitred square builds from a corner chain downward. Shrinking by two stitches on every row through a central decrease on the diagonal. This construction is the opposite of the granny square: instead of growing outward from a ring. The mitred square collapses inward from its widest edge to a single stitch at the tip.

The finished 10 cm square has a visible spine running corner to corner. In a single colour it reads as a subtle texture line. Worked in two colours split at the midpoint. The diagonal becomes a graphic stripe. Blocks join on any edge with whip stitch or mitred spine-to-spine alignment for a chevron layout.

subtitle: Three or more horizontal stripes across the mitred construction, each two rows wide
excerpt: Stripe colours change every two rows across the mitred square, giving horizontal bands that narrow toward the tip as the row count shrinks. Three colours in rotation produce six graduated stripes; the visible diagonal spine interrupts each stripe band for a graphic finish.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 2 (1887). Stripe construction is a standard adaptation of the mitred decrease square.

content.text: The striped mitred square changes colour every two rows. Producing horizontal bands that taper toward the lower corner as the row length shrinks through the central dc2tog. Three colours in a two-row stripe sequence give six visible stripes across the 10-row square.

title: Mohair Lace Shawl
subtitle: Shell lace on a chain-space net in lace weight mohair-silk blend on a 4mm hook
excerpt: A triangular shawl in lace weight mohair-silk blend worked on a 4mm hook for an intentionally open, halo-textured fabric. The pattern is shell lace over a chain-space net: each row of treble shells sits over the chain spaces of the row below.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. Shell lace over chain-net construction is a well-established technique with no single originating source.

content.text: This shawl is a top-down triangle. It measures approximately 140cm across the top edge and 70cm from the top to the lower point. The pattern uses two row types, worked in turns. A chain-net row creates open chain spaces. A shell row follows, placing 5-treble fans into those spaces. The 4mm hook is bigger than you would normally use for lace weight yarn. This is intentional: it opens the mesh, softens the drape, and lets the mohair halo show. Mohair is less stretchy than wool. Count your stitches at the end of each row. Fix mistakes before moving on, as unpicking mohair is harder than unpicking wool.

Mohair-silk blends shed fibres into each other as you work. Cut yarn cleanly with sharp scissors and soak ends in a tiny amount of hair conditioner before weaving in if the yarn is particularly slippery.

Yarn: approximately 200g of lace weight mohair-silk blend. These yarns are very light so 200g goes further than it sounds. Hook: 4mm (used oversize deliberately). You will also need a tapestry needle, scissors, tape measure, a foam blocking mat, and rust-proof pins.

One shell repeat (5 tr into a chain space) measures approximately 5cm wide on a 4mm hook with lace weight mohair-silk. The open gauge is intentional. Do not adjust to a smaller hook to tighten the fabric: the structure of the pattern depends on the chain spaces remaining open.
Shell: 5 tr in same ch sp
Chain net: dc + ch-3 sp alternating to form the open grid

The shawl starts at the top centre. The pattern alternates between a net row (which creates the open chain spaces) and a shell row (which fills them). The triangle grows by one shell at each edge on every shell row.
Ch 8, sl st to form a ring.
Ch 3 (counts as first tr), 4 tr in ring (half-shell at edge), ch 3, dc in ring, ch 3, 5 tr in ring (shell), ch 3, dc in ring, ch 3, 5 tr in ring (edge), turn. (3 shells, 4 ch-3 sps)

Ch 5 (counts as dc + ch 3), dc in centre tr of first shell, [ch 3, dc in ch-3 sp, ch 3, dc in centre tr of next shell] across, ch 3, dc in top of turning ch, turn. (creates ch-3 sps over each shell and between)

Ch 3 (counts as first tr), 4 tr in first ch-3 sp (new edge shell), [ch 3, dc in next ch-3 sp, ch 3, shell in next ch-3 sp] across, 4 tr in last ch-3 sp (new edge shell), tr in last dc, turn. (adds 1 shell at each edge)

Alternate Row 2 (net row) with Row 3 (shell increase row). Each shell row adds 2 shells to the total. Continue until the top edge measures approximately 140cm. At the stated gauge this is approximately 14 full shell rows (28 rows total), with approximately 29 shells across the final shell row. End with a net row.
Work one final row of dc along the top edge only, placing 1 dc per stitch and 1 dc per chain space for a neat finished edge. Fasten off.

Weave in all ends on the wrong side. Because mohair halo fibres interlock, ends can be trimmed close after weaving. Block thoroughly: soak in cool water for 15 minutes, press out excess moisture in a towel (do not wring), and pin to the stated dimensions on a foam mat. Pin each shell open at its full width. The halo will bloom and the triangular shape will set properly only once fully dry.

Hand wash in cool water with a gentle detergent suitable for mohair. Do not agitate or the fibres will felt. Press out moisture in a towel, reshape, and dry flat. Re-block after each wash to restore the triangular shape.

For a similar shell-over-chain construction in a more forgiving yarn, the classic prayer shawl uses DK weight with the same principle. For a lace shawl with more complex stitch work in the same weight yarn, the baby christening shawl uses a 2.5mm hook for a much finer, closer fabric. If you want to continue with mohair, a simple dc-mesh scarf on the same 4mm hook will give you more practice managing the yarn without a stitch pattern to track.

This shawl is a top-down triangle. It measures approximately 140cm across the top edge and 70cm from the top to the lower point. The pattern uses two row types, worked in turns. A chain-net row creates open chain spaces. A shell row follows, placing 5-treble fans into those spaces. The 4mm hook is bigger than you would normally use for lace weight yarn. This is intentional: it opens the mesh, softens the drape, and lets the mohair halo show. Mohair is less stretchy than wool. Count your stitches at the end of each row. Fix mistakes before moving on, as unpicking mohair is harder than unpicking wool.

Mohair-silk blends shed fibres into each other as you work. Cut yarn cleanly with sharp scissors and soak ends in a tiny amount of hair conditioner before weaving in if the yarn is particularly slippery.

Yarn: approximately 200g of lace weight mohair-silk blend. These yarns are very light so 200g goes further than it sounds. Hook: 4mm (used oversize deliberately). You will also need a tapestry needle, scissors, tape measure, a foam blocking mat, and rust-proof pins.

One shell repeat (5 tr into a chain space) measures approximately 5cm wide on a 4mm hook with lace weight mohair-silk. The open gauge is intentional. Do not adjust to a smaller hook to tighten the fabric: the structure of the pattern depends on the chain spaces remaining open.
Shell: 5 tr in same ch sp
Chain net: dc + ch-3 sp alternating to form the open grid

The shawl starts at the top centre. The pattern alternates between a net row (which creates the open chain spaces) and a shell row (which fills them). The triangle grows by one shell at each edge on every shell row.
Ch 8, sl st to form a ring.
Ch 3 (counts as first tr), 4 tr in ring (half-shell at edge), ch 3, dc in ring, ch 3, 5 tr in ring (shell), ch 3, dc in ring, ch 3, 5 tr in ring (edge), turn. (3 shells, 4 ch-3 sps)

Ch 5 (counts as dc + ch 3), dc in centre tr of first shell, [ch 3, dc in ch-3 sp, ch 3, dc in centre tr of next shell] across, ch 3, dc in top of turning ch, turn. (creates ch-3 sps over each shell and between)

Ch 3 (counts as first tr), 4 tr in first ch-3 sp (new edge shell), [ch 3, dc in next ch-3 sp, ch 3, shell in next ch-3 sp] across, 4 tr in last ch-3 sp (new edge shell), tr in last dc, turn. (adds 1 shell at each edge)

Alternate Row 2 (net row) with Row 3 (shell increase row). Each shell row adds 2 shells to the total. Continue until the top edge measures approximately 140cm. At the stated gauge this is approximately 14 full shell rows (28 rows total), with approximately 29 shells across the final shell row. End with a net row.
Work one final row of dc along the top edge only, placing 1 dc per stitch and 1 dc per chain space for a neat finished edge. Fasten off.

Weave in all ends on the wrong side. Because mohair halo fibres interlock, ends can be trimmed close after weaving. Block thoroughly: soak in cool water for 15 minutes, press out excess moisture in a towel (do not wring), and pin to the stated dimensions on a foam mat. Pin each shell open at its full width. The halo will bloom and the triangular shape will set properly only once fully dry.

Hand wash in cool water with a gentle detergent suitable for mohair. Do not agitate or the fibres will felt. Press out moisture in a towel, reshape, and dry flat. Re-block after each wash to restore the triangular shape.

For a similar shell-over-chain construction in a more forgiving yarn, the classic prayer shawl uses DK weight with the same principle. If you want to continue with mohair, a simple dc-mesh scarf on the same 4mm hook will give you more practice managing the yarn without a stitch pattern to track.

title: Mosaic crochet rectangle shawl
subtitle: Two-colour geometric patterning in DK using back-loop-only double crochet on a 4 mm hook
excerpt: Mosaic crochet builds geometric colourwork by working back-loop-only stitches in a contrast yarn to lift a column of colour from the previous row. This rectangle shawl measures 175 cm wide by 55 cm deep in DK weight on a 4 mm hook. Two colours of yarn, one row at a time, produce a graphic repeat without ever carrying yarn across the row.
sourceNotes: Mosaic crochet technique synthesised from established BLO colourwork principles. The back-loop-only row method for two-colour geometric patterns is documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet (1886) derivatives and in the wider fibre arts canon. No single prior source.

content.text: This rectangular shawl uses mosaic crochet to place a two-colour geometric repeat across 175 cm of DK fabric on a 4 mm hook. The method works one colour per row: on main-colour rows you work standard double crochet across all stitches. On contrast rows you alternate regular dc with BLO dc at the pattern positions. The BLO stitch reaches through only the back loop. Pulling a stitch of contrast colour up through the row above it. The result is a geometric colourwork surface with no floats and no colour-carrying across rows.

You carry the unused colour loosely up the side edge rather than fastening off after every row. Keep the carry tension consistent: too tight pulls the edge in; too loose leaves loops that catch. The pattern uses a 12-stitch repeat so any multiple of 12 plus 2 edge stitches produces a full repeat. The stated cast-on of 314 stitches gives the full 175 cm at gauge.

content.text: 18 dc x 20 rows = 10 x 10 cm in DK yarn on a 4 mm hook. Measured in the mosaic pattern after blocking. Work a swatch of at least 25 stitches across at least 24 rows in the mosaic pattern. Block it. And measure the central 10 x 10 cm. Gauge in the mosaic pattern runs slightly tighter than plain dc due to the BLO rows drawing in.
ch: chain -- UK and US shared.
sl st: slip stitch -- UK and US shared.
dc: double crochet -- the same move as US "single crochet". Yarn over once, insert hook, draw up loop, yarn over, draw through both loops.
: double crochet through the back loop only. Works exactly as dc but the hook enters only the back of the top two loops.
The shawl is worked flat in rows, turning at the end of each row. Colour A rows and colour B rows alternate throughout. The ch-1 turning chain does not count as a stitch in this pattern.
Ch 1. 1 dc in 2nd ch from hook. 1 dc in each ch across. Turn.
Ch 1. 1 dc in each st across. Drop colour A to the side. Turn.
Row 3 (right side, colour B -- mosaic row)
Join colour B. Ch 1. *1 dc in each of next 6 sts. 1 BLO dc in each of next 6 sts*; repeat from * to * to last 2 sts. 1 dc in each of last 2 sts. Drop colour B to side. Turn.
Ch 1. 1 dc in each st across. Drop colour B to side. Turn.
Row 5 (right side, colour A -- mosaic row)
Pick up colour A. Ch 1. *1 BLO dc in each of next 6 sts. 1 dc in each of next 6 sts*; repeat from * to * to last 2 sts. 1 dc in each of last 2 sts. Drop colour A. Turn.
Ch 1. 1 dc in each st across. Drop colour A. Turn.

Rows 3 to 6 form the four-row mosaic repeat. Continue repeating rows 3 to 6 until the work measures 55 cm from the foundation chain. Ending with a completed colour A wrong-side row. At 20 rows per 10 cm the shawl reaches 55 cm after about 110 rows total. Fasten off both colours and weave in ends.

Weave all ends in on the wrong side. Working along the backs of several stitches in different directions so they sit flat and will not work loose. Wet-block by soaking in cool water for 10 minutes. Pressing excess water out in a towel without wringing. Then pinning to the stated dimensions on a blocking mat. Allow to dry completely before removing pins.
Handwash in cool water with a mild wool or fibre wash. Do not tumble-dry. Lay flat on a clean towel, ease to shape, and leave until dry.

Once you can read the BLO column positions confidently. Try designing your own mosaic repeat on graph paper: each pair of rows is one design row. And the BLO positions in row 3 map to the contrast columns in the finished fabric. A corner-to-corner construction uses the same BLO principle in a diagonal format. Working the rectangle in lace-weight yarn on a 3 mm hook produces a finer. More translucent fabric from the same repeat.

title: Mosaic crochet square
subtitle: Two-colour geometric patterns built from alternating rows with spike stitches
excerpt: Mosaic crochet uses two colours worked in alternating rows, one colour per row, with spike stitches reaching down into the previous same-colour row to pull up the pattern. No yarn is carried across the row, each colour simply works its own rows and the spike stitches create the colour interaction from above.
sourceNotes: Mosaic crochet is a 20th-century development of earlier alternating-row spike stitch techniques documented in Victorian needlework manuals. The mosaic principle appears in Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 4 (1889), alternate-row fancy stitch chapter.

content.text: Mosaic crochet creates two-colour geometric patterns without carrying yarn across each row. Each colour works alternate rows. The mosaic spike reaches down through the previous row to pull the current colour to the surface. Creating the colour interaction.

The square below uses a simple diamond pattern: spike stitches at the corners of a diamond shape on even rows. Shifted by one position on odd rows. Once the spike placement is understood, mosaic charts read in the same way as any two-colour stitch map.

attrs.body: About 8 g colour A and 8 g colour B in DK-weight cotton. A 4 mm hook. Tapestry needle and scissors.

Work dc with mosaic spikes at shifted positions per chart. Continue alternating colours for 10 rows total, placing spikes per the diamond chart. Fasten off.
For simultaneous two-colour work, try the tapestry crochet square. For a different geometric approach, work the corner-to-corner diamond motif.

title: Chevron round motif
subtitle: Six increase points over four rounds giving a star-with-points disc
excerpt: Four rounds of double crochet with six concentrated increase points produce a 13 cm disc with clearly projecting points, sitting flat with blocking.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886). Weldon's Practical Crochet.

content.text: The chevron round works three double crochets into the same stitch at six evenly-spaced positions each round. Producing points that project outward while the fabric between them stays flat. Unlike the six-point star, this motif uses double crochet throughout. So the points are lower and the shape is a spiked disc rather than a sharp star. Blocking with a pin at each of the six points sharpens the profile considerably.
Yarn: DK weight cotton, about 26 m per motif. Hook: 4 mm. Notions: tapestry needle, scissors, blocking mat, 6 blocking pins.
4 rounds in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook = 13 cm across the widest point-to-point measurement. The disc between points is about 10 cm.
Mark the centre stitch of each triple-increase point with a stitch marker in round 2 and move it up each round. Ch 1 at the start of each round does not count as a stitch.
Make a magic ring. Ch 1. Work 12 dc into the ring. Pull tail to close. Join with sl st to first dc.
Ch 1. *Work 3 dc into the next st. 1 dc in the next st*; repeat from * to * 5 more times. Join with sl st.
*3 dc into the centre dc of the point group. 1 dc in each of the next 3 sts*; repeat from * to * 5 more times. Join with sl st.
*3 dc into the centre dc of the point group. 1 dc in each of the next 5 sts*; repeat from * to * 5 more times. Join with sl st. Fasten off.
Weave in tails. Wet-block by soaking. Removing excess moisture. Then pinning one pin at the tip of each of the six points and easing the sides between points to a smooth curve. Leave overnight.
Join chevron round motifs tip-to-tip using a sl st join at the point stitch. The curved bays between points of adjacent motifs form a negative-space pattern when several motifs are joined together.
Hand wash or machine wash at 30 °C gentle cycle. Pin to shape after each wash if the point definition needs refreshing.

title: Flat circle motif
subtitle: A classic six-increase disc in double crochet
excerpt: Four rounds of evenly distributed double crochet increases produce a flat 12 cm disc with no curling or puckering.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886). Weldon's Practical Crochet.

content.text: The flat circle motif relies on one rule: six double crochet increases per round. Staggered so they do not land in the same position twice. Stacking all increases in six columns produces a hexagon. Staggering them round by round keeps the edge circular. Four rounds from a magic ring give a 12 cm disc in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook. The motif is the base component for many crocheted flat shapes: rugs, coasters, applique flowers. And the foundation round of beret crowns.
Yarn: DK weight cotton, about 20 m per motif. Hook: 4 mm. Notions: tapestry needle, scissors, stitch marker, blocking mat and pins.

4 rounds in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook = 12 cm diameter. Gauge is not critical for a decorative motif, but a tighter tension produces a firmer, less pliable disc. If the circle cups, go up a hook size; if it ruffles, go down.
Make a magic ring. Ch 1. Work 6 dc into the ring. Pull the tail to close the ring. Join with a slip stitch to the first dc.
Ch 1. Work 2 dc in each of the 6 sts around. Join with sl st to first dc.
Ch 1. *2 dc in next st, 1 dc in next st*; repeat from * to * around. Join with sl st.
Ch 1. *2 dc in next st. 1 dc in each of next 2 sts*; repeat from * to * around. Join with sl st. Fasten off.

Cut yarn, leaving a 15 cm tail. Thread onto a tapestry needle and weave through the back loops of the final round at least twice to secure. Trim tail. Wet-block the motif by soaking in cold water. Pressing out excess moisture in a towel, then pinning flat to a blocking mat. Leave to dry completely.

Flat circles join to each other and to granny squares with a whip stitch through the outer edge loops. Or with a join-as-you-go slip stitch on the last round. When joining multiple circles. The gaps between them form decorative diamond shapes that can be filled with small chain-and-slip-stitch fill motifs.
Cotton DK: machine wash at 30 °C on a gentle cycle, or hand wash in cool water. Lay flat to dry. Do not tumble dry cotton motifs as heat causes them to pucker and shrink unevenly.

title: Solid treble granny square
subtitle: A granny square with no chain spaces between clusters
excerpt: Four rounds of treble clusters with no chain-1 gaps between them produce a fully solid 10 x 10 cm square, heavier and denser than a standard granny.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886). Weldon's Practical Crochet.

content.text: The solid treble granny removes both the chain-1 side gaps and the chain-2 corner space on the sides. Replacing every gap with a single treble worked into the top of the previous cluster stitch. Only the four corner ch-2 spaces remain open, as they are needed to keep the corners square. The result is a solid fabric, heavier and more insulating than a standard granny. And well suited for pot holders, cold-weather blankets. And any project where draping opacity rather than lightness is the goal.
Yarn: DK weight cotton, about 28 m per motif. Hook: 4 mm. Notions: tapestry needle, scissors, blocking mat and pins.

excerpt: Four rounds of standard granny corners combined with chain-3 arch sides produce an 11 x 11 cm open-work square that is fast to work and delicate in appearance.

title: Puff stitch square motif
subtitle: Granny corners with a raised puff at the centre of each side
excerpt: Four rounds of standard granny corners combined with a puff stitch at the centre of each side produce an 11 x 11 cm square with a rounded, pillow-like texture.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886). Weldon's Practical Crochet.

content.text: The puff stitch square places a puff stitch at the centre of each side on every round above round 1. Contrasting a soft, pillow-like bulge against the flat treble clusters and chain-2 corners. Puffs are softer and more rounded than bobbles. They bulge gently forward rather than projecting at a sharp angle. Giving the square a cushion-like character. The puff is worked as five half-completed trebles closed together: yarn over. Insert hook. Pull through. Yarn over, pull through two loops repeated five times, then yarn over and pull through all loops at once.
Yarn: DK weight cotton, about 32 m per motif. Hook: 4 mm. Notions: tapestry needle, scissors.

4 rounds in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook = 11 x 11 cm. Puffs pull in the fabric at their position slightly. If your puffs are very tight the square may measure smaller than 11 cm. Ease the tension on the closing loop of each puff stitch if needed.
Note: ch 3 counts as first tr throughout. Puff stitch: x5, yarn over and pull through all 11 loops on hook. Ch 1 to close.
Make a magic ring. Ch 3. 2 tr into ring. Ch 2. **; repeat 3 more times. Pull tail to close. Join with sl st to top of ch 3.
Sl st to corner sp. Ch 3. * into corner sp. Ch 1, work 1 puff stitch into the ch-1 sp between the two side clusters, ch 1*. Repeat from * to * 3 more times. Join with sl st.

Sl st to corner sp. Ch 3. * into corner sp. Along each side: ch 1. 3 tr into next ch-1 sp. Ch 1, 1 puff into top of puff from round 2, ch 1, 3 tr into next ch-1 sp, ch 1*. Repeat from * to * 3 more times. Join with sl st.
Sl st to corner sp. Ch 3. * into corner sp. Along each side: ch 1. 3 tr, ch 1, 3 tr, ch 1, 1 puff, ch 1, 3 tr, ch 1, 3 tr, ch 1*. Repeat from * to * 3 more times. Join with sl st. Fasten off.
Weave in tails. Light wet-blocking sets the corners square; avoid flattening the puffs under heavy tension as you pin. The puff dimension is part of the intended texture.
Join with a sl st seam through the top of the outer treble clusters on each side. Or use a join-as-you-go at the ch-1 spaces of the final round.
Hand wash in cool water. The puff stitches can flatten with machine washing; hand washing and reshaping while damp preserves their rounded profile.

The sunburst square motif also uses a raised element at the centre. But radiating outward rather than sitting at the sides. The lace square motif replaces the side clusters with chain arches for a completely different texture in the same square format.

title: Spiral round motif
subtitle: Continuous rounds without a join, tracked with a stitch marker
excerpt: Four rounds of continuous double crochet increases produce a 10 cm disc with no join bump, tracked by a single stitch marker.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886). Weldon's Practical Crochet.

content.text: The spiral round eliminates the join-bump that marks the start of each round in standard joined construction by never stopping to slip stitch. The hook works continuously; a stitch marker moved up at the start of each revolution keeps count. The finished disc looks identical to a joined-round circle from the top but has no visible jog at the round start. Which matters for colourwork and for motifs where the join would fall in an obvious position.
Yarn: DK weight cotton, about 20 m per motif. Hook: 4 mm. Notions: tapestry needle, scissors, stitch marker.
4 rounds in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook = 10 cm diameter. The stitch count and increase pattern are identical to the flat circle motif; only the construction method differs.
Slip stitch, used only to close the final round.
Make a magic ring. Work 6 dc into the ring. Pull the tail to close. Do not join. Place a stitch marker in the first dc of this round.
Work 2 dc in each of the 6 sts around. When you reach the stitch marker, move it to the first dc of this new round.
*2 dc in next st, 1 dc in next st*; repeat from * to * around. Move marker.
*2 dc in next st. 1 dc in each of next 2 sts*; repeat from * to * around. When you return to the marker, sl st to the next dc to close the final round. Fasten off.
Weave in both tails. The tail at the magic ring should be woven through the central stitches in two different directions to prevent the ring from loosening over time. Block flat if needed.
Join spiral circles the same way as joined-round circles: whip stitch or mattress stitch through the outer edges. The absence of a join seam on the face of the motif is the only visible difference.
Machine wash at 30 °C on a gentle cycle. Lay flat to dry.

Spiral construction also works for amigurumi bodies, hats, and tubular bags. Once the spiral flat circle is comfortable. Try working the same increase sequence in a colour-change yarn to see how the spiral construction handles the stripe jog differently from joined rounds.

title: Six-point star motif
subtitle: Sharp treble increases at six positions over four rounds
excerpt: Four rounds of treble crochet with triple-increase points at six evenly-spaced positions produce a 14 cm star that blocks flat with clearly projecting points.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886). Weldon's Practical Crochet.

content.text: The six-point star concentrates all its increases at six positions by working three trebles into the leading stitch of each point column on every round. Letting all other stitches stay at one. The points project clearly by round 3 and are fully defined by round 4. Blocking with a pin at the tip of each point is essential: the yarn wants to round the points unless it is pinned and dried under tension.
Yarn: DK weight cotton, about 30 m per motif. Hook: 4 mm. Notions: tapestry needle, scissors, blocking mat, 6 blocking pins.
4 rounds in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook = 14 cm point-to-point after blocking. Before blocking the points may measure only 11 cm; pinning each point individually under tension corrects this.
Note: ch 3 counts as first tr throughout. Mark the tip stitch of each point with a stitch marker on round 2 and move the markers up each round to keep track of the six point columns.
Make a magic ring. Ch 3. Work 11 tr into the ring. Pull tail to close. Join with sl st to top of ch 3.
Ch 3. *Work 3 tr into the next st. 1 tr in the next st*; repeat from * to * 5 more times. Join with sl st to top of ch 3. (24 tr, 6 groups of 3 tr at points, 6 single tr between points.).
Ch 3. *Work 3 tr into the first tr of the point group. 1 tr in each of the next 2 sts of the point group. 1 tr in the between-point tr*; repeat from * to * 5 more times. Join with sl st.
Ch 3. *Work 3 tr into the tip tr of the point. 1 tr in each of the next 4 sts*; repeat from * to * 5 more times. Join with sl st to top of ch 3. Fasten off.

Weave in tails. Wet-block by soaking, pressing out moisture, then pinning the motif to the blocking mat. Place one pin at the very tip of each of the six points and two pins on each side of the indentation between points to set the star silhouette. Leave to dry fully before unpinning.
Six-point stars join tip-to-tip at the point stitches, with a sl st join or a short chain link. The spaces between the points of adjacent stars form a secondary pattern of diamond-shaped gaps.
Hand wash in cool water. Block again after each wash to maintain the point shape.

title: Sunburst square motif
subtitle: Double treble spikes radiating from the magic ring into a granny square
excerpt: Double treble spikes worked back into the magic ring in round 2 create a spiked starburst at the centre of a standard granny square, producing a 12 x 12 cm motif.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886). Weldon's Practical Crochet.

content.text: The sunburst square works double treble spikes back into the magic ring in round 2. Producing tall spikes that radiate inward toward the centre and stand above the surrounding trebles of round 1. Working into the ring rather than into the round-1 stitches pulls the spike bases toward the centre. Giving a true starburst appearance. Rounds 3 and 4 return to standard granny construction. So the square edges are conventional and compatible with any granny blanket.
Yarn: DK weight cotton, about 35 m per motif. Hook: 4 mm. Notions: tapestry needle, scissors, blocking mat and pins.
4 rounds in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook = 12 x 12 cm. The spike round does not add much to the overall diameter. But it makes the centre visually much more prominent.
Note: ch 3 counts as first tr throughout rounds 1, 3, and 4. Double treble: yarn over three times, insert hook, four times.
Make a magic ring. Ch 3. Work 11 tr into the ring. Pull tail to close. Join with sl st to top of ch 3.

*Ch 1. Work 1 dtr directly into the magic ring. Ch 1. Sl st into the next tr of round 1*; repeat from * to * 11 more times. Each sl st anchors the spike to the round-1 treble. And each dtr stands above as a spike leaning back toward the centre.

Work this round into the spaces between the spike bases, at the level of round 1. Join yarn to the space between two spikes at a corner position. Ch 3. * into the corner space. Ch 1. 3 tr into the side space between the next pair of spikes. Ch 1*; repeat from * to * 3 more times. Join with sl st to top of ch 3.
Sl st to corner sp. Ch 3. * into corner sp. Ch 1. 3 tr into ch-1 side sp. Ch 1. 3 tr into next ch-1 side sp. Ch 1*; repeat from * to * 3 more times. Join with sl st to top of ch 3. Fasten off.

Weave in tails carefully; the spike round creates extra thread ends at the ring. Block flat with the four corners pinned to 90 degrees. The spikes will remain slightly raised from the face of the motif even when blocked. This is the intended texture.

The outer rounds are standard granny construction. So sunburst squares join to any other granny square using the same sl st or whip-stitch methods. The spike centre is contained within rounds 1 and 2 and does not affect joining.
Hand wash in cool water. Lay flat to dry. The dtr spikes are robust and hold their shape well after washing.

title: Neck cowl shawl hybrid
subtitle: A short wide rectangle in treble stitch with a picot border, worn as a neck scarf or draped shawl
excerpt: This DK-weight rectangle measures 130 cm wide by 30 cm deep and sits high on the shoulders, working equally well as a neck scarf, a looped cowl, or a small shawl. The body is worked in treble stitch on a 4 mm hook; a picot edging runs along all four sides. Finished size makes it a useful everyday piece that packs flat.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. Treble rectangle construction with picot edge is a widely established technique with no single source.

content.text: This rectangle works up quickly on a 4 mm hook in DK yarn and sits at the borderline between a neck scarf and a shawl. At 130 cm wide it will wrap once around the neck and still drape down the front, or lie flat across both shoulders with the ends tucked in. The treble body produces an open, lightly draped fabric; the picot border adds definition without bulk.
The construction is a plain rectangle: a foundation chain sets the width, then rows of treble build the depth. The
counts as the first treble throughout, which keeps each row clean and even. The picot border is worked as a final round around all four sides once the rectangle is complete.

attrs.body: Approximately 200 g DK-weight yarn. A 4 mm crochet hook (US G/6). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Tape measure. Optional: blocking mat and pins.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 18 tr x 10 rows = 10 x 10 cm in DK yarn with a 4 mm hook, measured unstretched. Work a swatch of at least 24 stitches and 14 rows, then measure the central 10 x 10 cm area. Adjust hook size if needed: one stitch per 10 cm off the stated gauge changes the finished width by about 7 cm.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
treble (tr): UK; the same move as US "double crochet" (dc).
: ch 3, sl st into base of chain.

The rectangle is worked flat in rows. The ch-3 turning chain at the start of every row counts as the first treble. Do not work into the top of that turning chain on the following row. Skip it and work the last stitch of every row into the top of the previous row's turning chain.
Ch 238. (This becomes 235 trebles after the first row, which gives 130 cm at the stated gauge.)
Ch 3 (counts as first tr). 1 tr in the 4th ch from hook. 1 tr in each remaining ch. Turn. (235 sts)
Ch 3 (counts as first tr). 1 tr in each st across, working the final tr into the top of the turning ch from the previous row. Turn. (235 sts)
After Row 30, the rectangle measures approximately 130 cm x 30 cm. Do not fasten off.
Work the picot border as a continuous round around all four edges. The sequence at corners allows the work to turn without puckering.

Round 1: do not turn. Join yarn at the top right corner. Work 1 dc (UK double crochet, the same move as US single crochet) into each stitch along the top edge to the corner. At each corner work (1 dc, ch 2, 1 dc) into the corner stitch. Continue down the short right side, working 1 dc into each row-end. Repeat along the bottom edge and up the short left side. Join with sl st to the first dc.

Round 2 (picot round): *1 dc in next dc, ch 3, sl st back into base of ch (1 picot made), 1 dc in each of next 2 dc*; repeat from * to * all the way round. At each corner chain space, work (1 dc, ch 3, sl st, 1 dc). Join with sl st. Fasten off.

Fasten off and weave in all ends securely through the backs of several stitches in different directions. Wet-block by soaking the finished piece in cool water for 10 minutes, gently pressing out excess water in a towel, then pinning to the finished dimensions on a blocking mat. Leave until completely dry before unpinning.
Handwash in cool water with mild wool wash. Lay flat to dry. Do not tumble-dry or hang while wet.

Work the same rectangle in a sport-weight linen blend on a 3.5 mm hook for a lighter summer version. Replace the plain treble body with a V-stitch (tr, ch 1, tr into the same st) for a more open mesh. A contrast colour picot border in a second DK shade gives a clean, two-tone finish.

title: Overlay stitch square
subtitle: Colour patterns applied over a solid base fabric using front-post spike stitches
excerpt: The overlay square crochets a plain dc grid first, then works front-post stitches in a contrast colour across the surface on a second pass, the overlay layer sits on top of the base without structurally changing it. Geometric diamond and stripe patterns emerge from the overlay without any colour-change complexity in the base.
sourceNotes: Overlay crochet techniques appear in Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 5 (1890), decorative surface chapter (Internet Archive).

content.text: The overlay stitch separates construction from decoration: work the base square in dc first. Then apply the pattern as a second pass in a contrast colour. No colour changes during the base rows; no complex counting while adding the pattern.

The front-post trebles of the overlay reach down one or two rows into the base fabric. Sitting proud of the surface. A diamond outline uses four overlay stitches placed at the corners of a tilted square. A stripe uses a row of overlay stitches across the full width every three rows.

On rows 4 and 6, work at positions 3 and 13. On rows 3 and 7, at positions 5 and 11. On rows 2 and 8, at positions 7 and 9. On row 1, a single fptr at position 8 closes the diamond.
For a fully integrated two-colour pattern, try the tapestry crochet square. Where both colours are worked simultaneously into each row.

title: Pineapple-centre square
subtitle: A square motif with a lace pineapple panel worked into the centre rounds
excerpt: A pineapple motif grows from the magic ring and fills the centre of the square, its graduated treble fans pointing outward from the magic ring. The outer rounds close the pineapple into a square with standard corner clusters. The pineapple read is strongest in a single colour against a plain background yarn.
sourceNotes: Pineapple crochet is a classic American and Victorian motif documented extensively in Weldon's Practical Needlework, Volume 7 (1892), and in early American thread-crochet booklets from the 1890s.

content.text: grow from the magic ring, one in each diagonal direction. Rounds 3 through 5 widen then narrow each fan, with each successive round working into alternate treble tops to decrease the fan by two stitches. The outer two rounds close the motif into a square.

Use fine cotton thread and a 2.5 mm hook for the classic thread-crochet scale. In DK yarn on a 4 mm hook the pineapple reads at 15 cm across, still useful but the detail is less precise. Block the finished motif firmly with all pineapple points pinned open.

Round 4: *dc between tr 1 and 2, ch 3, dc between tr 3 and 4, ch 3, dc between tr 5 and 6; ch 5* across each fan. (Fans narrow.)
Round 5: work 5 tr into each ch-5 sp (fan tips). Round 6: dc across, working corners with ch 2. Round 7: granny-style corner cluster border. Fasten off.

subtitle: A rectangle of traditional pineapple motifs in lace-weight yarn, worked across a long foundation chain
excerpt: Pineapple crochet is a Victorian lace tradition using clusters of double trebles fanned from a chain space to form a tapered pineapple shape. This rectangle works four pineapple motifs side by side across a 185 cm width, with a chain-arch mesh between them. Yarn is lace-weight on a 2.75 mm hook. The pattern is adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet (1886). Finished size is approximately 185 cm wide by 50 cm deep.
sourceNotes: Pineapple motif construction adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 3 (1887), 'Pineapple Crochet' and 'Shawl in Pineapple Stitch', Internet Archive. Double treble cluster fan arrangement updated for modern lace-weight yarn proportions.

content.text: Pineapple crochet is one of the most recognisable Victorian lace patterns. Each pineapple motif begins with a wide fan of double trebles at the base. Then tapers row by row through progressively smaller clusters until a single stitch closes the tip. This rectangular shawl places four pineapple motifs side by side with chain-arch mesh filling the spaces between them. The construction works from the wide base of the pineapples upward toward the tips. Then returns to base level on the flip side to close each motif symmetrically.

A double treble is wound three times before inserting the hook. Then drawn through pairs of loops four times. The pineapple base fan is 9 dtr fanned into a single chain space. Each next row pairs adjacent dtr into dtr clusters. Reducing the count until one final dc closes the pineapple tip.

attrs.body: about 350 g lace-weight yarn. A 2.75 mm crochet hook. Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Stitch markers. Blocking mat. Blocking pins. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: One complete pineapple motif = about 45 cm long x 10 cm wide at the widest point. After blocking. The chain-arch mesh between motifs: 4 arch rows = 5 cm deep. Work a single pineapple swatch and block it before beginning the full shawl.
slip stitch: UK and US shared.
double crochet: UK; the same move as US "single crochet".
treble: UK; the same move as US "double crochet".
double treble: UK; the same move as US "treble crochet". Yarn over 3 times before inserting hook.
double treble cluster: 2 dtr into the same space, joined at the top.

The shawl is worked flat. The foundation chain runs the full 185 cm width. The pineapple motifs are established in rows 1 to 3. Then taper through rows 4 to 12, with chain arches filling the spaces between motifs throughout. Four motifs sit at equal spacing across the width.
Ch 277. Mark every 69th chain: these mark the centre chain of each pineapple base.

Ch 5. Work 8 more dtr into the first marked chain. *Ch 5, skip 8 ch, 1 dc in next ch, ch 5, skip 8 ch. 9 dtr into the next marked chain*; repeat from * to * for remaining 3 pineapples. Ch 2, 1 tr in last ch to close. Turn.

Ch 4. Work [dtr-cl into same space as ch-4. Ch 1] across the first pineapple fan. Working a dtr-cl over each adjacent pair of dtr: 8 dtr-cl with ch-1 between each. *Ch 5, 1 dc into the mesh arch dc, ch 5. Work 8 dtr-cl with ch-1 between over next pineapple fan*; repeat across. Ch 2, 1 tr to close. Turn.

On each next row. Pair adjacent dtr-cl from the row below into a new dtr-cl. Reducing the cluster count by one on each side of the pineapple: row 3 has 7 dtr-cl, row 4 has 6. And so on down to row 11 with 1 dtr-cl. Between pineapples. The chain-arch mesh continues with ch 5 on each side of the mesh dc. Increasing the arch length by 1 ch every two rows to keep the mesh proportional. The stitch count per pineapple reduces by 1 dtr-cl each row.
Ch 4. *1 dc into the top of the single remaining dtr-cl. Ch 7, 1 dc into mesh arch dc, ch 7*; repeat across. 1 tr to close. Turn.
Work 4 rows of ch-5 arch mesh across the full width to bring the shawl depth to 50 cm: *1 dc into arch. Ch 5*; repeat across each row. Fasten off after row 16.

Fasten off and weave in all ends through the solid parts of the mesh. Wet-block by soaking fully in cool water for 15 minutes. Pressing gently, then pinning to 185 x 50 cm on a blocking mat. Pin each pineapple tip outward and pin the arch loops open. Leave until completely dry before unpinning.
Handwash in cool water with mild wool wash. Do not wring or tumble-dry. Press excess water out in a towel and lay flat to dry, repinning the pineapple tips if needed.

Work the same pineapple arrangement in a top-down triangle. Add one pineapple motif on each triangle increase row to grow the design. A single large pineapple motif worked as a standalone panel works well as a cushion cover centrepiece or a framed textile piece.

title: Pinwheel motif, basic
subtitle: A flat hexagonal motif with six angled blade sections worked in the round
excerpt: Six blade sections radiate from the centre ring and angle across the motif in the same direction, giving the pinwheel its rotating appearance. Each blade is a treble cluster worked into the previous round at an offset, pulling the fabric into the characteristic twist that holds flat after blocking.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 3 (1888), pinwheel motif construction (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), rotating-blade motif section.

content.text: The pinwheel motif works treble clusters into offset chain spaces on each round. Twisting six blade sections clockwise as the motif grows. The offset is small, each cluster enters the chain space from the adjacent blade rather than its own. But the cumulative effect across three rounds gives a clear propeller shape.
Use two colours to make the blades stand out: work rounds 1 and 2 in colour A and the border round in colour B. Block firmly, the offset construction wants to cup slightly before pinning flat.

attrs.body: About 8 g DK-weight cotton across one or two colours. A 4 mm hook. Tapestry needle, scissors, blocking mat, pins.
attrs.title: Materials for one motif

content.text: Magic ring. Ch 3. 1 tr into ring. *Ch 1, 2 tr into ring.* Rep from * 4 more times. Ch 1, sl st to top of beg ch-3. Pull to close ring.
Sl st into first ch-1 sp. Ch 3. Work 2 more tr into the NEXT ch-1 sp. *Ch 1, skip back one ch-1 sp, 3 tr into the following ch-1 sp.* Rep from * 4 more times. Ch 1, sl st to top of beg ch-3.
Join border colour. *3 dc into the next ch-1 sp. Ch 2.* Rep from * around all 6 sp. Sl st to join.
Add two more rounds with the offset method for the lacy pinwheel. Or work a fourth round of trebles per blade for the dense pinwheel.

title: Pinwheel motif, lacy
subtitle: Extended chain arches between blade tips give an open, airy pinwheel in 4-ply
excerpt: Chain-4 arches between each blade tip replace the dc border of the basic pinwheel, opening up the outer edge into a scalloped lace ring. Five rounds in 4-ply cotton produce a 10 cm motif light enough for shawls and collar edgings.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Needlework: Crochet, Volume 5 (1890), lace pinwheel chapter (Internet Archive).

content.text: The lacy pinwheel extends the basic offset-blade construction to five rounds. Replacing the dc border with chain arches between each blade tip. The outer edge becomes a scalloped lace ring rather than a solid dc border.
Work in 4-ply cotton on a 3 mm hook. The finer yarn keeps the arches delicate. Pin the motif firmly when wet-blocking, the chain arches need stretching open to show the scallop shape properly.
