title: Classic Prayer Shawl
subtitle: Simple shell-and-chain lace in DK weight, worked as a top-down triangle
excerpt: A classic triangular shawl worked from the centre top outward in a repeating shell-and-chain pattern. DK weight yarn on a 4mm hook produces open, drapey fabric. Based on a traditional construction documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet.
sourceNotes: Construction and stitch arrangement adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet (published 1886-1897), now in the public domain. Pattern updated to modern UK crochet terminology.

content.text: This shawl is a straightforward top-down triangle measuring about 165cm across the top edge and 65cm from the top to the lower point. You begin at the centre top with a small chain. Then work outward in rows, adding a shell at each side on every pattern row. The stitch pattern is a repeating sequence of 5-treble shells separated by chain spaces. DK weight yarn on a 4mm hook gives an open, drapey fabric. Construction is adapted from a classic triangular shawl documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet. A late nineteenth-century needlework series now in the public domain.

Yarn: about 450g of DK weight yarn (a smooth wool, cotton-blend, or bamboo-blend shows the shell pattern clearly). Hook: 4mm. You will also need a tapestry needle, scissors, and a tape measure. A foam blocking mat and rust-proof pins are useful for the final shaping.

One shell repeat measures about 5cm wide on a 4mm hook over the shell-and-chain pattern. Tension is not critical for a shawl: a tighter tension will produce a smaller. Denser piece; a looser tension will produce a larger, more open one.
Shell: 5 tr in same ch sp.

The shawl grows by two shells per right-side row: one shell is added at each edge. The centre stitch is marked and a shell always sits at the centre. Stitch counts given below refer to shells, not individual stitches, to keep the instructions readable.
Ch 6, sl st to form a ring.
Ch 4, [5 tr in ring, ch 2] twice, tr in ring, turn.
Ch 1, dc in first tr, ch 2, shell in next ch-2 sp, ch 2, dc in top of centre tr, ch 2, shell in next ch-2 sp, ch 2, dc in 3rd ch of turning ch, turn.
Ch 4, shell in first ch-2 sp, [ch 2, shell in next ch-2 sp] to last sp, ch 1, tr in last dc, turn.
Ch 1, dc in top of turning ch, [ch 2, shell in next ch-2 sp] across, ch 2, dc in 3rd ch of turning ch, turn.

Alternate Row 3 with Row 4, adding one extra shell on every right-side row. Continue until you have about 30 shells across one RS row. Or until the piece measures 165cm across the top edge. The increase rows are: ch 4 at start. Add a shell in the first ch sp, work shells across, ch 1, tr at end. The plain WS rows: dc at each edge, shells across. End with a WS row.
Work one round of dc evenly around the entire shawl edge. At each corner of the triangle, work 3 dc into the corner stitch to keep the fabric flat. Fasten off.

Weave in all ends securely on the wrong side. Block by soaking in cool water and pressing out excess moisture in a towel. Pin to the stated dimensions on a foam mat. Easing the top edge straight and the lower point sharp. Allow to dry fully before unpinning. Blocking opens the lace pattern and defines the triangular shape.
Hand wash in cool water with a gentle detergent. Reshape and dry flat. Press gently with a damp cloth if needed. Check the yarn label for fibre-specific guidance.

This pattern establishes the core skill of working into chain spaces rather than into stitch tops. Once that feels reliable, the V-stitch triangle shawl uses a similar top-down construction with a different increase structure. For a denser triangular fabric, try a DK asymmetric wedge where increases happen on one edge only. For a finer lace result, the mohair lace shawl uses the same shell-over-chain-net principle in lace weight yarn.

title: Puff stitch rectangle wrap
subtitle: Alternating 5-loop puff stitches and chain spaces in aran weight on a 5 mm hook, 170 cm x 55 cm
excerpt: A five-loop puff stitch creates a rounded, bobble-like cluster by drawing up five loops in the same stitch before closing them together. Set against chain spaces, the puffs sit in a regular grid that gives the fabric both texture and drape. This rectangle wrap uses aran weight yarn on a 5 mm hook and measures 170 cm wide by 55 cm deep.
sourceNotes: Puff stitch rectangle construction synthesised for Homemade. The five-loop puff stitch worked in alternating rows with chain-1 spaces is a standard fibre arts technique with no single original source.

content.text: This rectangular wrap is worked flat in rows, using an alternating pattern of

and chain spaces on every right-side row, with double crochet rows on every wrong-side row. Each puff uses five loops drawn up in the same space. The ch-1 that closes each puff counts as the chain space for the following row, so the puffs on alternate rows sit directly above the chain spaces of the previous puff row.

Aran weight yarn on a 5 mm hook produces substantial, warm fabric. The puff stitch draws in more yarn than a plain row, so tension matters: measure your gauge swatch across the full 10-repeat width before committing to the cast-on count. The stated foundation chain of 172 stitches gives 85 puff positions per puff row at gauge.

attrs.body: Approximately 600 g aran-weight yarn (a smooth, lightly twisted yarn shows the puff shapes most clearly). A 5 mm hook (US H/8). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Stitch markers. Blocking mat and pins. Tape measure.

content.text: 1 puff stitch + 1 ch-1 space = 2 cm wide; 1 puff row + 1 plain row = 2 cm tall. Over 10 puff repeats the work measures 20 cm wide. Work a swatch of at least 12 puff repeats across and 10 rows tall in the full puff-and-plain pattern, block it, and measure the central 10-repeat width and 5-row height.

sl st: slip stitch -- UK and US shared.
dc: double crochet (UK) -- worked on every plain row. The same move as US single crochet (sc).
: (yarn over, insert hook in ch-1 space, draw up a loop to 1 cm height) 5 times -- 11 loops on hook -- yarn over, draw through all 11 loops. Ch 1 to secure.

The wrap is worked from one short end to the other (the 55 cm measurement builds up over rows). The long measurement (170 cm) is the foundation chain width. The ch-1 turning chain does not count as a stitch in this pattern.

title: Ripple Chevron Shawl
subtitle: Traditional ripple stitch triangle in aran weight, increasing from the top down
excerpt: A triangular shawl worked in the classic ripple stitch: paired increases form the peaks and paired decreases form the valleys of each chevron row. Aran weight on a 5mm hook produces a bold, structured fabric with clear directional movement.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. Ripple chevron stitch is a well-established crochet technique with no single originating source.

content.text: This shawl is a top-down triangle measuring about 155cm across the top edge and 70cm from the top to the lower point. It is worked in the traditional ripple stitch: each row has alternating peaks. Where you place 3 trebles into one stitch. And valleys, where you work two trebles together twice in succession. The triangle grows because the outer two stitches of every row are worked as increases rather than as decreases. Adding one peak at each side on every other row. Aran weight yarn on a 5mm hook produces a firm, structured fabric with bold chevron movement. The pattern requires counting carefully: each peak and each valley must occur in the correct place for the chevron columns to align.

Yarn: about 550g of aran weight yarn. A smooth, lightly spun yarn shows the chevron ridges well. Hook: 5mm. You will also need a tapestry needle, scissors, a tape measure. And optional stitch markers, blocking mat, and rust-proof pins.

One ripple repeat measures about 7cm wide and 2 rows measure about 5cm in height. Using a 5mm hook over aran weight ripple stitch. Work a flat swatch of at least 30 stitches to check your tension before starting the full triangle.
Ripple: alternating 3-in-1 increases and tr2tog decreases.

Each ripple repeat is 10 stitches: 3 tr at the peak. Tr2tog twice for the valley, then 3 tr at the next peak. The triangle starts with one small repeat and grows by adding a repeat at each edge on every increase row. The ch-3 turning chain counts as the first tr throughout.
Ch 3, 2 tr in 4th ch from hook, tr in next 3 ch, tr2tog twice, tr in next 3 ch, 3 tr in last ch, turn.
Ch 3, 2 tr in first st, tr in next 3 sts, tr2tog twice, tr in next 3 sts, 3 tr in last st, turn.
Ch 3, 3 tr in first st, tr in next 3 sts, [tr2tog twice, tr in next 3 sts, 3 tr in peak st, tr in next 3 sts] across, 3 tr in top of turning ch, turn.

On every RS row. Add a new peak at each outer edge by working 3 tr into the first st and 3 tr into the top of the final turning ch. On every WS row, maintain the stitch count by working 2 tr at each outer edge. The valley positions stay fixed within each repeat. Continue adding repeats until the top edge measures about 155cm, ending on a WS row.

At the stated gauge, about 22 full ripple repeats across the top row gives a 155cm edge width. This requires about 44 total rows. Check width against the tape measure after every 10 rows and adjust if your tension differs.

Weave in all ends on the wrong side. Block firmly: soak in cool water. Remove excess moisture in a towel. Then pin the top edge to 155cm and the lower point to 70cm depth on a foam mat. The ripple chevrons need pinning at each peak and valley along the lower edge to set the wave. Allow to dry completely.
Hand wash in cool water with a wool-safe detergent. Reshape and dry flat. Do not tumble dry or wring. Re-block after washing if the chevron definition softens.

A multicolour ripple blanket uses exactly this approach and lets you practise stripe colour-changes. For a triangle with a single clean increase line rather than chevron movement. title: Ripple round motif
subtitle: A flat circular motif with a concentric wave pattern built from increases and decreases
excerpt: The ripple round alternates dc increase peaks and dc2tog decrease valleys on every other round, producing a flat circle with a concentric wave line across the surface. Four rounds in DK cotton make a 12 cm circle with one wave ring visible; six rounds make two visible rings.
sourceNotes: Ripple and chevron construction in circular form appears in Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 4 (1889), wave motif chapter (Internet Archive).

content.text: The ripple round motif alternates a standard flat-circle increase round with a ripple peak round. Where increases at peak positions and dc2tog at valleys create the wave texture while keeping the circle flat. The stitch count stays consistent because each ripple round adds as many stitches as it removes.

Work the flat rounds in one colour and the ripple rounds in a second colour to make the wave rings visible. Two ripple rounds nested inside a 12 cm circle require a careful stitch count. Mark the peak and valley positions after round 2 with stitch markers.

title: Rose motif, layered
subtitle: Three separate petal layers sewn together at the centre, 8 cm
excerpt: Three rounds of petals, small, medium, and large, are worked separately and stacked at the centre with a tapestry needle, then anchored through a dc ring base. The layered construction gives a more open, open-bloom look than the rolled rose, and the three petal sizes make the flower believably natural in scale.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 6 (1891), built-up flower motif chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crocheted flower construction.

content.text: The layered rose builds three separate petal rings at different heights, half treble, treble. And double treble, and stacks them with the inner ring on top. Because each ring is worked separately. The petal count and colour on each layer can vary. The standard version uses five petals per ring in three tones of the same colour.

Work each ring individually, pull the magic ring tail closed, and weave in the end before stacking. Stack them outer-ring-down. Middle on top. Inner on top of that. Then sew through all three centres with a tapestry needle to hold the arrangement. A button or bead in the very centre covers the sewing point.

half treble, UK; US "half double crochet".

Form a magic ring. *Ch 4. Work 6dtr into the ring. Ch 4. Sl st into the ring.* Repeat from * to * four more times. Pull tail to close. Fasten off.

Lay the outer ring flat. Place the middle ring on top, rotating it so its petals sit between the outer petals. Place the inner ring on top of the middle ring. Thread a tapestry needle with a length of any colour and take 4 stitches through the centre of all three rings. Sew a button or bead to the very top to cover the stitching point. Fasten off all sewing ends through the back of the outer ring.

title: Rose motif, rolled
subtitle: A flat spiral worked flat and rolled into a bud shape, 5 cm across
excerpt: The rolled rose works a long flat strip of shell stitches, then rolls it tightly from the starting end to form a layered bud. No special techniques beyond treble and chain; the roll itself shapes the flower. At 5 cm across it works as a corsage, a bag embellishment, or a garment button cover.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 5 (1890), rolled-petal flower chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crocheted flower section.

content.text: The rolled rose begins as a flat strip: a 36-chain foundation. Then two rows of shell stitches where the shells in row 2 are larger than the shells in row 1. Rolling the strip tightly from the short end automatically stacks the larger outer shells around the smaller inner shells. Creating the layered-petal look without any three-dimensional joining techniques.

The strip must be rolled evenly: too loose and the rose is open and floppy. Too tight and the base buckles. A good rule is to roll until the spiral feels firm but the petals can still move slightly. Secure through the base layers with a tapestry needle rather than trying to slip stitch. The needlework hold is more adjustable.

attrs.body: About 8 g of DK-weight cotton in a single colour or two tones. A 4 mm crochet hook. Tapestry needle. Scissors.
attrs.title: Materials for one rose

content.text: Each finished rolled rose measures 5 cm across in DK-weight cotton with a 4 mm hook.
chain, slip stitch, UK and US shared.
Ch 36. Dc into 2nd ch from hook and into every ch to end. Turn.
Ch 1. *Work 5tr into next dc. Sk 1dc. Sl st into next dc.* Repeat from * to * to end of row. about 9 shells. Turn.

Work into the foundation row only. Inserting the hook into the dc below the sl-st connector of each shell: *Work 7tr into the dc below the sl st. Sl st into the dc below the centre of the next shell.* Repeat from * to * to end. about 9 large shells. Fasten off, leaving a 30 cm tail.

Starting from the short starting end. Roll the strip tightly with the right side on the outside of the roll. Hold the base as you roll to keep the layers even. Thread the 30 cm tail through a tapestry needle and take 4 to 5 stitches through the base of the coil to hold the shape. Weave the tail through the base and trim.

title: Shell and fan triangle shawl
subtitle: Top-down triangle shawl in DK with a 5-treble fan separated by ch-1 spaces on a 4 mm hook
excerpt: A top-down triangular shawl worked entirely in a 5-treble fan stitch set in ch-2 corner spaces, separated by single chain stitches. The shawl grows from a short chain spine at the neck to a full triangle 150 cm wide and 72 cm deep. The fan repeat is two rows: a fan row and a chain-space return row.
sourceNotes: Shell and fan stitch construction from Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 1 (1886), which describes fan-stitch shawls worked from a central neck chain with increasing fan widths per row (Internet Archive). Fan stitch construction also in Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886).

content.text: This triangular shawl starts from a short
at the neck and grows downward by adding one

on each side of the spine on every fan row. The construction is top-down, worked flat in rows and turned at each edge. The ch-1 turning chain does not count as a stitch. The repeat is two rows: a fan row, where you work 5-treble fans into the ch-2 spaces of the previous row; and a return row, where you work dc and ch spaces across to set up the next fan row.

The fan stitch is accessible to beginners who are confident with treble crochet, chaining, and basic counting. The main skill to practise is placing each fan accurately in the correct ch-2 space. Stitch markers are essential at the spine chain position and at the two edge fan positions.

attrs.body: Approximately 400 g DK-weight yarn (cotton or cotton-blend gives good stitch definition in the open fan repeat). A 4 mm hook (US G/6). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Stitch markers (3 minimum). Blocking mat and pins. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 1 fan (5 tr) + 1 ch-1 space measures 3 cm wide; 2 rows (fan row + return row) measure 2.5 cm tall in DK on a 4 mm hook. Work a swatch of 5 fans across for 6 rows (3 fan rows + 3 return rows), block it, and measure. At gauge, 5 fans should measure 15 cm wide and 6 rows should measure 7.5 cm tall.
ch: chain -- UK and US shared.
sl st: slip stitch -- UK and US shared.
dc: double crochet (UK) -- used on return rows. The same move as US single crochet (sc).
tr: treble (UK) -- the main stitch of the fan. The same move as US double crochet (dc).
: 5 tr in the same ch-2 space.
The shawl is worked flat, turning at the end of each row. Mark the spine chain at the centre with a stitch marker. Move the marker up each row.
Ch 5. Mark the 3rd ch from the hook with a stitch marker. This is the spine position.
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in first ch. Ch 2. 1 dc in marked spine ch (move marker to this dc). Ch 2. 1 dc in last ch. Turn. (3 dc, 2 ch-2 spaces)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in first dc. Ch 2. 1 dc in spine dc (move marker). Ch 2. 1 dc in last dc. Turn. (3 dc, 2 ch-2 spaces)

Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in first dc. Ch 1. 5 tr in first ch-2 space (first fan). Ch 2. 5 tr in second ch-2 space (second fan). Ch 1. 1 dc in last dc. Turn. (2 fans, 2 ch-2 spaces, 2 edge dc)

Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in first dc. Ch 2. 1 dc in ch-1 space between fan and centre. Ch 2 (spine position -- move marker to this dc). 1 dc in ch-1 space between centre and second fan. Ch 2. 1 dc in last dc. Turn. (4 dc, 3 ch-2 spaces)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in first dc. Ch 1. *5 tr in next ch-2 space. Ch 1.* Repeat from * to * twice more (3 fans total). 1 dc in last dc. Turn. (3 fans, 3 ch-1 separators, 2 edge dc)

Continue the two-row repeat: on every return row (even rows), work dc in each gap between fans with ch-2 between, adding a ch-2 space at both edges; on every fan row (odd rows), work 5 tr in each ch-2 space with ch-1 between, and dc at each edge. Each fan row adds two fans to the total count (one per side of the spine). Work until you have 25 fans across on the fan row (approximately 57 rows total). The shawl should measure 150 cm wide at this row. (25 fans)
Work the final return row after the 25-fan row to set the last row of ch-2 spaces. Fasten off. The total depth from the neck to the lower point is approximately 72 cm.

Fasten off and weave in all ends. Wet-block by soaking in cool water for 10 minutes, pressing water out gently in a towel, then pinning to the stated dimensions on a blocking mat. Pin the two top corners first, then pin the point at the base, then pin the two diagonal edges at 10 cm intervals.
Handwash in cool water with mild soap. Do not tumble-dry. Lay flat and ease to shape while damp. DK cotton holds its block well; wool-blend yarn may need re-pinning after the first wash.

A 7-treble fan in the same construction produces a more dramatic open arc shape. Working the same fan repeat in a lace-weight yarn on a 3 mm hook produces a fine summer shawlette in far fewer grams. Adding a picot border along the lower diagonal edges (ch 3, sl st in base of ch 3) gives the fan edge a decorative finish.

title: Shetland-style triangle with shell border
subtitle: A treble lace body with a shell-stitch border, inspired by Shetland shawl construction, in natural grey DK
excerpt: This triangular shawl draws on Shetland shawl construction: a lace body worked from the centre out with a deep shell-stitch border applied separately around all three edges. The body is an openwork treble lace in DK weight natural grey on a 4 mm hook. The border adds approximately 8 cm of depth to each edge. Finished size is 145 cm wide by 68 cm deep. Requires confident lace counting and border pick-up.
sourceNotes: Construction inspired by traditional Shetland shawl technique, documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volumes 2 and 3 (1886-1887), which describe lace-body shawls with applied shell borders (Internet Archive). Lace body structure adapted from de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886).

content.text: Traditional Shetland shawls separate the centre body from the border: the body uses one stitch pattern and the border uses a different. Often denser one. This crochet interpretation uses the same principle. The lace body is a V-stitch grid that produces an open, lightweight fabric. The applied border is a five-treble shell worked directly into the edge stitches of the finished body.

title: Shoulder wrap in cluster stitch
subtitle: A square of treble clusters separated by ch-1 spaces in DK weight, worn folded as a triangle
excerpt: This square wrap is worked in rows of three-treble clusters separated by ch-1 spaces on a 4 mm hook with DK yarn. The 90 x 90 cm square folds diagonally and is worn as a shoulder triangle. The cluster stitch creates an open, textured fabric that is lighter than solid treble but more structured than a mesh.

content.text: This shoulder wrap is a 90 cm square worked in rows of three-treble clusters separated by ch-1 spaces. Fold it diagonally before wearing and drape the long straight edge across the back of the neck; the two corners of the fold hang in front. At DK weight on a 4 mm hook the fabric is open enough to show the cluster texture but warm enough for cooler weather. The whole piece is one rectangle with no shaping.

is three trebles worked into the same ch-1 space, all joined at the top. Each cluster sits in a ch-1 space from the previous row; on each new row you work into the spaces from the row below, not into the cluster tops. The pattern repeat is: 1 cl in next ch-1 space, ch 1; worked across the row.

content.text: 5 cluster repeats (cl + ch 1) x 8 rows = 10 x 10 cm in DK yarn with a 4 mm hook, measured unstretched. Work a swatch of at least 20 clusters wide and 16 rows deep, measure the central 10 cm, and adjust hook size before beginning.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
treble (tr): UK; the same move as US "double crochet" (dc).
treble cluster (cl): 3 trebles into the same space, joined at the top as described above.
The square is worked flat. The foundation chain is one side of the square; the rows build the other side. The stitch count in clusters stays constant throughout at 45 clusters per row.
Ch 137. (This gives 45 cluster positions plus selvedge chains.)
Ch 4 (counts as 1 tr + ch 1). Skip 3 ch. *1 cl in next ch-3 group (insert into the centre chain), ch 1, skip 2 ch*; repeat from * to * to last 3 ch. 1 tr in last ch. Turn. (45 cl, 46 ch-1 spaces)
Ch 4 (counts as 1 tr + ch 1). *1 cl in next ch-1 space, ch 1*; repeat from * to * to end. 1 tr in the top of the ch-4 turning chain. Turn. (45 cl, 46 ch-1 spaces)
Repeat row 2 until the piece measures 90 cm from the foundation chain edge, approximately 72 rows. The stitch count remains 45 cl throughout. Fasten off.

Fasten off and weave in both ends securely. A single row of double crochet worked around all four edges gives clean, stable selvedges. Wet-block by soaking, pressing out water, then pinning to 90 x 90 cm. Check that all four corners are true right angles before leaving to dry.
Handwash in cool water with mild soap. Lay flat to dry. Do not tumble-dry.

Increase the cluster to five trebles for a larger, more open texture. Work the square in two colours by alternating stripes of two rows each; the ch-1 spaces pick up both colours cleanly. A pointed fringe along two sides of the square transforms it from a shoulder wrap into a triangular shawl.

title: Snowflake, advanced
subtitle: A six-branch lace snowflake with secondary branches and picot tips
excerpt: This advanced snowflake extends each of the six main branches with two secondary branches, giving the motif its characteristic feathered appearance. Picot tips at each branch end sharpen the silhouette. Five rounds in 4-ply cotton produce a 14 cm snowflake that blocks flat and crisp.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Needlework, Volume 7 (1892), snowflake lace chapter (Internet Archive). Victorian snowflake motifs appeared as Christmas decorations and as applique for net veiling.

content.text: The advanced snowflake works the six main branches as chain-10 arches in round 1. Then fills each branch with dc and adds secondary branches and picot tips on round 2. Each main branch gets two secondary branches at one-third and two-third positions along its length.

Use 4-ply cotton and a 2.5 mm hook. Work at a relaxed, even tension, tight tension makes the chain arches short and stiff. Block the finished snowflake by wetting, pinning all 18 branch tips to the blocking mat. And leaving to dry for several hours.

title: Star motif, eight point
subtitle: An eight-pointed star worked in the round with pointed spike sections
excerpt: Eight evenly spaced points radiate from the centre ring, each built by stepping up to a treble tip then decreasing back down. Four rounds in DK cotton produce a 12 cm star with a compact centre and sharp outer points suitable for Christmas decorations and applique panels.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 4 (1889), eight-point star chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886).

content.text: to form each of the eight points: dc at the base, htr on the slope, tr at the tip. The tip chain gives the sharpest point. Valley slip stitches pull the indentations tight between each point.

title: Striped triangle shawl in three colours
subtitle: A top-down triangle in DK with colour stripes on every sixth row, using three alternating shades
excerpt: This triangular shawl grows from the top centre to 150 cm wide and 72 cm deep in DK yarn. The body is plain treble, with the three yarn colours changing every six rows to create bold horizontal stripes across the triangle. Worked on a 4 mm hook. Requires confidence with carrying and joining yarn at the row edge.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. Top-down triangular shawl construction with stripe sequencing is a widely established technique with no single source.

content.text: This shawl uses the same top-down triangular construction as the Chunky Throw Shawl. It is worked in DK yarn on a 4 mm hook with three colours. The colours change every six rows. The stripes run horizontally across the triangle. Each stripe is wider near the base of the triangle where the rows are longer. Near the neck the rows are shorter, so the stripes narrow. This gives the finished shawl a gradual taper effect across each colour band.
Colours are labelled A, B, and C. The stripe sequence is: 6 rows A, 6 rows B, 6 rows C, repeat. At six rows per stripe you can carry the unused colours up the side edge without cutting: a
of up to 6 rows keeps a neat side selvedge. If you prefer cleaner edges, fasten off each colour and

Stitch marker. Blocking mat and pins. Tape measure.

content.text: 18 tr x 10 rows = 10 x 10 cm in DK yarn with a 4 mm hook, measured unstretched. Swatch in each of your three colours and check they match in tension; different dye lots of the same yarn rarely differ, but different yarn bases can. Use the same hook size for all three colours.

treble (tr): UK; the same move as US "double crochet" (dc).
The shawl is worked flat in rows. The ch-3 turning chain counts as the first treble on every row. Place a stitch marker in the central spine stitch and move it up on each row.
Using colour C, ch 4. Place a stitch marker in the 2nd ch from the hook. This is the spine chain.
Ch 3 (counts as first tr). 1 tr in the 4th ch from hook. 2 tr in the marked spine ch. 1 tr in the last ch. Turn. (5 sts)

Ch 3 (counts as first tr). 1 tr in each st to 1 st before the spine st. 2 tr in the st before the spine. 1 tr in the spine st (move marker). 2 tr in the st after the spine. 1 tr in each st to end, working the final tr into the top of the turning ch. Turn. (2 sts added)

Work the increase row throughout. Change colour at the start of a row: at the end of the last row in the current colour, complete the final tr until 2 loops remain on hook, then draw through with the new colour. Leave a 15 cm tail to weave in later.

Rows 1 to 6: colour C. Rows 7 to 12: colour B. Rows 13 to 18: colour A. Rows 19 to 24: colour C. Rows 25 to 30: colour B. Rows 31 to 36: colour A. After approximately 72 rows the widest row has approximately 149 sts and the width is 150 cm. After approximately 72 rows the depth is 72 cm. End on a complete stripe of any colour. Fasten off.

title: Summer cotton stole
subtitle: A long open-mesh rectangle in fingering-weight cotton, worked in a ch-1 skip-1 dc grid
excerpt: This rectangular stole uses a ch-1, skip-1, dc mesh pattern on a 3.5 mm hook with fingering or sport-weight cotton. The open grid creates a light, airy fabric that sits flat without blocking. Finished size is approximately 200 cm long by 50 cm wide, giving enough length to wrap, drape, or loop over the shoulders.

content.text: This stole works a ch-1, skip-1, dc repeat across a long rectangle, producing an open grid fabric that is airy enough for warm weather but structured enough to hold a drape. The yarn is fingering or sport-weight cotton on a 3.5 mm hook. At 200 cm by 50 cm the finished piece wraps as a stole, folds as a scarf, or drapes across both shoulders.

repeats over an even number of foundation chains. On every row each dc sits above a ch-1 space from the previous row, not above a stitch, so the pattern stays consistent and the grid aligns naturally.

attrs.body: Approximately 300 g fingering or sport-weight cotton yarn. A 3.5 mm crochet hook (US E/4). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 14 mesh repeats (dc, ch 1) x 14 rows = 10 x 10 cm in fingering-weight cotton with a 3.5 mm hook, measured unstretched. Work a 15 x 15 cm swatch in the mesh pattern, count the central 10 cm, and adjust the hook size if needed before starting the foundation chain.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
double crochet (dc): UK; the same move as US "single crochet" (sc).

The stole is worked flat along its length, so the foundation chain is the short end (50 cm width) and the rows build the 200 cm length. This orientation means you work fewer, longer rows rather than many short ones, which keeps the work manageable on the hook.
Ch 143. (This gives 71 mesh repeats across 50 cm of width.)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in the 2nd ch from hook. *Ch 1, skip 1 ch, 1 dc in the next ch*; repeat from * to * to end. Turn. (72 dc, 71 ch-1 spaces)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in the first dc. *Ch 1, 1 dc in the next ch-1 space*; repeat from * to * to last dc. 1 dc in the last dc. Turn. (72 dc, 70 ch-1 spaces)

Repeat row 2 on every subsequent row. The pattern is: ch 1 (does not count as stitch), 1 dc in the first dc, *ch 1, 1 dc in next ch-1 space*, repeat to last dc, 1 dc in last dc. Turn. (72 dc, 70 ch-1 spaces each row)
Continue row 2 pattern until the piece measures 200 cm from the foundation chain edge, measured flat. At 14 rows per 10 cm this is approximately 280 rows in total. Fasten off.

Fasten off and weave in both ends. Thread the tail through several stitches along the selvedge, pulling gently to secure. Cotton does not felt so ends must be woven in a minimum of 5 cm. The mesh fabric sits flat without blocking; if the edges curl, lightly spray and pin to shape while damp.
Machine-wash at 30 degrees on a gentle cycle, or handwash in cool water. Cotton can be tumble-dried on a low setting. Lay flat to dry for best results.

content.text: 14 mesh repeats (dc, ch 1) x 14 rows = 10 x 10 cm in fingering-weight cotton with a 3.5 mm hook, measured unstretched. Work a 15 x 15 cm swatch in the mesh pattern, count the central 10 cm, and adjust the hook size if needed before starting the foundation chain.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
double crochet (dc): UK; the same move as US "single crochet" (sc).

The stole is worked flat along its length, so the foundation chain is the short end (50 cm width) and the rows build the 200 cm length. This orientation means you work fewer, longer rows rather than many short ones, which keeps the work manageable on the hook.
Ch 143. (This gives 71 mesh repeats across 50 cm of width.)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in the 2nd ch from hook. *Ch 1, skip 1 ch, 1 dc in the next ch*; repeat from * to * to end. Turn. (72 dc, 71 ch-1 spaces)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in the first dc. *Ch 1, 1 dc in the next ch-1 space*; repeat from * to * to last dc. 1 dc in the last dc. Turn. (72 dc, 70 ch-1 spaces)

Repeat row 2 on every subsequent row. The pattern is: ch 1 (does not count as stitch), 1 dc in the first dc, *ch 1, 1 dc in next ch-1 space*, repeat to last dc, 1 dc in last dc. Turn. (72 dc, 70 ch-1 spaces each row)
Continue row 2 pattern until the piece measures 200 cm from the foundation chain edge, measured flat. At 14 rows per 10 cm this is approximately 280 rows in total. Fasten off.

Fasten off and weave in both ends. Thread the tail through several stitches along the selvedge, pulling gently to secure. Cotton does not felt so ends must be woven in a minimum of 5 cm. The mesh fabric sits flat without blocking; if the edges curl, lightly spray and pin to shape while damp.
Machine-wash at 30 degrees on a gentle cycle, or handwash in cool water. Cotton can be tumble-dried on a low setting. Lay flat to dry for best results.

title: Sunburst motif, advanced
subtitle: A four-round sunburst with shell border, 14 cm, in DK cotton
excerpt: Four rounds extend the basic sunburst to 14 cm. The fourth round fills the gaps between spokes with five-treble shells, turning the open geometric tile into a denser, more decorative square-compatible motif. Works well as a cushion centrepiece or in a throw with the basic version for scale contrast.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 5 (1890), extended radiating motifs chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet motif section.

content.text: The advanced sunburst adds a fourth round of five-treble shells to the three-round basic version. Taking the motif from 10 cm to 14 cm and filling the open chain arches with a fanning border. Rounds 1 through 3 match the basic sunburst exactly. So both sizes can be worked from the same starting sequence before diverging at round 4.

Two-colour working reads most clearly: rounds 1 and 2 in the spoke colour. Round 3 onward in the border colour. Single-colour gives a more unified look. The shells in round 4 close the motif enough to join in a grid rather than a honeycomb.

title: Sunburst motif, basic
subtitle: A six-spoke radiating motif in DK cotton, worked in three rounds
excerpt: Six treble clusters radiate from the centre like spokes on a wheel, giving this 10 cm motif its sunburst shape. Three rounds in a single colour produce a graphic geometric tile; swap the centre round for a contrast colour and the spokes read as rays against a ring border.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 3 (1888), radiating-spoke motif chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet motif section.

content.text: The sunburst motif builds six treble cluster spokes from a tight magic ring. Then extends each spoke outward across two rounds until the motif reaches 10 cm. The geometry is stable: six spokes divide the round equally. And the chain arches between them hold the shape flat without curling. It works as a stand-alone coaster, as a tile in a throw. Or as a centrepiece in a more complex block.
Two colours give a crisper read: work round 1 in a contrast. Rounds 2 and 3 in the main colour. One colour gives a quieter, more textural result.

title: Tapestry crochet square
subtitle: A two-colour geometric square where both yarns are carried simultaneously across each row
excerpt: Tapestry crochet carries both yarn colours across every row, crocheting over the unused colour so it is caught inside the stitches. Switching between colours mid-row produces crisp geometric pixel patterns with a neat, reversible wrong side. This square works a simple diamond chart in dc.
sourceNotes: Tapestry crochet with carried yarn is documented in South American craft traditions and appears in early 20th-century American crochet handbooks. The carry-yarn principle in European crochet appears in Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 5 (1890).

content.text: Tapestry crochet keeps both colours in hand at all times. Carrying the yarn not in use over the top of the previous row. Colour switches happen within the dc stitch itself: work the stitch until the final pull-through. Drop one colour and pick up the other. The carried yarn is completely hidden inside the stitches when done correctly.

Tension is the main challenge. The carried colour must stay relaxed. Not pulled tight enough to pucker the fabric. Not so loose it shows as a loop on the surface. Work a 5-stitch swatch carrying one colour over the other before starting the motif.

Diamond peak is at position 8, row 8. From row 2. Begin introducing colour B at the chart positions: switch at the last pull-through. Carry the unused colour inside all dc until the next switch.

title: Heart motif, basic
subtitle: A flat applique heart in DK cotton, 8 cm wide
excerpt: The basic heart motif is worked in two symmetrical halves from a centre chain, with dc rows forming each lobe, then joined at the base with a V-point. At 8 cm wide in DK cotton the silhouette is clean and unmistakable. Used for Valentine's Day decorations, children's blanket appliques, and scatter motifs on throws.

. Then joins them along the bottom and works decrease rows down to a single V-point. Each lobe is a ch-4 slip-stitch ring with 10 dc worked around the outside of the ring in a semicircle. The flat base of each semicircle is the joining line.

title: Pumpkin motif
subtitle: A flat applique pumpkin with a green stem and rib panels, 9 cm wide
excerpt: The pumpkin motif is a flat disc with four orange dc rib panels separated by slip-stitch vertical lines to mimic the pumpkin's lobed sides, topped with a small green stem. At 9 cm wide in DK cotton it is a bold and recognisable Halloween and harvest applique for blankets, tote bags, and seasonal cushion covers.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from flat disc and vertical rib construction. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 9 (1894), seasonal and novelty applique chapter (Internet Archive).

content.text: The pumpkin body is a simple flat disc from a magic ring, increased each round to stay flat. Four vertical rib lines are added afterward by working a slip stitch column through the disc from top to bottom. Pulling the surface inward to create the lobed pumpkin shape. The rib lines are the key technique, without them the disc is just a circle. A small green stem is worked from the top centre.

attrs.body: About 10 g of orange DK cotton, 2 g of green for the stem. A 4 mm hook. Tapestry needle. Scissors.
attrs.title: Materials for one motif

content.text: Each finished pumpkin motif measures 9 cm wide and 8 cm tall including stem in DK-weight cotton with a 4 mm hook.
chain, slip stitch, magic ring, UK and US shared.

Form a magic ring. Ch 1. Rnd 1: 8dc. Sl st to join. Rnd 2: 2dc in each. Sl st to join. Rnd 3: *Dc. 2dc in next.* Repeat 8 times. Sl st to join. Rnd 4: *Dc. Dc. 2dc in next.* Repeat 8 times. Sl st to join. Fasten off.

Identify 4 evenly spaced stitches around the outer edge at the top of the disc. With orange yarn and a tapestry needle. Take a stitch through the disc from the top edge dc straight down to the centre ring. Then back up to the top, this draws a vertical groove on the disc surface. Repeat at each of the 4 rib positions. The four lines divide the disc into 4 equal lobes.
Join green at the top centre of the disc. Ch 4. Dc in 2nd, 3rd, and 4th ch from hook. Sl st back into the top of the disc. Fasten off.

title: Star wreath motif
subtitle: Five five-pointed stars joined in a ring, 25 cm across
excerpt: The star wreath links five crochet stars at adjacent points into a circular arrangement, leaving a pentagonal opening at the centre. Each star is a five-pointed piece worked from a magic ring with treble spokes and chain tip loops. The finished wreath at 25 cm in DK cotton works as a door wreath, Christmas wall hanging, and table centrepiece.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 4 (1889), star and wreath motif chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet star and joined motif construction.

content.text: Each star in the wreath has five treble cluster spokes from a magic ring. With a ch-5 point at the end of each spoke tipped with a dc. Stars 2 through 5 replace two of their five tip dc stitches with chain joins into the adjacent star. Closing the wreath. The first star is complete and free. Star 5 joins to both stars 4 and 1 to close the ring.

attrs.body: About 30 g of DK cotton for all five stars. A 4 mm hook. Tapestry needle. Scissors. Optional: hanging ring and ribbon.
attrs.title: Materials for one wreath

content.text: Each individual star measures 10 cm across. The joined wreath measures 25 cm across in DK-weight cotton with a 4 mm hook.
chain, slip stitch, magic ring, UK and US shared.
treble cluster, three trebles drawn together.

Form a magic ring. Ch 3. Work 2 more tr into ring, draw together. *Ch 2. 3tr-cl into ring.* Repeat 3 more times. Ch 2. Sl st to top of first cluster. For each of the 5 points: *Sl st into ch-2 sp. Ch 5. Dc into 2nd ch from hook. Ch 3. Sl st back into the ch-2 sp.* Repeat 4 more times. Fasten off.

Work the centre clusters as for star 1. For 3 free points, work as star 1. For the 2 joined points: Ch 5. Ch 3. Sl st into the corresponding tip of the adjacent star. Ch 3. Sl st back to the ch-2 space. This links the tip without a separate dc point, the adjacent star's dc serves as the shared tip.
Work 2 free points and 2 joined points to stars 4 and 1. Check placement before working the closing joins.

title: Toddler shawl in double crochet
subtitle: A 75 cm square in DK-weight double crochet for ages 2 to 4, worked flat with no shaping
excerpt: This toddler shawl is a 75 cm square of double crochet in DK yarn on a 4 mm hook, sized for ages 2 to 4. The construction is entirely plain double crochet with no shaping. The square folds diagonally and is worn as a triangle draped over small shoulders. It is the most structurally direct entry point for double crochet on a usable project.

content.text: This is a 75 cm square of

in DK yarn on a 4 mm hook. The square has no shaping: every row is the same. Once finished, fold it diagonally and drape it over a toddler's shoulders. The only technique required is dc and managing the
correctly at the start of each row.

The turning chain in double crochet is ch 1 and does not count as a stitch. This means the first dc of each row goes into the first actual stitch of the previous row, not into the turning chain. Getting this right from row 1 keeps the stitch count stable across all 165 rows.

attrs.body: Approximately 250 g DK-weight yarn in a soft fibre suitable for a child (cotton, cotton-blend, or machine-washable treated wool). A 4 mm crochet hook (US G/6). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 18 dc x 22 rows = 10 x 10 cm in DK yarn with a 4 mm hook, measured unstretched. Work a 15 x 15 cm swatch, measure the central 10 cm in each direction, and adjust hook size before starting. One stitch per 10 cm off changes the finished square from 75 cm by about 4 cm.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
double crochet (dc): UK; the same move as US "single crochet" (sc).
The shawl is worked flat. The foundation chain is one side of the square. Every row is identical. The stitch count stays at 135 dc throughout.
Ch 136. (This gives 135 working stitches, which measures 75 cm at the stated gauge.)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch throughout). 1 dc in each ch across. Turn. (135 sts)
Ch 1 (does not count as stitch). 1 dc in the first st (not the turning chain). 1 dc in each st across to end. Turn. (135 sts)

Check the stitch count at the end of every 10th row while you are learning the pattern. Count the tops of the stitches along the row just completed. You should have 135 every time. A count of 134 means you missed the first stitch; a count of 136 means you worked into the turning chain by mistake.
Continue repeating row 2 until the piece measures 75 cm from the foundation chain edge, approximately 165 rows at 22 rows per 10 cm. Fasten off. (135 sts)

Fasten off and weave in both ends securely. Thread the tail through the backs of stitches in different directions for at least 5 cm. A single row of dc worked around all four edges with a contrast colour gives a neat frame and hides the foundation chain edge. Wet-block to 75 x 75 cm if the square is not lying flat.
Machine-wash at 30 degrees on a gentle cycle if the yarn is machine-washable. Otherwise handwash in cool water with mild soap. Lay flat to dry.

A crochet border of shell stitch worked into the selvedge stitches turns the plain square into a mini heirloom piece. title: Triangle shawl with shell border
subtitle: A top-down triangle in half treble, finished with a shell-stitch border in DK cotton
excerpt: This top-down triangular shawl grows from a chain-2 spine into a full triangle in half treble, then gains a shell-stitch border along the lower two edges. Finished size is roughly 145 cm wide and 70 cm deep in DK cotton on a 4.5 mm hook. The half treble body gives a dense, warm fabric; the shell border adds decorative width.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 2 (1886), triangular shawl construction from a centre-chain spine (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet shawl chapter.

content.text: This triangular shawl grows from a two-chain spine at the neck down to a full-width point, worked in half treble on a 4.5 mm hook with DK cotton. The body fabric is dense enough to drape without stretching out of shape. The shell-stitch border runs along both diagonal edges and turns the corners cleanly.
The construction is top-down: you start at the top centre with a short chain, place a stitch marker on the centre chain (the
), and increase by one half treble on each side of it on every row. The shawl is 70 rows deep before the border.

attrs.body: Approximately 400 g DK-weight cotton yarn. A 4.5 mm crochet hook (US 7). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Stitch marker. Blocking mat and pins. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 16 htr × 12 rows = 10 × 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4.5 mm hook, measured unstretched. Work a 15 × 15 cm swatch in half treble, measure the central 10 × 10 cm area, and swap hook size if the tension misses by more than one stitch per 10 cm. The gauge (older British patterns call this a tension square) controls the finished width.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
half treble (htr): UK; the same move as US "half double crochet" (hdc).
treble (tr): UK; the same move as US "double crochet" (dc).
The shawl is worked flat, turning at the end of each row. The spine sits at the centre of every row; mark it with a stitch marker that you move up each row.
Ch 4. Place a stitch marker in the 2nd ch from the hook, this is the spine chain.

Ch 2 (does not count as a stitch). 1 htr in each of the 2 foundation chains before the spine. Move marker to the spine ch. 1 htr in the spine ch. 1 htr in each of the remaining 2 foundation chains. Turn. (5 sts)

Ch 2 (does not count as a stitch). 1 htr in each st to 1 st before the spine st. 2 htr in the st before the spine. 1 htr in the spine st (move marker). 2 htr in the st after the spine. 1 htr in each st to end. Turn. (7 sts)

Repeat Row 2 on every row. On every row, two stitches increase (one on each side of the spine). At the end of Row 70 you have 145 sts. Move the marker up the spine on each row to keep track of the centre.
along both diagonal edges of the shawl. Do not work along the straight top edge.

Starting at the top right corner: join yarn. *Sk 2 sts (or 2 row-ends), 5 tr in the next st (or row-end), sk 2 sts (or row-ends), 1 sl st in the next st (or row-end)*; repeat from * to * along the right diagonal edge to the bottom point. At the bottom point, work (5 tr, ch 2, 5 tr) into the single bottom stitch to turn the corner. Continue the shell repeat up the left diagonal edge to the top left corner. Fasten off.

Fasten off and weave in all ends through the backs of several stitches in different directions. To wet-block, soak the shawl in cool water for 10 minutes. Gently press out excess water in a towel. Pin the shawl to a blocking mat at the finished dimensions. Leave until completely dry.
Handwash in cool water with mild soap. Do not tumble-dry. Lay flat on a clean towel and ease to shape while damp.

Work the same construction in lace-weight yarn on a 3 mm hook for a finer, more open fabric. Swap the half treble body for treble stitch throughout to add height and drape. A contrast colour for the shell border gives a clean two-tone finish.

title: Tunisian rectangle wrap
subtitle: A dense rectangle in Tunisian simple stitch on an aran-weight yarn, using a long Tunisian hook
excerpt: This wrap uses Tunisian simple stitch worked on a long Tunisian crochet hook with aran-weight yarn. Each row is worked in two passes: a forward pass picks up loops across the row, and a return pass works them off. The resulting fabric is dense, warm, and knit-like in appearance. Finished size is approximately 170 cm wide by 50 cm deep. A long Tunisian hook (or extension cable hook) is required.

content.text: Tunisian crochet is worked with a long hook that holds all the live loops of a row at once. This wrap uses Tunisian simple stitch throughout, producing a dense, knit-like fabric with a clear vertical rib on the right side. Each row of the pattern is two passes: the forward pass picks up one loop per stitch across the row without working them off, and the return pass works through all those loops from right to left. A dedicated long Tunisian hook (at least 50 cm, or a standard hook with an extension cable) is needed to hold 80 or more live loops.
picks up loops through the vertical bars of the previous row on the
works them off. Unlike standard crochet, you do not turn the work between passes: both passes travel in the same direction across the same face of the fabric.

attrs.body: Approximately 500 g aran-weight yarn. A 5.5 mm Tunisian crochet hook at least 50 cm long, or a standard 5.5 mm hook fitted with a flexible extension cable. Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Blocking mat and pins. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 16 Tss sts x 14 rows = 10 x 10 cm in aran-weight yarn with a 5.5 mm Tunisian hook, measured after blocking. Each 'row' here counts as one forward pass plus one return pass. Tunisian fabric curls before blocking; swatch and block the swatch before measuring.
chain (ch): UK and US shared, used for foundation chain.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared, used for cast-off.
Tunisian simple stitch (Tss): worked in two passes as described above.

The wrap is worked flat from one short end to the other. The foundation chain is the 50 cm depth; the rows build the 170 cm width. You do not turn the work at the end of each row in Tunisian crochet: the fabric is always facing you on the right side.
Ch 81. (This gives 80 working stitches across the 50 cm depth.)
Insert hook into 2nd ch from hook, yarn over, pull up loop (keep on hook). *Insert hook into next ch, yarn over, pull up loop*; repeat from * to * to end. Do not turn. (81 loops on hook)
Yarn over, pull through 1 loop. *Yarn over, pull through 2 loops*; repeat from * to * to end until 1 loop remains on hook. (80 sts)

Skip first vertical bar (this is the selvedge edge). *Insert hook under next vertical bar from front to back, yarn over, pull up loop (keep on hook)*; repeat from * to * across all 79 remaining vertical bars. Insert hook under both loops of the last stitch at the far edge, yarn over, pull up loop. Do not turn. (81 loops on hook)
Yarn over, pull through 1 loop. *Yarn over, pull through 2 loops*; repeat from * to * to end until 1 loop remains on hook. (80 sts)
Repeat row 1 (forward pass + return pass) until the piece measures 170 cm from the foundation chain edge, approximately 238 rows. The stitch count remains 80 sts throughout.
Work a slip-stitch cast-off row: *insert hook under next vertical bar, yarn over, pull through bar and loop on hook (1 sl st made)*; repeat from * to * across all stitches. Fasten off.

Fasten off and weave in both ends through the back of several Tss stitches. Tunisian fabric curls at the edges before blocking. Wet-block by soaking thoroughly, pressing out excess water, and pinning flat to 170 x 50 cm on a blocking mat. The fabric flattens completely once blocked and dry.
Handwash in cool water with mild wool wash. Do not tumble-dry. Lay flat to dry. Blocking after each wash keeps the fabric flat.

Tunisian full stitch (Tfs) uses the same two-pass structure but inserts through the space between vertical bars rather than the bar itself, giving a more open, mesh-like fabric. Colour-change stripes are straightforward in Tunisian: change yarn at the start of a return pass. A narrow standard dc border worked around all four edges after blocking tidies the curl-prone selvedges.

excerpt: Tunisian crochet uses a long hook to pick up all stitches across the row in the forward pass, then works them off one by one in the return pass. sourceNotes: Tunisian (Afghan) crochet is documented in Weldon's Practical Needlework, Volume 1 (1885), Afghan stitch chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Afghan crochet section.

content.text: to build a dense, flat fabric with a woven-grid surface. The forward pass picks up all 20 loops across the row; the return pass works them off two at a time. Unlike standard crochet, the work is never turned.

Worked into the chain space of the V-stitch below. Because every V sits over the previous V. The pattern is self-correcting: if you can see where the last V sat. You know exactly where to place the next one. DK weight yarn on a 4mm hook produces a light. Open fabric that drapes well as a shoulder wrap or evening layer.

Which counts as 1 tr plus ch 1 and forms the left-hand arm of the first V at the edge. A matching tr is placed at the end of the row to form the right-hand arm of the last V.

title: Victorian collar shawlette
subtitle: A small scallop-lace collar shawlette in fingering-weight cotton, adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet
excerpt: This collar shawlette works a scalloped lace edging in fingering-weight cotton on a 3 mm hook. Each scallop unit is dc, ch 3, sl st, repeated across the row, with a shallow curve built by short-row shaping on the straight upper edge. Finished size is approximately 80 cm wide by 25 cm deep. The pattern is adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet (1886).
sourceNotes: Collar shawlette construction and scallop edging adapted from Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 1 (1886), 'A Crochet Collar' and 'Scalloped Edging' chapters (Internet Archive). Adapted for fingering-weight cotton; original used white crochet thread.

content.text: This collar shawlette sits close to the shoulders and neck in the style of the decorative lace collars found in Weldon's Practical Crochet from 1886. The body is worked in rows of double crochet with short-row shaping to build extra depth at the centre back. A row of scallop units runs along the lower edge and the two front ends. Fingering-weight cotton on a 3 mm hook gives a fine, crisp fabric that holds the collar shape without stiffening.
is: 1 dc into the fabric, ch 3, sl st into the base of the ch-3. This forms one small pointed loop. Work these across the lower edge with 3 dc between each scallop. The
in the body ensures the straight upper edge curves to follow the shoulder line rather than sitting flat.

attrs.body: Approximately 100 g fingering-weight cotton yarn. A 3 mm crochet hook (US C/2 or D/3). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Blocking mat. Blocking pins. Tape measure.
attrs.title: Materials

content.text: 22 dc x 26 rows = 10 x 10 cm in fingering-weight cotton with a 3 mm hook, measured unstretched. The collar is a small piece so accurate gauge is essential for the finished 80 cm width.
slip stitch (sl st): UK and US shared.
double crochet (dc): UK; the same move as US "single crochet" (sc).
picot (ch 3, sl st to base of chain): used in scallop units.

The shawlette is worked from the straight upper edge downward. The foundation chain is the full 80 cm width. Short rows add extra depth at the centre of the piece. The scallop border is worked separately along the lower edge once the body is complete.
Ch 177. (This gives 176 working stitches across the 80 cm width.)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch throughout). 1 dc in each ch across. Turn. (176 sts)
Ch 1 (does not count as stitch). 1 dc in each st across. Turn. (176 sts each row)
Short row A: Ch 1. 1 dc in each of next 88 sts (centre half of the row). Turn. Do not work to the end of the row. (88 sts worked)
Short row B: Ch 1. 1 dc in each of the 88 sts just worked. Turn. (88 sts)
Short row C: Ch 1. 1 dc in each of next 66 sts (centre third). Turn. (66 sts worked)
Short row D: Ch 1. 1 dc in each of the 66 sts just worked. Turn. (66 sts)
Ch 1 (does not count as stitch). 1 dc in each st across the full 176 sts. Turn. (176 sts each row)

Do not fasten off. Work the scallop border along the lower (row 16) edge, then down each short front end. Starting at the bottom-right corner: *1 dc in next st, ch 3, sl st into the base of the ch-3 just made (1 scallop unit formed), 1 dc in each of next 3 sts*; repeat from * to * across the full lower edge. Work 1 dc into each row-end along the right front, then the same scallop sequence down the right front. Mirror for the left front if desired. Fasten off.

Fasten off and weave in all ends. Wet-block by soaking in cool water for 10 minutes, pressing out excess water, and pinning to 80 x 25 cm on a blocking mat with the scallop points individually pinned outward. Leave until fully dry.
Handwash in cool water with mild soap. Cotton can be lightly pressed with a damp cloth and a cool iron to restore crispness. Lay flat to dry.

Work a second row of scallops offset from the first for a deeper, more layered border. Replace the dc body with an open filet grid (dc and ch-1 alternating) for a lighter, lace-like collar. A small button and loop at each front corner holds the shawlette in place when worn.

title: Vintage wheel square
subtitle: A circular wheel motif centred in a square border, worked in the round
excerpt: A circular wheel of radiating treble spokes fills the centre of the motif, then a square border round closes the circle into a square. The wheel spokes and the square corners are offset, giving the motif a compass-rose quality. Five rounds in DK cotton produce a 12 cm tile.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 3 (1888), wheel-and-square motif chapter (Internet Archive). Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), spoke motifs.

content.text: The vintage wheel square builds eight radiating spokes in the first three rounds. Then uses a circle-to-square transition on round 4 to anchor four corner clusters onto the wheel. Converting the circular motif to a square. Round 5 adds the outer granny-style border.

The transition round places corner clusters at every other spoke position. The intermediate 4 spokes become mid-side positions on the square border. Producing a subtle octagonal shadow inside the square outline.

title: Willow tree motif
subtitle: A flat applique tree in three shades of green with a brown trunk, 10 cm tall
excerpt: The willow tree works a tapered trunk in brown, then builds three tiers of drooping chain loops upward to form the characteristic weeping silhouette. Worked flat in rows with colour changes at each tier, it reads as a recognisable tree at 10 cm tall and 8 cm wide. Used as an applique on cushions, blankets, and garment panels.
sourceNotes: Synthesised from flat applique tree construction. Weldon's Practical Crochet, Volume 7 (1892), applied motif chapter (Internet Archive).

content.text: The willow tree applique builds upward from a narrow trunk rectangle, adding three tiers of foliage. Each tier is a wider dc base row with drooping chain-loop fronds hanging from the working edge. The fronds on the lowest tier are longest. Giving the weeping silhouette; the upper tier has shorter fronds to narrow the canopy toward the top.

Three shades of green from dark to light give the canopy depth. A single green works too but loses the dimensional look. The colour change at each tier requires a fasten-off and re-join rather than a carry. Since the trunk colour must be restarted separately.

Working along this full 18-dc base: ch 1. *Dc into next dc. Ch 6. Sl st back into the same dc. Dc into next dc. Dc into next dc.* Repeat from * to * five more times. Fasten off.

title: Crocodile stitch accent blanket
subtitle: Scale-like crocodile stitch panels on a treble background.
excerpt: Crocodile stitch wraps trebles around a base stitch pair to make overlapping scale shapes. Worked in panels across an accent blanket in chunky yarn on a 6 mm hook.
sourceNotes: Crocodile stitch is a modern technique. No direct Weldon source; synthetic from contemporary technique documentation.

content.text: accent blanket is 60 x 80 cm. Each scale wraps five trebles down one leg of a
and five more up the other, forming an overlapping tile. The scales sit on a plain treble background.

Chunky yarn on a 6 mm hook makes scales large enough to see clearly. The scale structure means the blanket is heavier than its size suggests. Total yardage is around 400 g chunky. This is a slow pattern to work; it takes longer per row than a plain treble blanket.
4 scales x 3 rows = 10 x 10 cm in chunky with a 6 mm hook. Work a test swatch of two full scale rows before starting the blanket.
Chain 61. Work *tr, ch 2, tr* into every 4th chain. This creates the base V pairs for the first scale row. (15 Vs.)

Work 5 tr down the right leg of the first V (counting from the top). Rotate work. Work 5 tr up the left leg of the same V (back upward). One scale made. Sl st to the ch-2 space of the next V. Repeat for every V across the row.
After the scale row, work a new base V row offset by half a repeat, placing each new V over the sl st join between two scales below. This offsets the scale rows for a true tile pattern.
Alternate scale rows and offset base rows. Work until piece measures 80 cm (approximately 8 scale rows). Fasten off.
. The crocodile stitch forms a self-finished edge; no additional edging is needed.
Handwash chunky wool cool. Dry flat. Machine wash acrylic 40 degrees; the scale structure holds.
The bobble blanket is a more accessible raised-texture pattern at the same advanced level. Or try the puff stitch throw for a softer three-dimensional texture.

title: Double crochet mesh table runner
subtitle: A filet-style cotton runner in double crochet and chain spaces
excerpt: A lightweight cotton table runner worked in a simple dc and chain-space mesh grid. The open mesh keeps the pattern light and lets the table surface show through. Cotton DK on a 4 mm hook.
sourceNotes: Open filet mesh is documented in Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, filet crochet chapter. The dc-and-chain-space grid is the base construction of all filet work.

content.text: A double crochet mesh table runner is a 30 × 120 cm cotton strip worked in

: a regular open-mesh grid of double crochets and two-chain spaces. The result is lightweight enough to layer over a tablecloth or use alone on a bare table; the mesh allows the surface underneath to show. Works in any DK cotton; a neutral colour or a natural undyed cotton suits most tables.

The runner is worked flat, back and forth, in rows. Each row starts with ch 5 (counts as first tr + ch 2) and ends with a tr into the last dc of the previous row. Block the finished runner wet for a flat, even mesh: cotton relaxes and the mesh squares become regular.
200 m DK cotton (100% cotton or linen-cotton blend). Two 100 m balls cover one runner in a single colour.
One mesh unit (1 dc + ch 2 + 1 dc) = 1.5 cm wide in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook, blocked. 8 rows = 10 cm tall, blocked. Work a 10-unit × 8-row swatch to check width and height before starting.
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
Treble (tr). UK term; US equivalent is double crochet (dc). Used only for the turning chain edge stitches.
Ch 63. (The foundation chain is a multiple of 3 plus 3 for the turning chain. 63 ch = 20 mesh units wide.)
1 tr into 6th ch from hook (counts as tr + ch 2 space), *ch 2, skip 2 ch, 1 tr into next ch; repeat from * to end (20 tr + 19 ch-2 spaces = 20 mesh units). Turn.
Ch 5 (counts as tr + ch 2). *1 tr into next tr, ch 2; repeat from * across, ending 1 tr into top of turning ch. Turn. (20 mesh units per row.)
Work rows until the runner measures 120 cm from the foundation chain, ending with a right-side row. At the stated gauge, this is approximately 96 rows. Fasten off.
Work one round of dc evenly around all four edges, with 3 dc into each corner. Sl st to join. Fasten off. The edging firms up the perimeter and keeps the mesh from rolling at the edges.

Weave in both ends. Wet-block the runner by submerging in cool water, squeezing gently, then pinning to size on a blocking mat. Pin the long edges straight and the short ends square. Leave until completely dry: usually several hours. The mesh squares become regular and the runner lies flat after blocking.
Machine-wash on a 30°C gentle cycle. Reshape and dry flat, or re-pin if needed after heavy washing.

title: Drawstring dry goods bag
subtitle: A closed-base cotton bag for storing loose grains, nuts, or coffee
excerpt: A 15 × 20 cm closed-base drawstring bag in DK cotton, for storing loose dry goods in the pantry or taking to a refill shop. Worked in double crochet in the round with a drawstring top. Beginner skill.
sourceNotes: Original pattern. Drawstring storage bags in cotton have been a domestic convention for centuries.

content.text: A drawstring dry goods bag is a 15 × 20 cm closed-base cotton bag worked in double crochet from a

. The base is worked as a small flat circle, then straight sides are worked up in the round, ending with a chain-space drawstring channel and a cord closure. Suitable for loose grains, nuts, coffee, or refill-shop dry goods. One 100 m ball makes two bags.
50 m DK cotton per bag. Plus 60 cm cotton cord or ribbon for the drawstring.
16 dc × 20 rows = 10 × 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook.
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
Round 2: 2 dc in each st (12 dc).
Round 3: *1 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (18 dc).
Round 4: *2 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (24 dc). Sl st to join.
Round 5: ch 1, 1 dc in each st, working into back loop only (24 dc). This creates a visible ridge at the base of the sides and helps the base lie flat. Sl st.
Rounds 6, 37: ch 1, 1 dc in each st through both loops (24 dc). Sl st each round. Work 32 rounds = approx. 16 cm of straight sides.
Round 38: ch 1, *1 dc, ch 2, skip 1; repeat from * around (12 ch-2 spaces). Sl st.
Round 39: ch 1, 1 dc in each dc, 2 dc in each ch-2 sp (24 dc). Sl st. Fasten off.
Weave in ends. Thread the 60 cm cord through the ch-2 drawstring spaces, entering and exiting at the same gap. Knot cord ends.
Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle. Hang to dry. Empty before washing: dry goods can be weighed out and transferred to jars between uses.

title: Filet crochet shawl
subtitle: A triangular shawl worked in filet mesh with solid block details.
excerpt: Filet crochet alternates open mesh squares with solid block squares to build pictures or geometric patterns into the fabric. This triangular shawl uses a simple diamond grid as its centrepiece worked in lace weight on a 3.5 mm hook.
sourceNotes: Filet crochet as a domestic craft is documented from the 1890s in Weldon's Practical Needlework series (Internet Archive). The open-mesh solid-block grid is the foundational technique of 20th-century filet pattern books. This shaping and chart are original to Homemade.

content.text: A filet crochet shawl is a triangular piece 170 cm across the wingspan and 80 cm deep at the centre back. The fabric is a grid of
squares, each one either open or filled in. Open squares let light through; solid squares build up the pattern.
The shawl is worked from the top back neck edge downward, increasing by two
squares per row at each side edge. A diamond grid sits in the centre panel, with
tracing the diamond outline against an open mesh background.

items.name: Lace weight yarn

content.text: 10 mesh squares x 10 rows = 10 x 10 cm in lace weight with a 3.5 mm hook, blocked. Work a 20-square-wide swatch across 15 rows, block it, and measure. The gauge determines the finished width. At 10 squares per 10 cm, the shawl reaches 170 cm at 170 squares wide.
: 1 tr, ch 2, skip 2 sts, 1 tr at the far edge
Ch 7 (counts as 1 open mesh square: 1 tr, ch 2, 1 tr in turning chain). Turn.

Ch 8 (counts as 1 increase open mesh at left edge). Work 1 tr into the ch-4 base of row 1 to close the new increase mesh. Ch 2, skip 2, 1 tr into the last ch. Ch 5. Work 1 tr into the same last ch (increase open mesh at right edge). Turn. (3 open mesh squares.)

Each right-side row increases by one open mesh at each edge using the ch-8 turn-and-fill method. Each wrong-side row mirrors the right side. Work in pattern following the chart: read right-side rows from right to left, wrong-side rows from left to right. The centre diamond appears from Row 15. Work 80 rows total.

Rows 15 to 45: The centre 11 squares of each row trace a diamond outline. On Row 15, the centre square is a solid block. On Row 16, the two squares either side of centre are solid. Continue expanding by two solid squares per row until Row 30 (the widest row of the diamond), then mirror back in to Row 45. All surrounding squares remain open mesh.
Work one row of double crochet around all three edges of the triangle.

title: Filet crochet table runner
subtitle: Traditional filled-and-open mesh in fine cotton thread
excerpt: A traditional filet crochet table runner in fine cotton thread: a 25 × 80 cm runner worked in trebles and chain spaces, with a simple border motif in filled squares across each end.
sourceNotes: Traditional filet crochet technique from Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, Chapter XI: Crochet. Filet table covers and runners are among the most extensively documented items in de Dillmont.

content.text: A filet crochet table runner is a 25 × 80 cm piece in size 10 cotton thread: a traditional table covering worked entirely in

, with a repeating geometric border motif of filled squares across each short end. The body of the runner is open mesh. Traditional filet work requires patience and attention to count: blocked flat, it has the look of drawn-thread work or cutwork linen.

items.label: 1.75 mm crochet hook (or as needed for thread)

content.text: 300 m size 10 crochet cotton thread (100% cotton). Approximately two 150 m balls in white or ecru.
1 mesh square (1 tr + ch 2 + 1 tr) = 0.7 cm wide in size 10 crochet cotton with a 1.75 mm hook. 10 mesh squares tall = 7 cm. Work a 10 × 10-square swatch to confirm before starting.
Treble (tr). UK term; US equivalent is double crochet (dc)
Double treble (dtr). UK term; US equivalent is treble (tr). Used for border lacets.
1 tr, ch 2, skip 2 sts or ch spaces, 1 tr (one open square = 1 mesh unit).
1 tr, 2 tr in the previous ch-2 space, 1 tr (one filled square = 4 tr together).
Ch 111. (35 mesh units wide requires 35 × 3 ch + 6 for turning chain = 111 ch.)
1 tr in 6th ch from hook, *ch 2, skip 2, 1 tr in next ch; repeat from * across (35 open squares). Turn.

Work all rows as open mesh: ch 5 (counts as tr + ch 2), *1 tr in next tr, ch 2; repeat across, ending 1 tr in top of turning ch (35 open squares per row). Turn. Repeat until the runner body measures approx. 55 cm from the foundation chain.
Border motif (worked over 20 rows at each short end)

Work the first 10 and last 10 rows as a simple repeating diamond motif: on border rows, replace alternating open squares with filled squares on a diagonal grid. Diamond motif (5 squares wide, 5 squares tall): open, open, filled, open, open / open, filled, filled, filled, open / filled, filled, filled, filled, filled / open, filled, filled, filled, open / open, open, filled, open, open. Repeat this 5-wide diamond 7 times across the 35-wide mesh, centred. Work the centre of the runner as plain open mesh between the two border ends.

Weave in both ends. Wet-block by submerging in cool water, squeezing out without wringing, and pinning to size on a blocking mat. Traditional filet linen is pinned using a scalloped edge along the treble posts. Leave until completely dry. This can take 12 hours or more for thread-weight cotton.
Handwash in cool water. Reshape and re-pin when needed. Fine cotton thread may be starched very lightly for table use: a thin starch solution adds body and keeps the mesh open between washes.

title: Filet mesh baby blanket

excerpt: Filet crochet uses a grid of open chain spaces and filled treble squares to make text or pictures. This baby blanket version works a simple heart motif in a treble grid.
sourceNotes: Filet crochet grid from Weldon's Practical Needlework (series 10, 1895). Internet Archive.

content.text: A filet mesh baby blanket is 70 x 80 cm. The fabric is a grid of trebles:
sit on the same base to make pictures or text. This version works a heart at the centre of a plain mesh.
Filet in DK cotton on a 3.5 mm hook gives a firm, clear grid with well-defined squares. The tighter hook than normal for DK stops the mesh from going too open. Total yardage is around 300 g.
14 mesh squares x 14 rows = 10 x 10 cm in DK cotton with a 3.5 mm hook. One mesh square = one open or filled unit. Measure 14 units across, not individual trebles.
An open square on the chart means work 2 ch, skip 2, 1 tr. A filled square means work 2 tr instead of the chain. Each square in the chart is one unit of your grid.
Chain 199 (66 mesh squares x 3 chains + 1 turning chain).
Ch 5 (counts as tr + 2 ch). Skip 3 ch. *Work tr, ch 2, skip 2, tr*. Repeat across. Turn. (66 open squares.)

Follow the grid chart, working filled squares where the heart falls and open squares everywhere else. The heart sits at rows 30 to 50, centred in the 66-square-wide grid. All other rows are plain open mesh.
Work 2 rounds of dc (UK) around the perimeter: 1 dc into each tr, 2 dc into each ch-2 space, 3 dc into corners.
. Block firmly by wet-blocking: pin to the stated dimensions while damp and allow to dry fully. The grid squares only show clearly when blocked.
Machine wash 30 degrees gentle. Reshape and dry flat. Reblock if the grid squares distort.
