title: Granny square, basic three rounds
subtitle: The starter motif behind every granny blanket
excerpt: The Victorian three-round granny square in DK cotton, twelve clusters of three trebles, separated by chain spaces, building outward from a magic-ring centre. The classic motif that joins into blankets, cushions, bags, and bunting. Twenty minutes per finished square once the rhythm is in the hands.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Crochet, volumes covering the 1880s, 1900s, the granny square as a household motif appears in multiple Weldon's volumes alongside afghan-square assembly instructions. Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), crochet chapter, documents the cluster-of-trebles construction that the granny square formalises. The three-round count and the colour-block convention come from twentieth-century afghan tradition; the underlying stitch structure is Victorian.

content.text: The granny square is the most-made motif in crochet. Three rounds of

, separated by single chains, build outward from a closed centre. The finished square is the building block of granny blankets, granny bags, granny cushion fronts, and the ubiquitous granny bunting. This pattern is the three-round starter: a single square at about 10 × 10 cm in DK cotton, the size most older afghan patterns assume.

The pattern below is written in UK terminology. UK "treble" is US "double crochet"; UK "double crochet" does not appear here. The renderer offers a UK / US terminology toggle for readers more comfortable in the US convention. The stitch counts and structure are identical either way.

About 20 g of the centre colour and 20 g of the outer colour will make one square with a margin to spare. Mercerised cotton (Drops Paris, Scheepjes Cahlista, Yarn and Colors Must-Have) gives the cleanest stitch definition. The pattern works in any DK yarn, but cotton holds the square shape best after blocking. The exercise here is the structure; the colour choice is the reader's.
Standard DK pairing. If your tension runs loose, drop to 3.5 mm to keep the square at 10 × 10 cm; if your tension is tight, move up to 4.5 mm.
Tapestry needle, sharp scissors, soft measuring tape.
The tapestry needle weaves in the cut ends, at minimum two per square (start tail and final tail), more when changing colour at each round.
A foam tile or a folded towel and four T-pins are enough. Blocking sets the cotton fibres into a true square and is the difference between a slightly-wonky motif and a precise one.

Each three-round granny square measures 9, 10 cm across the diagonal in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook, before blocking. Blocked, the squares settle to 10 × 10 cm with crisper corners. The gauge is not optional: a blanket of forty-five granny squares depends on the squares being the same size, and a single square that comes off 1 cm bigger throws every join and seam across the whole project. Make one square, measure, and adjust the hook size before committing to a full set.
the adjustable starting loop. The first round of the square is worked into the ring; the tail pulls it closed.
and as the chain spaces that separate clusters and form corners.
the main pattern stitch. Three trebles worked into a single chain space make one cluster.
joining stitch. Used to close each round into a circle and to move the hook across the work to the next start position.

The chart above shows the three rounds in symbol form. Read it alongside the written pattern below, the chart speaks the structure and the written speaks the detail. Either is enough on its own; together they cross-check each other.

. Ch 3 (counts as first treble), 2 tr into the ring, ch 2 (first corner space), [3 tr into the ring, ch 2] three more times. Sl st to the top of the beginning ch-3 to join. (12 tr, 4 ch-2 corner spaces.) Pull the tail to close the ring. Fasten off centre colour, leaving a 10 cm tail.

Join the outer colour with a sl st into any ch-2 corner space. Ch 3 (counts as first treble), [2 tr into the same corner space, ch 2, 3 tr into the same corner space], the first corner is now formed. The pattern for round 2 from here: ch 1, then *(3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr) all into the next ch-2 corner space, ch 1, repeat from * twice more. Sl st to the top of the beginning ch-3 to join. (8 clusters of 3 tr, 4 ch-2 corner spaces, 4 ch-1 side spaces.)

Sl st across the next 2 trebles to bring the hook to the corner space. Ch 3 (counts as first treble), 2 tr into the corner space, ch 2, 3 tr into the same corner space (first corner formed). *Ch 1, 3 tr into the next ch-1 side space, ch 1, (3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr) into the next ch-2 corner space*, repeat from * to * twice more. Ch 1, 3 tr into the final ch-1 side space, ch 1. Sl st to the top of the beginning ch-3 to join. (12 clusters of 3 tr, 4 ch-2 corner spaces, 8 ch-1 side spaces.)
Fasten off, leaving a 10 cm tail for weaving in. Square is complete.

Thread each tail onto the tapestry needle. Weave through three stitches in the back of the work, take a small backstitch to lock the tail, then weave another two stitches in the opposite direction. Trim the tail close to the work. With four tails (the magic-ring start, the centre-colour fasten-off, the outer-colour join, and the outer-colour fasten-off), one square needs about three minutes of finishing work, more than the crochet itself takes once the rhythm is in.

Pin the four corners to a foam blocking mat with the square stretched gently to 10 × 10 cm, measure the diagonal from corner to corner; it should be 14 cm (the diagonal of a 10 × 10 cm square). Hold a steam iron 2-3 cm above the pinned work and
for ten seconds, do not touch the iron to the fabric. Leave to dry pinned out (an hour or two in a warm room). Cotton blocks crisply and holds the square shape.

Granny squares in cotton handwash cool with wool wash or mild soap. Lay flat to dry, reshaping to the blocked dimensions if the wash distorts the corners. Machine washing on a wool cycle works for sturdy DK cotton but the cycle should be cool (30°C) and the spin gentle; the join seams between assembled squares are the failure point in machine washing, not the squares themselves.

The three-round granny is the entry point to a long line of variations. A six-round granny gives a 20 × 20 cm cushion-front-sized square; a continuous-colour granny is worked from a single colour for a more uniform finish; the solid granny replaces the chain spaces with extra trebles for a denser fabric. Once forty-five identical three-round squares stack up, a blanket-from-grannies is the natural next project, joining methods (whipstitch, slip stitch seam, or join-as-you-go) become the next thing to learn.

title: Granny square join blanket
subtitle: Classic four-round granny squares joined edge to edge.
excerpt: Forty-two classic four-round granny squares, joined as you go on the final round. Each square is 15 cm and the finished blanket is 90 x 105 cm in DK cotton.
sourceNotes: Granny square construction from Weldon's Practical Crochet (1st series, 1880s). The four-round square is the standard Victorian pattern square. Internet Archive.

content.text: A granny square join blanket is made from 42 classic four-round squares. Each 15 cm across, joined edge to edge as you crochet the final round of each new square. The finished piece is 90 x 105 cm, which drapes a standard single bed to the pillow line.

The join-as-you-go method means no sewing at the end: when you reach a corner or side chain on the final round. You slip stitch into the matching point on the neighbouring square instead of chaining. Work all squares in the same colour for a clean grid look. Or change colour square by square for a patchwork effect. Yardage for the solid version is 400 g DK cotton on a 4 mm hook.

One four-round granny square = 15 x 15 cm with a 4 mm hook in DK cotton, unblocked. Make one test square and measure across the centre from edge to edge. If it measures more than 15 cm, go down one hook size; if less, go up. At 15 cm per square, 6 across x 7 down gives 90 x 105 cm.
gr-cl: granny cluster, 3 tr into the same chain space.
Round 1: Ch 3. Work 2 tr into the ring. Ch 2. *3 tr into the ring, ch 2*. Repeat 3 more times. Sl st to top of ch-3 to close. Pull ring closed.
Round 2: Sl st across to first ch-2 corner space. Ch 3. Work into same corner space. *Ch 1. Work into next corner space*. Repeat from * to * twice more. Ch 1. Sl st to close.
Round 3: Sl st to corner. Ch 3. Work into corner. *Ch 1. Work 3 tr into ch-1 side space. Ch 1. Work into next corner*. Repeat 3 more times ending with ch 1. Sl st to close.
Round 4: Work as Round 3, adding one more ch-1 and 3-tr cluster on each side. Fasten off leaving a tail for weaving.

On the final square in a row or when placing a square adjacent to a completed square. Replace each joining ch-2 corner with "ch 1. Sl st into matching corner space of adjacent square, ch 1". And replace each joining ch-1 side with "sl st into matching side space of adjacent square". This creates a flat, invisible join.

Make the first 6 squares individually, then join each next square on Round 4 to its left-hand neighbour. When starting a new row. Join each new square to the square above as well as to the left. Work 7 rows of 6 squares each.

After joining. Work one round of dc around the entire blanket border: 1 dc into each stitch. 1 dc into each ch-1 side space, 2 dc into each ch-2 corner. And 1 dc into each join point. This smooths the outer edge and ties the squares into one fabric.

Use weaving in ends with the tapestry needle to secure all tails. Block: wet-block the cotton by submerging in cool water, squeezing out excess. And pinning flat to the stated dimensions. Allow to dry completely before unpinning.
Machine wash 30 degrees, gentle cycle. Reshape while damp and dry flat. DK cotton does not tumble dry well.
Try the granny hexagon blanket next, or the c2c blanket for a diagonal take on the same stitch.

content.text: A granny square placemat is four classic 15 cm squares in DK cotton, each built from a

centre and joined with a flat slip stitch seam. Finished size is 30 × 30 cm. Block each square flat before joining for a neat result. Works in a single colour throughout or in alternating colours per square.
80 m DK cotton per placemat (approx. 20 m per square). One 100 m ball makes one placemat plus a square or two extra.
Each granny square measures 15 × 15 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook, blocked. Four joined squares = 30 × 30 cm.
Treble (tr). UK term; US equivalent is double crochet (dc). Worked in clusters of 3.
MR: ch 3, 2 tr, ch 2, *3 tr, ch 2; repeat 3 more times. Sl st to top of ch 3. Pull tail to close ring. (4 clusters, 4 ch-2 corners)

Round 2: sl st to ch-2 corner sp. Ch 3, 2 tr, ch 2, 3 tr in same sp (first corner). *Ch 1, [3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr] in next ch-2 sp; repeat from * twice. Ch 1, sl st to ch 3. (8 clusters, 4 corners, 4 ch-1 side spaces)

Round 3: sl st to ch-2 corner sp. Ch 3, 2 tr, ch 2, 3 tr in same sp. *Ch 1, 3 tr in ch-1 sp, ch 1, [3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr] in ch-2 corner sp; repeat from * twice. Ch 1, 3 tr in last ch-1 sp, ch 1. Sl st to ch 3. (12 clusters)

Round 4: sl st to ch-2 corner sp. Ch 3, 2 tr, ch 2, 3 tr. *Ch 1, [3 tr in ch-1 sp, ch 1] twice, [3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr] in corner; repeat from * twice. Ch 1, [3 tr in ch-1 sp, ch 1] twice. Sl st to ch 3. Fasten off. (16 clusters)

Block all 4 squares. Lay them in a 2 × 2 grid. Holding two squares RS together, work a slip stitch seam through both back loops of matching ch-1 side spaces along one edge, pulling gently to avoid puckering. Join the four squares in two pairs, then seam the two pairs together to form the placemat.
Weave in all ends. Wet-block the assembled mat flat if needed.
Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle. Lay flat to dry.

content.text: A granny square sampler throw is 90 x 105 cm made from 42 squares, each 15 cm, in six different designs. All squares use the same
start and four rounds. They are joined with a
on the wrong side after blocking.

The six designs include the classic granny, a solid granny (no chain corners), a flower centre, a sunburst, a cross stitch granny, and a cluster granny. Use one yarn colour or several; a single colour shows the stitch differences most clearly. Total yardage is around 800 g in aran.
One four-round granny square = 15 x 15 cm with a 5 mm hook in aran yarn. Make one test square of each design to confirm consistent sizing before making all 42.
Classic granny: tr clusters with ch-2 corners, open sides
Solid granny: same as classic but ch-1 corners only, no open chain spaces

title: Granny strip table runner
subtitle: Granny squares joined into long strips for the table
excerpt: A table runner built from rows of granny squares joined together, 4 squares wide, 10 squares long. Each square is the classic three-round granny in DK cotton, joined with a slip-stitch seam.
sourceNotes: Granny square construction from Weldon's Practical Crochet, Series 2 (1886), Internet Archive. The join-as-you-go and slip-stitch seam methods are documented in Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776.

content.text: A granny strip table runner is 40 classic granny squares, 4 wide by 10 long: joined into a 36 × 90 cm table runner. Each square is worked from a
; the squares are joined with a slip-stitch seam. Works in one colour for a clean, modern look or in random leftover colours for a traditional patchwork effect.
300 m DK cotton in total. For a single-colour runner, three 100 m balls of the same colour. For a multi-colour runner, 8 m per square = approx. 320 m across as many colours as needed.
Each finished granny square measures 9 × 9 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook, lightly blocked.
Treble (tr). UK term; US equivalent is double crochet (dc)
Granny cluster: 3 tr into a ch-2 corner space
MR: ch 3 (counts as tr), 2 tr, ch 2, *3 tr, ch 2; repeat 3 more times, sl st to top of ch 3 to join (4 clusters, 4 ch-2 corner spaces).

Round 2: sl st to ch-2 corner space. Ch 3, 2 tr, ch 2, 3 tr into same corner space (first corner). *Ch 1, [3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr] into next corner space; repeat from * twice, ch 1, sl st to top of ch 3 (8 clusters: 2 per corner + 4 ch-1 side spaces).

Round 3: sl st to ch-2 corner. Ch 3, 2 tr, ch 2, 3 tr into corner. *Ch 1, 3 tr into side ch-1 space, ch 1, [3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr] into next corner; repeat from * 3 times, omitting last corner on final repeat, sl st to top of ch 3 (12 clusters: 2 per corner + 2 per side). Fasten off.

Arrange 40 squares in a 4-wide × 10-long grid. Hold two squares wrong sides together and work a sl st seam along one edge through both outer loops. Join squares row by row, 4 squares across, then join the rows lengthwise. The seam sits on the right side as a small raised ridge; reverse the direction alternately to prevent the runner from curling.
Weave in all ends: there will be at least 2 per square (40 squares = 80 ends minimum). Light wet-blocking on a mat evens the squares and flattens the seams. Pin to size and leave until dry.
Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle. Lay flat to dry. The cotton softens slightly with each wash.

title: Granny stripe baby blanket
subtitle: A simple stripe worked row by row in treble clusters.
excerpt: Rows of treble clusters in alternating colours make a fast, stretchy baby blanket in DK cotton. No joining, no motifs, just one long stripe after another.
sourceNotes: Stripe construction draws on the Victorian striped afghan tradition documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet (2nd series, 1880s, Internet Archive). Treble-cluster stripe is a modern simplification of the Victorian long-stitch strip.

content.text: A granny stripe baby blanket is 75 x 90 cm. Each row is a strip of treble clusters. The colours swap every row to build up the stripe.
The clusters are three trebles into the same chain space, the same move as a granny square corner. Each

happens at the end of a row, keeping the join on the wrong side. The finished fabric is stretchy and machine-washable. At the stated gauge it drapes a standard cot mattress lengthways with a little overhang.

content.text: 16 tr x 8 rows = 10 x 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook, unblocked. Work a 20-stitch swatch across 10 rows to check. If your swatch comes out wider than 10 cm, go down a hook size; if narrower, go up. At this gauge the blanket reaches 75 x 90 cm. Join Colour B to the ch-3 turning chain of Row 1. Ch 3. *Work 3 tr into the next ch-1 space, ch 1*. Repeat across. Work 1 tr into the top of the turning chain. Turn. Cut Colour A leaving a 15 cm tail. (40 gr-cl.)
Join Colour C. Work as Row 2. Cut Colour B. (40 gr-cl.)
Continue working one row per colour in the order A, B, C, A, B, C. Work 72 rows total (24 repeats of the three-colour stripe). Fasten off.

For a wider blanket: add stitches in multiples of 4 to the foundation chain. For a longer blanket: work more rows. Each 3-row stripe adds about 3.5 cm in height at this gauge. A single-bed size (90 x 120 cm) needs a foundation chain of 157 and 102 rows.

title: Half treble baby blanket
subtitle: A dense, drapey fabric halfway between double crochet and treble.
excerpt: Half trebles worked back and forth make a thick, compact fabric that sits between a double crochet and a treble in height. Good for baby blankets where warmth matters more than drape.
sourceNotes: Half treble stitch documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet (1st series, 1880s). Baby blanket application is modern. Internet Archive.

content.text: baby blanket is a 75 x 90 cm rectangle of htr worked back and forth on a 4 mm hook in DK cotton. The stitch produces a denser, more compact fabric than plain treble, which makes it slightly warmer and less prone to holes. The wrong side of a htr fabric shows a distinctive horizontal bar that some makers use intentionally as the right side.

DK cotton gives the best balance of softness and washability for a baby blanket in this stitch. Total yardage is about 380 g, slightly more than a treble blanket of the same size because the rows are shorter.

16 htr x 12 rows = 10 x 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook. At this gauge a foundation chain of 121 gives a 75 cm finished width. Check a swatch: htr gauge is noticeably tighter than treble gauge in the same yarn.
htr (UK) / hdc (US): half treble, one yarn-over before inserting the hook, then all three loops pulled through together
Row 1: Work 1 htr into the 3rd ch from hook (the first 2 ch count as 1 htr). Work 1 htr into every remaining ch. Turn. (120 htr.)
of ch 2 (counts as 1 htr). Skip the first stitch. Work 1 htr into every stitch across. Work 1 htr into the top of the turning chain at the end. Turn. (120 htr.)
Repeat Row 2 until piece measures 90 cm (approximately 108 rows). Fasten off.
Work one round of dc (UK) around the perimeter: 1 dc into each stitch and row end, 3 dc into each corner.
. Block lightly with steam if needed.
Machine wash 30 degrees gentle. Dry flat. The htr fabric holds its shape well without blocking.

The third-loop half treble blanket uses the same stitch inserted differently to produce a flat, fabric-like texture with no visible ridges. Or try the full treble blanket for a faster, more open fabric.

title: Heirloom lace shawl
subtitle: A fine lace weight shawl in shell and picot lace, advanced skill level.
excerpt: This heirloom shawl combines deep shell fans with picot arches and a six-row lace border to create a piece that can be passed down. Worked in lace weight on a 3.5 mm hook, the finished shawl is 180 cm wingspan and 85 cm deep at centre back.
sourceNotes: Shell and picot lace is one of the most enduring crochet traditions, documented in Irish crochet sources from the 1890s and in Weldon's Practical Needlework. Heirloom-quality lace shawls with detailed borders are well represented in early 20th-century pattern booklets (Internet Archive). This construction and border are original to Homemade.

content.text: An heirloom lace shawl is the most refined piece in the lacework collection. The body is a repeating column of seven-treble
. The border is six additional rows of increasing complexity, finishing with a deep scalloped
along the lower triangle edge. Worked in lace weight on a 3.5 mm hook and fully
, the shawl reaches 180 cm wingspan and 85 cm deep at the

This is an advanced pattern. Each body row has multiple stitch types in a fixed sequence and the border chart requires reading a six-row repeat without losing position. Set aside uninterrupted time for the border rows.

items.name: Lace weight yarn
items.substitutions: A fine merino or merino-silk lace weight takes blocking beautifully. Avoid very springy yarns as the fans compress back after pinning.

content.text: 1 shell fan (7 tr) + picot arch = 5 cm wide in lace weight with a 3.5 mm hook, blocked. Work one full body repeat swatch and block it before starting. The fan width determines the total wingspan at full stitch count. An unblocked fan is only 3.5 cm; blocking opens it to the full 5 cm.
dtr (UK): double treble, two yarn-overs before inserting hook

Ch 7. Work (3 tr, ch 3, 4 tr) into 7th ch from hook (first shell fan half at spine). Turn.
Ch 6. Work 1 dc into the 4th tr of the previous fan half. Work a
(ch 4, ch 3 sl st to base, ch 4). Work 1 dc into the turning ch space. Work (3 tr, ch 3, 4 tr) into the ch-3
space (spine increase fan). Work dc into turning ch of far side. Picot arch. Dc into 4th tr of the far fan half. Ch 6. 1 tr into the foundation base. Turn.

Each row grows by one shell fan on each side. The sequence for every row is: ch-6 edge arch, dc into far fan tr, picot arch, dc into ch-3 space between fans, *7-tr shell fan into dc position, dc into ch-3 space, picot arch, dc, picot arch, dc*, repeat to spine, spine fan (7 tr, ch 3, 7 tr), mirror back to right edge, ch-6 arch at right. Turn.
Continue working until the body measures 70 cm deep from the spine, measured straight down the centre back line. At this point work one plain dc row across the bottom edge to set the border start.
Row B1: Dc across the full bottom edge, 1 dc per stitch and 2 dc into each chain space. Turn.
Row B2: Ch 5. *Skip 2 dc, 1 tr into next, ch 2*. Repeat across. Turn. (Open mesh row.)
Row B3: Sl st into first ch-2 space. *7 tr into next space (shell fan), ch 3, dc into next space, ch 3.* Repeat across. Turn. (
Row B4: Dc into first tr. *Ch 3, picot (ch 3, sl st to base), ch 3, 1 dc into 4th tr of fan, ch 3, picot, ch 3, 1 dc into ch-3 arch.* Repeat across. Turn. (
Row B5: Work one row of plain dc, placing 1 dc per stitch and 3 dc into each picot loop. Turn.

Soak the shawl for 30 minutes, press out excess water in a towel, and pin aggressively. Pin each border scallop point separately using T-pins. Pin the wingspan corners first to 180 cm apart, then the centre spine point to 85 cm. Fill all border scallops between. Leave 24 hours to dry.

This is an advanced pattern. Each body row has multiple stitch types in a fixed sequence and the border chart requires reading a six-row repeat without losing position. Set aside uninterrupted time for the border rows.

items.name: Lace weight yarn
items.substitutions: A fine merino or merino-silk lace weight takes blocking beautifully. Avoid very springy yarns as the fans compress back after pinning.

content.text: 1 shell fan (7 tr) + picot arch = 5 cm wide in lace weight with a 3.5 mm hook, blocked. Work one full body repeat swatch and block it before starting. The fan width determines the total wingspan at full stitch count. An unblocked fan is only 3.5 cm; blocking opens it to the full 5 cm.
dtr (UK): double treble, two yarn-overs before inserting hook

Ch 7. Work (3 tr, ch 3, 4 tr) into 7th ch from hook (first shell fan half at spine). Turn.
Ch 6. Work 1 dc into the 4th tr of the previous fan half. Work a
(ch 4, ch 3 sl st to base, ch 4). Work 1 dc into the turning ch space. Work (3 tr, ch 3, 4 tr) into the ch-3
space (spine increase fan). Work dc into turning ch of far side. Picot arch. Dc into 4th tr of the far fan half. Ch 6. 1 tr into the foundation base. Turn.

Each row grows by one shell fan on each side. The sequence for every row is: ch-6 edge arch, dc into far fan tr, picot arch, dc into ch-3 space between fans, *7-tr shell fan into dc position, dc into ch-3 space, picot arch, dc, picot arch, dc*, repeat to spine, spine fan (7 tr, ch 3, 7 tr), mirror back to right edge, ch-6 arch at right. Turn.
Continue working until the body measures 70 cm deep from the spine, measured straight down the centre back line. At this point work one plain dc row across the bottom edge to set the border start.
Row B1: Dc across the full bottom edge, 1 dc per stitch and 2 dc into each chain space. Turn.
Row B2: Ch 5. *Skip 2 dc, 1 tr into next, ch 2*. Repeat across. Turn. (Open mesh row.)
Row B3: Sl st into first ch-2 space. *7 tr into next space (shell fan), ch 3, dc into next space, ch 3.* Repeat across. Turn. (
Row B4: Dc into first tr. *Ch 3, picot (ch 3, sl st to base), ch 3, 1 dc into 4th tr of fan, ch 3, picot, ch 3, 1 dc into ch-3 arch.* Repeat across. Turn. (
Row B5: Work one row of plain dc, placing 1 dc per stitch and 3 dc into each picot loop. Turn.
): Ch 1. *1 dc into dc, ch 3, picot, ch 3, skip 2 dc.* Repeat across. Fasten off.

Soak the shawl for 30 minutes, press out excess water in a towel, and pin aggressively. Pin each border scallop point separately using T-pins. Pin the wingspan corners first to 180 cm apart, then the centre spine point to 85 cm. Fill all border scallops between. Leave 24 hours to dry.

title: Herringbone half treble placemat
subtitle: Diagonal herringbone texture in cotton, 30 × 40 cm
excerpt: A 30 × 40 cm rectangle in herringbone half treble: a twisted variation of the half treble that creates a dense, diagonal texture. DK cotton on a 4.5 mm hook. Intermediate skill for the stitch technique.
sourceNotes: Original pattern. Herringbone half treble is a well-established stitch variant; this application to a placemat is an original composition.

content.text: A herringbone half treble placemat is a 30 × 40 cm rectangle worked in

: a stitch that pulls the working yarn through the first loop only before completing, producing a tight diagonal texture. The result is denser than standard htr with a woven look. DK cotton on a 4.5 mm hook gives a flexible, slightly padded placemat.
100 m DK cotton per mat. One 100 m ball per placemat, with a little left over.
18 hhtr × 16 rows = 10 × 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4.5 mm hook. The herringbone stitch pulls in more than standard htr. Use a slightly larger hook than usual.

Herringbone half treble (hhtr): yarn over, insert hook, draw up a loop (3 loops on hook), yarn over and draw through the first loop only (still 3 loops on hook), yarn over and draw through all 3 loops. This is the stitch throughout.
Row 1: ch 2 (t-ch, does not count as st), hhtr in 3rd ch from hook, hhtr in each ch across (54 hhtr). Turn.

All subsequent rows: ch 2 (t-ch), hhtr in each st across. The ch-2 turning chain does not count as a stitch. Work the first hhtr into the base of the ch-2 and the last hhtr into the last st of the previous row (54 hhtr). Turn.
Continue until mat measures 40 cm (approx. 64 rows). Fasten off.
The herringbone stitch has a strong directional pull. The mat may lean slightly to one side off the hook. This disappears completely with wet-blocking.
Weave in ends. Wet-block by pinning to size on a blocking mat and leaving until dry. This straightens the herringbone lean and softens the cotton.
Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle. Lay flat to dry.

title: Hexagon lace shawl
subtitle: Geometric hexagon motifs joined into a crescent shawl.
excerpt: Individual hexagon motifs in fingering weight are joined as you go into a crescent shape. The open mesh between motifs keeps the fabric airy and the geometric lines give it a modern edge.
sourceNotes: Hexagon motif construction draws on traditional Continental European hexagon lace traditions documented in 19th-century pattern books (Weldon's Practical Crochet series, Internet Archive). Crescent shaping and JAYG method are modern interpretations.

content.text: A hexagon lace shawl is built from individual
into a crescent shape. Each motif is 8 cm point to point after
. The finished shawl is 160 cm across the wingspan and 45 cm deep at the centre back.

The motifs are arranged in rows that increase by one hexagon on each row until the widest point is reached. Flat-joining keeps the surface smooth on both sides. The gaps between the motifs become part of the design, creating a lattice of open

items.name: Fingering weight yarn
items.substitutions: Any smooth lace or fingering yarn in natural or plant fibre blocks well.

content.text: One hexagon motif = 8 cm point to point with a 3.5 mm hook in fingering yarn, blocked. Work one motif and block it before starting the full shawl. If your motif is wider than 8 cm, go down one hook size. If narrower, go up. The crescent shaping depends on accurate motif size to stay flat.
dc (UK): double crochet, insert hook, pull through, two loops off together
tr (UK): treble, one yarn-over before inserting, three loops worked off two at a time
Foundation ring: ch 6, sl st to first ch to form a ring.
Round 1: Ch 3 (counts as 1 tr). Work 2 tr into ring, ch 2. *3 tr into ring, ch 2*. Repeat 5 more times. Sl st to top of ch-3 to close. (6 clusters, 6 ch-2 corner spaces.)

Round 2: Sl st into first ch-2 corner space. Ch 3. Work (2 tr, ch 2, 3 tr) into same space. Ch 1. *(3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr) into next corner, ch 1*. Repeat around. Sl st to close. (12 clusters, 6 ch-2 points, 6 ch-1 sides.)

Round 3: Sl st to corner. Ch 3. Work (2 tr, ch 2, 3 tr) into corner. *(Ch 1, 3 tr into ch-1 side space, ch 1, (3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr) into next corner)*. Repeat around. Sl st. Fasten off. (18 clusters, 6 points, 12 sides.)
The shawl is built in diagonal rows with the flat edge of the crescent at the top.
Row 2: Work 2 motifs side by side. On the second motif's Round 3,
to the first along one shared side: replace the ch-2 point with ch 1, sl st into matching point of adjacent motif, ch 1. Fasten off.

Continue adding one more motif per row. Each new row joins to the row above along the top points. Stagger the motifs so each one sits in the gap between two motifs in the row above, like a brick course. Work 9 rows total to reach the 160 cm wingspan.

Weave in all tails with the tapestry needle. Block the finished shawl by soaking in cool water for 20 minutes, pressing out excess water in a towel, and pinning each hexagon point to the blocking mat at the stated dimensions. Leave to dry fully before removing pins.
opens the chain spaces and makes the points sharp.

title: Hexagon motif table runner
subtitle: Joined flat hexagons in cotton, for a six-place table
excerpt: A table runner built from 18 flat hexagon motifs joined in two staggered rows. Each hexagon is 12 cm across, worked in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook. The finished runner is 24 cm wide and 90 cm long.
sourceNotes: Hexagonal motif construction from Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, crochet chapter. Victorian hex runners were worked in fine cotton thread; this version adapts the construction to DK weight.

content.text: A hexagon motif table runner is 18 flat hexagons in two staggered rows, each motif 12 cm across and joined with a
seam on the final round. The finished runner is 24 × 90 cm: long enough for a six-place table and wide enough to see. Each motif is worked from a
through four rounds. Block each motif flat before joining, and block the assembled runner once more at the end.
280 m DK cotton (approx. 15 m per hexagon for a single colour). Works equally well in a neutral or in alternating colours.
Each finished hexagon measures 12 cm across (flat side to flat side) in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook, blocked.
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
Treble (tr). UK term; US equivalent is double crochet (dc)
Hexagon motif (make 18 for the standard runner)
MR: ch 3 (counts as tr), 11 tr into ring, sl st to top of ch 3 (12 tr).
Round 2: ch 3 (counts as tr), tr in same st, ch 1, *2 tr in next st, ch 1; repeat from * 10 times, sl st to top of ch 3 (12 pairs, 12 ch-1 spaces).
Round 3: sl st to ch-1 sp. Ch 3, 2 tr in same sp, ch 1, *3 tr in next ch-1 sp, ch 1; repeat from * 10 times, sl st to ch 3 (12 clusters, 12 ch-1 spaces).

Round 4 (points): sl st to ch-1 sp. [Ch 3, 2 tr, ch 2, 3 tr] into same sp (one hex point). Ch 1, 3 tr into next sp, ch 1. Repeat this 2-step sequence 5 more times, 6 points and 6 flat sides. Sl st to top of ch 3. Fasten off.

Block all 18 hexagons to 12 cm flat before joining. Arrange in two staggered rows of 9: offset the top row by half a hexagon width. On the final round of each new hexagon, when you reach a joining side, replace the ch 2 at the hexagon point with ch 1, sl st into the corresponding point of the neighbouring hexagon, ch 1. At flat-side joins, replace ch 1 between clusters with sl st into the matching ch-1 space of the neighbour.
Weave in all ends. Wet-block the assembled runner and pin to size on the blocking mat. Leave until completely dry.
Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle. Lay flat to dry. Re-pin if needed to keep the hexagons flat after heavy washing.

in two separate rounds to give a layered look.

Round 2: 2 dc in each st (12 dc).
Round 3: *1 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (18 dc).
Round 4: *2 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (24 dc).
Round 5: *3 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (30 dc).

subtitle: An open-mesh pocket that holds a dish sponge near the sink
excerpt: A small open-mesh pocket that clips over the rim of a sink or hooks on a suction cup: holds a dish sponge and lets it drip-dry. Worked in fingering cotton in a simple mesh on a 3 mm hook. Beginner skill.
sourceNotes: Original pattern. Crocheted dish-sponge holders are a practical domestic convention.

content.text: A kitchen sponge holder is a small open-

pocket in fingering cotton: two small mesh rectangles joined at three sides, with a folded hanging loop at the top corner. The sponge tucks in, drips dry between washes, and the cotton holder machine-washes with your kitchen cloths. One 50 m ball of fingering cotton makes four holders.
15 m fingering cotton per holder. One 50 m ball makes four holders.
Gauge is not critical. The mesh should allow water to drain freely while holding the sponge securely.
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
Row 1: 1 dc in 6th ch from hook, *ch 2, skip 2, 1 dc in next; repeat from * across (6 mesh squares). Turn.
Rows 2, 8: ch 4 (t-ch, counts as dc + ch 2), *1 dc in dc, ch 2; repeat from * ending 1 dc in t-ch (6 mesh squares). Turn.

Hold two panels WS together. Sl st through both layers along the bottom edge and both side edges, leaving the top edge open (3 sides joined). At the top corner, ch 20 and sl st back to the same corner to form a hanging loop. Fasten off.
Weave in all ends. Hook the hanging loop on a suction hook near the sink, or loop over the tap. Tuck the sponge in through the open top.
Machine-wash on 40°C standard cycle together with kitchen cloths. The mesh dries quickly hanging in place.

excerpt: A linked treble connects each stitch to the one before by picking up a loop from the middle of the previous stitch. The resulting fabric has no gaps between stitches.
sourceNotes: Linked treble from Weldon's Practical Crochet (series 2, 1880s). Internet Archive.

content.text: baby blanket is 75 x 90 cm. Each stitch picks up a loop from the side of the previous stitch before completing the treble. The fabric has no side gaps and lies almost as flat as woven cotton.
DK cotton shows the dense fabric quality clearly. Total yardage is around 380 g. The linked stitch uses slightly more yarn than a standard treble because the extra loop adds height to each stitch.
How to work a linked treble

Yarn over. Insert hook into the upper horizontal loop on the side of the previous stitch. Pull up a loop (3 loops on hook). Yarn over, insert hook into the next stitch, pull up a loop (5 loops on hook). Yarn over, draw through 2. Yarn over, draw through 2. Yarn over, draw through 2. One linked treble made.

title: Magic ring granny motif blanket
subtitle: Small 4-round granny motifs joined as you go using the magic ring start.
excerpt: Each granny motif starts from a magic ring and is joined to its neighbours on the final round. The blanket is built motif by motif without a separate joining step.
sourceNotes: Granny square motif from Weldon's Practical Crochet (series 3, 1880s). Magic ring is a modern technique. Join-as-you-go is a modern joining method. Internet Archive.

content.text: A magic ring granny motif blanket is approximately 88 x 88 cm built from 121 small 4-round granny motifs. Each motif starts with a
and is joined to its neighbours on round 4 using

No sewing is needed to assemble the blanket. Each new motif is attached as its final round is worked. Total yardage is around 800 g in aran. Using two or three colours in rotation gives a scrappy or planned-colour result.
Round 1: Magic ring. Ch 3, 2 tr into ring, ch 2. *3 tr into ring, ch 2*. Repeat 3 times. Sl st to top of ch 3. Pull ring closed. (4 groups of 3 tr with ch 2 corners.)
Round 2: Sl st to corner space. Ch 3, 2 tr, ch 2, 3 tr into same space (corner made). *Ch 1, 3 tr, ch 2, 3 tr into next corner space*. Repeat 3 times. Ch 1. Sl st. (4 corners, 4 side ch-1 spaces.)
Round 3: Work corners as before. Work 1
into each side ch-1 space. Ch 1 between clusters. Sl st. (4 corners, 8 side clusters.)
Round 4: Repeat Round 3 structure, adding one more cluster to each side. Fasten off.

Work rounds 1-3 as normal. On round 4, when working the side that meets an existing motif: replace each ch-2 corner with ch 1, sl st into matching corner space, ch 1. Replace each ch-1 side gap with sl st into matching ch-1 space. This joins the motifs on the go.
Work in rows of 11 motifs. First row: 11 standalone motifs. Each subsequent motif in row 2 onward joins to the motif above and to the left on round 4.
Work one round of dc (UK) around the full blanket perimeter. Work 3 dc into each corner of each motif at the outer edge. Work 3 dc into each outer blanket corner.
. Block each motif as it is made if using wool. Block the finished blanket flat.
Machine wash 40 degrees normal. Dry flat. The join-as-you-go seams are as strong as the motif stitches.
The granny square join blanket uses the same motifs sewn together rather than joined live. Or try the granny stripe baby blanket for a continuous-row approach using granny clusters without motifs.

title: Mesh produce bag
subtitle: An open-mesh drawstring bag for fruit and vegetables
excerpt: An open-mesh drawstring bag for loose fruit and vegetables: worked in a simple chain-space mesh in fingering cotton from the base upward. One size fits most produce. A beginner pattern in one ball.
sourceNotes: Original pattern. Open-mesh reusable produce bags in cotton are a well-established domestic convention.

content.text: A mesh produce bag is an open-mesh drawstring bag in fingering cotton: worked in the round from a small base, with a simple chain-1 mesh throughout and a larger chain-3
near the top. The finished bag is 20 × 30 cm. Machine-washable, lightweight, and packs flat. One 50 m ball of fingering cotton makes one bag.
50 m fingering weight cotton. Plus 60 cm of thin cord or twisted cotton twine for the drawstring.
Exact gauge is not critical for a mesh bag. At ch-1 mesh on a 3 mm hook, each mesh square is approx. 0.7 × 0.7 cm.
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
Round 2: 2 dc in each st (12 dc).
Round 3: *1 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (18 dc).
Round 4: *2 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (24 dc).
Round 5: *3 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (30 dc). Sl st to join.
Round 6: ch 1, *1 dc in st, ch 1, skip 1 st; repeat from * around (15 mesh spaces). Sl st to ch 1. This starts the open mesh.
Rounds 7, 34: ch 1, *1 dc in dc of previous round, ch 1; repeat from * around (15 mesh spaces per round). Sl st each round. Continue until bag measures approx. 28 cm from base.
Round 35: ch 1, *1 dc in dc, ch 3, skip 1 st; repeat from * around (15 × ch-3 spaces). Sl st. This creates larger spaces for the drawstring cord.
Round 36: 1 dc in each dc and 2 dc in each ch-3 sp around. Sl st. Fasten off.
Weave in ends. Thread the 60 cm cord through the ch-3 drawstring channel spaces, entering and exiting at the same gap so both ends emerge on the same side. Knot the cord ends together.
Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle in a mesh laundry bag to prevent the drawstring cord tangling. Hang to dry.

subtitle: A 30 × 40 cm oval worked from a foundation chain in double crochet
excerpt: A 30 × 40 cm oval placemat in DK cotton, worked outward from a foundation chain in double crochet. Beginner-friendly and machine-washable: one 100 m ball covers two mats.
sourceNotes: Original pattern. Oval construction from a foundation chain is a standard crochet technique with no single primary source.

content.text: An oval cotton placemat is a 30 × 40 cm mat worked in double crochet outward from a foundation chain using

. Stitches are worked along both sides of the starting chain, then increased at each short curved end to keep the oval flat. A beginner technique. The shaping is methodical and the increases are easy to count. One 100 m ball of DK cotton makes two mats.
50 m DK cotton per mat. One 100 m ball covers two mats.
16 dc × 20 rows = 10 × 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook. For oval placemats, tension evenness is more important than exact gauge: check the oval lies flat after a few rounds.
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
Work in a continuous spiral with a stitch marker on the first st of each round. Ch 25.

title: Oven mitt pair
subtitle: A pair of double-layer oven mitts in 100% cotton
excerpt: A pair of simple rectangular oven mitts in 100% aran cotton: double-layer construction for heat resistance, with a hanging loop. 18 × 30 cm each. Intermediate skill for the double-layer finishing.
sourceNotes: Original pattern. Rectangular crochet oven mitts with double-layer heat resistance are a well-established domestic convention.

content.text: An oven mitt pair is two rectangular oven mitts, each with

: four panels in total, each worked flat in double crochet, then joined in pairs with a dc edging. 18 × 30 cm per mitt. 100% cotton only: synthetic blends are a fire risk. Two 100 m balls of aran cotton makes one pair.
200 m aran weight 100% cotton: two 100 m balls. Must be 100% cotton for safety.
14 dc × 18 rows = 10 × 10 cm in aran cotton with a 5 mm hook. Each panel: 25 sts × 54 rows = approx. 18 × 30 cm.
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
Row 1: ch 1 (t-ch), 1 dc in 2nd ch from hook, 1 dc in each ch across (25 dc). Turn.
All rows: ch 1 (t-ch), 1 dc in each st (25 dc). Turn.

Hold two panels WS together. With the 5 mm hook, work dc through both layers across the bottom (short) edge to seal the base (25 dc). Continue dc up the first long side, across the top (open end. Do not close), and down the second long side. Sl st to base dc. Fasten off.
At the open (wrist) end, work a round of dc through both layers around the opening to neaten. Make a hanging loop at one corner: ch 12, sl st to same st. Sl st to join. Fasten off.
Weave in all ends between the double layers. Repeat for the second mitt.
Machine-wash on 40°C standard cycle. Lay flat to dry. Replace mitts when the double layer becomes thin or worn: reduced fabric thickness means reduced heat protection. Do not use on open flames.

title: Overlay mesh shawl
subtitle: Surface overlay stitches worked across a lace mesh ground in fingering weight.
excerpt: An overlay mesh shawl has two layers of crochet: a lace mesh ground worked first, then a second layer of surface stitches worked on top to create a raised geometric pattern. The result looks woven from a distance and lacework close up.
sourceNotes: Overlay crochet technique developed in the late 20th century as an extension of traditional surface crochet, itself documented from the early 20th century. This shawl pattern is original to Homemade.

content.text: An overlay mesh shawl is made in two passes. In the first pass you work a triangular
of chains and trebles from the top down, increasing at each edge to build the triangle. In the second pass you work
across the ground using a contrasting or matching yarn to create the
pattern on top of the foundation.

The overlay gives the fabric a raised geometric quality: diamonds, chevrons, or grid lines appear to float above the lace mesh below. The work is advanced because you must read both the mesh grid and the overlay chart simultaneously.

items.name: Fingering weight yarn, main colour (MC)
items.substitutions: A smooth single-ply or lightly plied fingering in wool or cotton works best for the ground.

items.name: Fingering weight yarn, contrast colour (CC)
items.substitutions: Can also use MC for a tone-on-tone effect.

content.text: 18 mesh sts x 12 rows = 10 x 10 cm in fingering weight with a 3.5 mm hook, blocked. Work the gauge swatch in the MC only. The overlay adds body but does not significantly change the dimensions.
Mesh square: 1 tr, ch 2, skip 2, 1 tr
Foundation: ch 7. Work (2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr) into 5th ch from hook. Turn. This is the centre spine.

Increase row: Ch 5. 1 tr into first tr (left edge increase). Work mesh squares across to spine. Work (2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr) into spine ch-2 space. Continue mesh to end. Work (1 tr, ch 2, 1 tr) into turning ch space (right edge increase). Turn.
is 75 cm deep. Block the ground lightly before working overlay.
Attach CC at the top right corner of the blocked mesh ground. Insert hook from front to back through the first mesh square. Pull up a loop (

Diamond overlay repeat: *Cross diagonally up-right across 2 mesh squares (skip one, insert into the second). Cross diagonally down-right 2 squares. This makes one diamond half.* Continue across, building diamonds that are 4 squares wide and 4 rows tall. At each row of the ground, secure the overlay thread with a slip stitch before continuing the diagonal.
Work the overlay across the full width of the ground. Fasten off CC at the left edge. Reattach at the top of the next overlay row and repeat.
After overlay is complete, soak the full shawl and block to 160 x 75 cm.
melds both layers together. Pin the overlay threads gently so they sit flat against the ground without pulling.

items.cause: Losing track of the mesh square count

items.fix: Work overlay in short segments of 10 diamonds at a time. Cut CC and rejoin rather than carrying it across long distances.

title: Overlay mosaic throw
subtitle: Surface slip stitches overlay a base fabric to add a second colour pattern.
excerpt: Overlay crochet adds surface slip stitches on top of a plain treble background. Working rows of surface stitches in a second colour creates a simple geometric pattern without changing yarns mid-row.
sourceNotes: Surface slip stitch documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet (series 3, 1880s). Overlay pattern application is modern. Internet Archive.

content.text: An overlay mosaic throw is 90 x 100 cm. The base is a plain treble fabric in Colour A. After completing the base,
in Colour B are worked along the rows of the base to add a geometric pattern.

The two-step method avoids mid-row colour changes: the base is one solid colour and the overlay is applied separately. A simple diamond or stripe pattern is easiest for a first overlay project. Total yardage is around 600 g A and 150 g B.
14 tr x 8 rows = 10 x 10 cm in aran with a 5 mm hook for the base fabric.
surface sl st: slip stitch worked on the surface of the base
of ch 3. Work 1 tr into every stitch across. Tr into turning chain. Turn. Repeat until piece measures 100 cm (approximately 80 rows). Fasten off. Block the base fabric flat.

Using Colour B and holding yarn behind the work, insert the hook from front to back between the posts of two stitches on Row 1. Pull a loop through to the front. *Insert hook into the next space, pull a loop through and through the loop on the hook (surface sl st made)*.

Work horizontal lines of surface stitches every 4 rows across the base. Add diagonal lines crossing the horizontal at every 4th stitch for a diamond grid pattern. Cut Colour B between each line, leaving 10 cm tails.
Secure all Colour B tails with
on the wrong side. Work one round of dc (UK) around the perimeter in Colour A. Work 3 dc into each corner.
Machine wash 40 degrees normal. Dry flat. The surface stitches are secured through the base and hold through washing.
The staggered stripe throw adds colour mid-row using a different method. Or try the c2c blanket for a diagonal colour-block approach that needs no surface work.

title: Shell lace prayer shawl
subtitle: A wide, comforting shawl in dk weight shell lace, beginner-friendly.
excerpt: A prayer shawl in shell lace is wide, warm, and simple to make. This dk weight version uses a four-row shell repeat that is easy to memorise. The finished shawl wraps around the shoulders with plenty of fabric to spare.
sourceNotes: Shell lace is one of the oldest crochet stitch families, documented in Weldon's Practical Crochet (1880s) and Priscilla Crochet publications (early 1900s, Internet Archive). Prayer shawl knitting and crochet became a popular charity and spiritual practice from the 1990s onward. This pattern is original to Homemade.

content.text: A shell lace prayer shawl is 180 cm long and 70 cm wide, worked flat in rows. The
is four rows that are easy to remember after the first few: shell into chain space,
into shell centre, and back again. DK weight on a 4 mm hook gives a warm, drapy fabric.

itself is five trebles into one space. It fans out from a narrow base to a wide top and the shells stack on top of each other row by row, anchored in between by single double crochets. The rhythm is satisfying and meditative once established.

items.name: DK weight yarn
items.substitutions: Any soft DK in a wool-acrylic or bamboo blend works. Avoid very textured yarns as they hide the shell definition.

content.text: 1 shell (5 tr) + 1 dc = 4.5 cm wide in dk weight with a 4 mm hook. The row height is about 4 cm per two-row repeat. Work one shell repeat and measure before starting. At 4.5 cm per repeat, the shawl needs 40 shell repeats to reach 180 cm.
: 1 dc into centre tr of shell below

Ch 3 (counts as 1 tr). 2 tr into first dc (half shell at edge). *1 dc into centre tr of next shell, 5 tr (shell) into next dc.* Repeat to last shell. 1 dc into centre tr of last shell. 3 tr into last dc (half shell at edge). Turn.
Ch 1. 1 dc into first tr. *5 tr (shell) into next dc, 1 dc into centre tr of next shell.* Repeat across. End with 1 dc into top of turning ch. Turn.
Repeat Rows 1 and 2 until the shawl measures 180 cm. Fasten off and weave in all ends.
Work one row of dc (UK) along each short end: pick up one dc per row end, working into the side of each row. Fasten off. This gives the short ends a firm, even edge.
Follow the yarn label. Most DK wool-acrylic blends are machine washable on a gentle 30-degree cycle. Lay flat to dry to preserve the shell shapes. Do not tumble dry.

sourceNotes: Original pattern. Concentric granny-round construction is adapted from the classic granny square technique.

content.text: A round granny bath mat is a 50 cm disc built as a single large granny motif: concentric rounds of three-treble clusters from a central

Treble (tr). UK term; US equivalent is double crochet (dc). Worked in groups of 3.
MR: ch 3, 11 tr into ring, sl st to ch 3 (12 tr). Pull tail closed.
Round 2: ch 3 (counts as tr), tr in same st, ch 1, *2 tr in next st, ch 1; repeat from * 10 times. Sl st to ch 3 (12 pairs, 12 ch-1 sps, 24 tr).
Round 3: sl st to ch-1 sp. Ch 3, 2 tr in same sp, ch 1, *3 tr in next sp, ch 1; repeat from * 10 times. Sl st to ch 3 (12 clusters, 12 ch-1 sps).

Round 4: sl st to ch-1 sp. Ch 3, 2 tr in same sp, ch 1, 3 tr in same sp again (double cluster: two clusters in this sp for the first time). Ch 1, *[3 tr, ch 1, 3 tr] in next sp, ch 1; repeat from * 10 times. Sl st to ch 3 (24 clusters, 24 ch-1 sps).

Rounds 5, 7: each round, work 3 tr into every ch-1 sp from the previous round, with ch 1 between clusters. Add one extra cluster into a sp roughly every 12th sp to keep the mat lying flat and to slightly increase the circumference each round. Sl st to join each round. After round 7, measure, approx. 50 cm diameter. Fasten off.
If the mat starts to cup (go bowl-shaped), add an extra cluster into a sp every 8th cluster on the next round. If it ruffles, skip one sp every 10th cluster.
Weave in all ends. The chunky cotton lies flat without extensive blocking, but a light steam press around the edge helps.
Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle. Lay flat to dry. Use a non-slip bath mat underlay on wet bathroom floors.

Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
Treble (tr). UK term; US equivalent is double crochet (dc). Used in shells only.
Shell: 5 tr into the same st
Row 1: ch 1 (t-ch), 1 dc in 2nd ch from hook, 1 dc in each ch across (48 dc). Turn.
All rows: ch 1 (t-ch), 1 dc in each st (48 dc). Turn.
Work 80 rows total. Do not fasten off: proceed to the shell border.
Work in one round around all four sides, placing a shell every 6 sts (or 6 row-ends on the long sides) and a corner shell into each corner st.
Along the top edge: ch 1, 1 dc in corner, *skip 2 sts, shell (5 tr) in next st, skip 2 sts, 1 dc in next st; repeat from * 7 times along the 48 sts (8 shells across the top).

Sl st to ch 1 to join round. Fasten off.
Weave in both ends. The mat lies flat without blocking, but a light steam press opens the shells.

excerpt: A 120 x 150 cm aran-weight throw in plain treble rows. Nothing to count except the stitch total and the length. Finishes in a weekend on a 5 mm hook.

content.text: A simple treble throw is a 120 x 150 cm rectangle of plain treble rows worked back and forth in aran-weight yarn on a 5 mm hook. It is a one-stitch project: no stitch pattern to follow, no colour changes required. The only task is counting the row total and checking the length occasionally.

Aran-weight yarn covers ground quickly; at the stated gauge the throw reaches full length in around 105 rows. Wool or wool-blend aran produces a warmer, drapier fabric; acrylic is machine washable and cheaper. Total yardage is about 700 g.

of ch 3 (counts as 1 tr). Skip the first stitch. Work 1 tr into every stitch across. Work 1 tr into the top of the turning chain at the end. Turn. (167 tr.)

14 tr x 7 rows = 10 x 10 cm in aran yarn with a 5 mm hook. Make a 20-stitch swatch. At this gauge, a foundation chain of 169 gives a 120 cm finished width. If your gauge is tighter or looser, adjust the chain count accordingly.
tr (UK) / dc (US): treble, the single stitch used throughout
Row 1: Work 1 tr into the 4th ch from hook (the first 3 ch count as 1 tr). Work 1 tr into every remaining ch. Turn. (167 tr.)
of ch 3 (counts as 1 tr). Skip the first stitch. Work 1 tr into every stitch across. Work 1 tr into the top of the turning chain at the end. Turn. (167 tr.)
Repeat Row 2 until the piece measures 150 cm, approximately 105 rows. Fasten off.
For a neater edge, work one round of dc (UK) around the perimeter. Work 1 dc into each stitch along the top and bottom. Work 1 dc into each row-end on the sides. Work 3 dc into each corner.
, threading each tail along 3-4 stitches in the fabric. Block wool with steam. Acrylic needs no blocking.
Wool: handwash cool, squeeze in a towel, dry flat. Acrylic: machine wash 40 degrees, tumble dry low.

title: Small coiled rope basket
subtitle: A flat-bottomed basket made by coiling rope and joining with dc stitches.
excerpt: The coiled rope basket wraps rope in a spiral and joins the rounds with dc worked over the rope as a core. The dc anchors the rope coils together and adds colour.
sourceNotes: Coiled rope construction is a traditional basketry method adapted for crochet. No direct Weldon source. Contemporary documentation.

content.text: A small coiled rope basket is 18 cm across and 8 cm tall.
DC stitches worked over a rope core
join each new coil to the previous round while wrapping the rope in a contrasting colour of DK cotton. The result looks like traditional coiled basketry.
Use approximately 10 m of thick cotton washing line or similar rope (5-6 mm diameter) and 50 m of DK cotton for the joining yarn. A 4 mm hook works the dc over the rope.
Coil the rope into a tight circle about 3 cm across. Work dc stitches all around the coil to lock the centre tight. Approximately 12 dc for the first coil.
For each new round: hold the rope coil next to the previous round. Work 1 dc over the rope and into the stitch of the previous round (
). Space the stitches so the rope curves naturally without gaps or bunching. Add extra dc over the rope between the join stitches on wider rounds to keep it flat.

After round 6 (approximately 18 cm diameter), stop adding extra dc between joins. Work dc over rope and into previous round only. The sides will naturally begin to rise. Continue for 6 more rounds (approximately 8 cm tall). Cut rope, tuck end inside last dc, secure with sl st.
. Trim rope end closely inside the basket.
Spot clean. Do not machine wash rope baskets. Reshape while damp.
The basic round basket uses the same dc-in-spiral technique without the rope core. Or try the oval basket for a larger coiled version.

Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
Round 2: 2 dc in each st (12 sts).
Round 3: *1 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (18 sts).
Round 4: *2 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (24 sts).
Rounds 5, 7: 3 rounds straight dc (24 sts). These rounds form the cup side.
Round 8 (hanging slots): *3 dc, ch 3, skip 3; repeat 4 times (4 slots made). Sl st to join.
Thread a 50 cm length of yarn through the 4 chain slots to form the gathering cord. Draw up tight. Tie the two ends through the curtain rod or ring. Fasten off and weave in.
Weave in the magic ring tail. The cup can be lightly steam-blocked to firm the base.
Handwash in cool water. Reshape the cup while damp. Lay flat to dry before rehanging.

title: Solomon's knot throw
subtitle: Extended loop knots form an open lace-like mesh across an aran throw.
excerpt: Solomon's knot pulls a long loop and locks it with a dc, then repeats to build an open knotted mesh. The result is a lightweight lace-like throw in aran weight.
sourceNotes: Solomon's knot from Weldon's Practical Crochet (series 4, 1880s). Open knot mesh. Internet Archive.

content.text: throw is 90 x 100 cm. Each knot is one long pulled loop locked with a dc. Rows of knots connect at their lock stitches to build an open mesh that looks like lace.

Aran weight makes the knots large enough to work comfortably. The mesh uses much less yarn than solid fabric. Total yardage is around 450 g. Solomon's knot is considered advanced because the open mesh has no defined base row and the lock points can shift if the long loops are not pulled to a consistent height.

Pull the working loop up to about 2 cm (the knot height). Yarn over and draw through (chain made). Insert hook under the back loop of this long chain. Yarn over and draw up a loop (2 loops on hook). Yarn over and draw through both loops. One knot made.
5 knots x 6 rows = 10 x 10 cm in aran with a 5 mm hook. Pull every knot to exactly the same 2 cm height for an even mesh. Practice on a test swatch until the knot height is consistent.
dc (UK) / sc (US): double crochet (lock stitch of each knot)
Make a slip knot and work 46 SK in a chain. This forms the base of the mesh (one row of knots).
of 2 SK at end of foundation. *Work 1 dc into the lock dc of every 2nd knot, then 2 SK*. Repeat across. Turn. (22 mesh pairs.)
Work 2 SK, *1 dc into the lock dc between two knots from below, 2 SK*. Repeat. Turn.
Continue until piece measures 100 cm. Fasten off.
Work one round of dc (UK) around the perimeter: 1 dc into each lock stitch and 2 dc across each knot gap. Work 3 dc into each corner.
. Block firmly by wet-blocking and pinning to the stated dimensions.
Handwash cool. Pin flat while damp. The mesh structure opens when wet and must be pinned back to size.

Pull up an elongated loop (about 1 cm) from each of 5 consecutive stitches. (6 loops on hook.) Yarn over and draw through all 6 loops. Ch 1 to lock. One spider cluster made from 5 stitches.

title: Square lace shawl
subtitle: A flat square worked from one corner in fingering weight open mesh.
excerpt: Starting from a single chain at one corner and increasing on every row builds a flat square shawl in fingering weight lace mesh. Simple but elegant, the geometry is self-evident from the first row and the shawl can stop at any size.
sourceNotes: Corner-to-corner square shawl construction is a classic format documented in early 20th-century American and British pattern booklets. Lace mesh ground and picot border are traditional finishing elements. This version is original to Homemade.

content.text: A square lace shawl starts at one corner with a single chain and is worked diagonally outward, increasing at the corner on every row, until the square reaches 130 x 130 cm. The fabric is plain
: one treble, two chains, skip two chains, repeated. Nothing more complex than that.
at the start and end of every row is the one technique that needs attention. Everything else is the same mesh repeat all the way to the final row. A
edging along all four sides finishes the corners sharply.

At 15 squares per 10 cm, the shawl needs 195 squares across the widest row to reach 130 cm. The shawl grows by 2 squares per row, so it takes 97 rows to reach full width.

into that turning ch space (right corner increase). Turn. (Each row adds 2 mesh squares.)
Work until the piece measures 65 cm diagonally from the starting corner to the current row edge. At this point the full 130 cm diagonal is halfway complete. Continue to 97 rows total.

made), skip 1 dc*. Repeat around. Fasten off.
Soak the shawl, press out water without wringing, and lay flat on blocking mats. Pin each of the four corner points to form a true square at 130 x 130 cm. Pin along each edge every 5 cm.

title: Staggered stripe throw
subtitle: Offset colour blocks in short treble sections make a brick-like stripe.
excerpt: Working short sections of colour across each row and offsetting them by half a repeat every two rows makes a staggered brick-stripe pattern on an aran-weight throw.
sourceNotes: Brick-pattern intarsia from the colour-section family. No direct Weldon source; synthetic from colour-block construction principles.

content.text: A staggered stripe throw is 90 x 100 cm. Each row has sections of 14 trebles in Colour A and 14 in Colour B. The sections offset by 7 stitches every two rows to make a brick-like stagger across the fabric.

method uses a separate bobbin for each colour section. This avoids long floats on the back. A two-colour version with strong contrast gives the clearest brick pattern. Total yardage is around 700 g (350 g per colour).
14 tr x 8 rows = 10 x 10 cm in aran with a 5 mm hook.
mid-row: work the last tr of the old colour until 2 loops remain on the hook. Drop old colour to the back and pull the new colour through the final 2 loops. The new colour begins.
Using Colour A, chain 127 (126 tr + 1 turning chain).
Ch 3. Work 13 tr in Colour A. *Change to Colour B, work 14 tr. Change to Colour A, work 14 tr*. Repeat. Turn. (9 x A sections, 9 x B sections approximately.)
Shift the colour boundary by 7 stitches to the right at the start of this row and every 2 rows. This creates the stagger. Carry the change across all rows.
Continue for 80 rows (100 cm). Fasten off and close all bobbins.

content.text: A striped half treble table runner is 30 × 90 cm of two-colour stripes worked flat in half treble crochet. The stripes are two rows wide throughout; a

on the final yarn-over of each two-row stripe keeps the edges clean. At the stated gauge, the runner takes 90 rows total, 45 two-row stripe pairs. Works equally well in two neutrals or in a bold contrast.
150 m DK cotton in colour A (main). 150 m DK cotton in colour B (contrast). Two 100 m balls of each colour, with some left over from each.
18 htr × 14 rows = 10 × 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook, lightly blocked.
Half treble (htr). UK term; US equivalent is half double crochet (hdc)
With colour A, ch 57. (The foundation chain sets the width, 54 ch for the htr stitches, plus 3 turning chain. Each htr occupies approximately 0.55 cm at this gauge; 54 htr = approx. 30 cm.)
Row 1 (colour A): ch 3 (t-ch, counts as htr), htr in 3rd ch from hook, htr in each ch across (54 htr). Turn.

Row 2 (colour A): ch 2 (t-ch, does NOT count as a stitch. Work first htr into the base of this ch 2), htr in each st to end, htr into top of t-ch from row 1 (54 htr). On the final yarn-over of the last htr, pull through with colour B. Drop colour A at the side. Turn.
Rows 3, 4 (colour B): same as rows 1, 2. Change to colour A on final yarn-over of row 4.
Continue alternating 2 rows colour A / 2 rows colour B until the runner measures 90 cm from the foundation chain (approx. 90 rows total, 45 stripe pairs). Fasten off both colours.

Carry the yarn not in use up the side edge rather than cutting it at every stripe change. Loop the carried yarn loosely around the working yarn at the turn so it doesn't pull the edge in. This halves the number of ends to weave in.
Weave in all ends along the side edges. Light wet-blocking lays the runner flat and sharpens the stripe edges. Pin to size and leave until dry.
Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle. Lay flat to dry. The cotton softens with each wash.

title: Third loop half treble blanket
subtitle: Working into the third loop of htr makes a flat ribbed surface.
excerpt: The half treble has three loops at the top instead of the usual two. Inserting the hook into the third loop only makes a flat, ribbed fabric with a fabric-like hand on both sides.
sourceNotes: Third-loop htr is a modern technique refinement. No direct Weldon source. Synthetic from technique documentation.

content.text: htr baby blanket is 75 x 90 cm. The hook goes into the extra loop that sits below the two normal top loops of each half treble. Both sides of the fabric look the same and the surface is flat and smooth with a subtle horizontal rib.
DK cotton shows the flat rib most clearly. The third-loop stitch uses slightly more yarn than regular htr because the loop is a little tighter. Total yardage is around 400 g.

With the right side facing and the row just completed lying flat, look at the top of each htr. You will see two front loops as normal. Tilt the work away from you slightly: the third loop is the horizontal strand running behind and below the two main loops. Insert the hook under this loop only.

title: Three-tier cascading plant hanger
subtitle: Three cups at staggered heights, one hanging cord
excerpt: A three-tier cotton plant hanger with cups at three heights: works for trailing plants or a cascade of small succulents and herbs. Worked in worsted cotton with a 5 mm hook.
sourceNotes: Original design derived from staggered-tier plant hanger conventions common in 1970s craft publications. No single primary source.

content.text: A three-tier cascading plant hanger holds three pots at staggered heights on one hanging cord. The top holds a small 10 cm pot, the middle and bottom hold 13 cm pots. Each cup is worked in the round from a
, then connected by a single cord that runs up through all three cups to a gathered top ring. The hanger works best with trailing plants at the bottom and compact ones above.

The cord runs as one continuous length: work the bottom cup, cord up to the middle cup, cord up to the top cup, then gather and hang. Total yarn: roughly 200 m of aran cotton. A single 200 m ball covers the whole hanger.
200 m aran cotton (100% cotton). One ball is enough for all three cups and the cord.
1 metal ring, 2, 3 cm diameter, for the hanging loop.
14 dc × 18 rows = 10 × 10 cm in aran cotton with a 5 mm hook, unblocked. Gauge is approximate. The cup size adjusts by changing chain count. A looser tension gives a more open, airy cup.
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
Treble (tr). UK term; US equivalent is double crochet (dc)
Start with the bottom cup. Work each cup in a continuous spiral with a stitch marker on the first st of each round.
Round 2: 2 dc in each st (12 sts).
Round 3: *1 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (18 sts).
Round 4: *2 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (24 sts).
Round 5: *3 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (30 sts).
Round 6: *4 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (36 sts).
Rounds 7, 10: work 4 rounds straight, no increases (36 sts).
Sl st to join. Do not fasten off: proceed straight to the cord.
Cord from bottom to middle cup
Ch 3 (counts as tr), 1 tr into next st, 1 tr into next st (3 tr). Turn.
Ch 3, 2 tr in the 3-tr group. Turn. Repeat for 22 rows, or until the cord measures 20 cm.

At the end of the cord, sl st the cord to itself to form a joining bar, then pick up stitches around that bar and work the middle cup the same as the bottom cup (rounds 1, 10, 36 sts). When the middle cup is done, work another cord section of 18 rows (approx. 18 cm).
Round 2: 2 dc in each st (12 sts).
Round 3: *1 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (18 sts).
Round 4: *2 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (24 sts).
Round 5: *3 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (30 sts).
Work cord: ch 3, 1 tr in each of next 2 sts, turn. Ch 3, 2 tr in group. Repeat for 14 rows (approx. 14 cm).
Thread the tail through the metal ring and knot tightly. Fasten off.
Weave in all ends. Check that each cup hangs level. The pot should sit flat without tipping. If a cup hangs at an angle, re-position the cord attachment point one stitch over.
Handwash in cool water. Rinse and squeeze gently. Hang to dry. Cotton is machine-washable on a 30°C gentle cycle: remove the pots first.

to create an open lace fabric. The

3 fan repeats x 8 rows = 10 x 10 cm after blocking. Gauge is approximate in lace; finished size is more important than row count.

Fan repeat (worked over 9 sts): dc, ch 3, skip 3, 5 tr in next st, ch 3, skip 3, dc. On the following row work chain spaces into the tr cluster. The spine increase is 3 tr into the centre chain space on every right-side row.

title: Triple herb window hanger
subtitle: Three small cups in a row on a kitchen window rod
excerpt: Three small 8 cm cups crocheted in DK cotton and threaded onto a wooden dowel or curtain rod, for keeping three small herb pots at the kitchen window. Simple in-the-round construction.
sourceNotes: Original design. No primary source.

content.text: A triple herb window hanger keeps three small 8 cm herb pots at the kitchen window on a wooden dowel or curtain rod. Each cup is worked in double crochet in the round from a
; the top edge has chain loops that thread directly onto the rod. Works well with basil, thyme, and rosemary side by side.
90 m DK cotton total (one 100 m ball is enough for all three cups, with some left over). Work in one colour or use a different colour for each cup.
A wooden dowel or narrow curtain rod, 35 cm minimum length.
16 dc × 20 rows = 10 × 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook, unblocked.
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
Round 2: 2 dc in each st (12 sts).
Round 3: *1 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (18 sts).
Round 4: *2 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (24 sts).
Rounds 5, 7: 3 rounds straight dc (24 sts). Cup walls.
Round 8 (rod slots): *2 dc, ch 5, skip 2; repeat 6 times (6 chain loops) (24 sts + 6 loops). Sl st to join. Fasten off.

Thread the rod through the chain loops on the top round of each cup, spacing the cups evenly along the rod: about 10 cm between centres. Hang the rod on two hooks, curtain rings, or cord tied to each end.
Weave in all ends. The cups may be lightly steam-blocked to keep the base flat.

title: Triple treble lap blanket
subtitle: Very tall stitches make a dramatic open lattice in chunky yarn.
excerpt: Triple trebles need three yarn-overs and are nearly twice the height of a double treble. Worked in chunky yarn they form a dramatic open lattice that makes a quick lap blanket.
sourceNotes: Triple treble stitch from Weldon's Practical Crochet (series 1, 1880s). Internet Archive.

content.text: lap blanket is 80 x 90 cm. The very tall stitches mean the blanket needs only about 27 rows to reach 90 cm in chunky yarn. The gaps between stitches are large and give the fabric a dramatic open look.

Chunky yarn keeps the open stitch from becoming too flimsy. A fine yarn would produce a lacework-like fabric; chunky gives enough body for a lap blanket. Total yardage is around 350 g because the tall open stitch uses less yarn than a dense fabric.
How to work a triple treble
Yarn over 3 times. Insert hook into stitch. Pull up loop (5 loops on hook). *Yarn over, draw through 2 loops*. Repeat 4 times. One trtr made.
7 trtr x 3 rows = 10 x 10 cm in chunky with an 8 mm hook. Each row gains a lot of height; check after 5 rows to confirm the pace.
of ch 5. Work 1 trtr into every chain from the 6th. Turn. (56 trtr.)
Ch 5. Skip the first stitch. Work 1 trtr into every stitch. Work 1 trtr into the top of the turning chain. Turn.
Repeat Row 2 until piece measures 90 cm (approximately 27 rows). Fasten off.

Work 2 rounds of dc (UK) around the perimeter. Work 1 dc into each trtr along top and bottom. Work 3 dc into each row-end gap on the sides. Work 3 dc into each corner. The edging closes the very open side edges.

title: Tunisian lace shawl
subtitle: A rectangular shawl in Tunisian simple stitch with openwork panels.
excerpt: Tunisian crochet uses a long hook to hold all live stitches across the row like knitting, then works them off in a return pass. This shawl alternates solid Tunisian simple stitch columns with openwork chain panels for a woven-looking lace fabric.
sourceNotes: Tunisian crochet (also called Afghan stitch) is documented from the 1860s in British needlework manuals. Openwork-panel variations appear in 20th-century pattern booklets. This shawl construction and panel repeat are original to Homemade.

content.text: A Tunisian lace shawl is a flat rectangle 180 cm long and 55 cm wide worked entirely in Tunisian crochet with a long-tail or interchangeable hook. The fabric alternates bands of solid
of chains and single stitches that run the full length of the shawl. Blocked, the panels open into wide lace ladders.
Every row has two phases. The
picks up loops across the row from right to left, leaving them all on the hook. The
then works them off from left to right until one loop remains. This is the engine of all Tunisian work.

items.name: 5 mm Tunisian crochet hook (long, at least 40 cm)

content.text: 18 Tss x 16 rows = 10 x 10 cm in sport weight with a 5 mm Tunisian hook, unblocked. Tunisian fabric does not change dramatically with blocking, but does relax slightly. Work a 25-stitch swatch across 20 rows and measure unblocked.
: Tunisian simple stitch, insert hook behind front vertical bar, pull up loop
: return pass, ch 1, *yo, pull through 2 loops* to end

Ch 100. FP: insert hook into 2nd ch from hook, pull up loop. Continue pulling up 1 loop from each ch across. (100 loops on hook.) RP: ch 1, *yo, pull through 2 loops*. Repeat to end. (1 loop remains.)

The pattern repeats across 10 stitches: 6 Tss, then 1 ch-2 openwork panel (skip 2, ch 2, pick up 1 Tss), then 1 Tss to anchor. Work this repeat across all 100 foundation stitches (10 repeats of 10). Follow with RP.
On the next row, work 6 Tss over the Tss column. For the openwork section, insert the hook into the ch-2 space and pull up one loop as if it were a stitch. This is the
repeat that keeps the ladders aligned on every row.

Continue working FP and RP with the 10-stitch pattern until the piece measures 180 cm. At 16 rows per 10 cm, this is approximately 288 rows. The fabric will bias slightly. This is normal for Tunisian and corrects on blocking.
On the final forward pass, instead of leaving loops on the hook, work sl st into each Tss and ch-2 space across. This is the Tunisian cast-off row. Fasten off.
Soak, press out water, and pin the rectangle to 180 x 55 cm on blocking mats. The Tunisian bias flattens on blocking. The openwork panels open into full-width lace ladders only after wet blocking.

title: Twin-pot plant hanger
subtitle: Two side-by-side cups on one hanging bar
excerpt: Two cups hang side by side on a single horizontal bar hanger: holds two 10, 12 cm pots at the same height. Worked in DK cotton on a 4 mm hook.
sourceNotes: Original design. Side-by-side dual-pot hangers are a contemporary convention with no historical primary source.

content.text: A twin-pot plant hanger holds two 10, 12 cm pots side by side on a horizontal crochet bar. Each cup is worked in double crochet in the round from a
; the cups attach to a central bar that hangs from a single cord. The pair balance well with herbs of similar weight, or one trailing plant and one compact upright.
150 m DK cotton. A single 100 m ball plus a small leftover ball covers the piece.
1 wooden dowel, 30 cm long, 1 cm diameter, for the hanging bar. A bamboo skewer or craft dowel works well.
16 dc × 20 rows = 10 × 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook, unblocked.
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
Work both cups identically. A stitch marker on the first stitch of each round helps track the spiral.
Round 2: 2 dc in each st (12 sts).
Round 3: *1 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (18 sts).
Round 4: *2 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (24 sts).
Round 5: *3 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (30 sts).
Sl st to join, fasten off leaving a 60 cm tail.
Thread the tail from each cup through the rim stitches at 4 points (quarter-points around the top rim).
Draw the tails through and wrap them tightly around the dowel at a point 5 cm in from each end. Knot securely.
Weave in the tails or trim and wrap with a small length of yarn.
Cut two 70 cm lengths of yarn. Loop each over the dowel, 3 cm from each end. Tie a square knot at the top of each loop.
Bring the four yarn ends together at the top and tie in a single knot at the height where the hanger should balance. This forms the hanging loop.
Weave in all ends. Test the balance with both pots filled: adjust the hanging knot position until the bar hangs level.
Remove pots before washing. Handwash in cool water, reshape the cups, and lay flat to dry. Rehang when dry.
