content.text: blanket is a 75 x 90 cm piece made by working two trebles with one chain between them into the chain space of each V from the previous row. The result is an open, semi-lacy fabric that is lighter than a solid treble blanket and shows the stitch repeat cleanly in smooth DK cotton.

DK cotton in a pale colour works best here because the open structure is the visual interest. In a variegated yarn the V pattern disappears into the colour changes. Total yardage is around 280 g, less than a solid blanket of the same size because of the open gaps.
8 V-sts x 8 rows = 10 x 10 cm in DK cotton with a 4 mm hook. Work a sample of 16 V-sts across 8 rows to check. Each V is about 1.2 cm wide; at this gauge 60 V-sts across gives 75 cm.
V-st: (tr, ch 1, tr) all into the same space
of ch 3. Skip 2 ch. Work (tr, ch 1, tr) into next ch (one V-st made). *Skip 2 ch. Work V-st into next ch*. Repeat to last 3 ch. Skip 2 ch. Tr into last ch. Turn. (75 V-sts.)
Ch 3. *Work V-st into the ch-1 space of each V-st from previous row*. Tr into top of turning chain. Turn. (75 V-sts.)
Repeat Row 2 until piece measures 90 cm (about 72 rows). Fasten off.
Work one round of dc (UK) around the perimeter: 1 dc into each tr, 1 dc into each ch-1 space, 2 dc into each corner. This fills the open edges and stabilises the border.
with the tapestry needle. Block lightly with steam to open the V spaces.
Machine wash 30 degrees gentle. Dry flat.

title: Waterfall lace shawl
subtitle: Cascading chevron lace rows worked top down in fingering weight.
excerpt: Chevron lace rows angle downward from the spine to create a cascading waterfall effect across a crescent shawl. The repeat is a four-row pattern that is straightforward to memorise after the first few repeats.
sourceNotes: Chevron lace construction synthesised from traditional zigzag lace principles present in 19th-century Shetland and Irish crochet sources. Top-down crescent shaping is a modern adaptation. Original pattern by Homemade.

content.text: A waterfall lace shawl is a crescent worked top down from the back neck edge. A central

of double increases grows the width as you go; chevron lace rows angle outward from it to create a cascading diagonal effect. The finished shawl is 155 cm across and 50 cm deep at centre back, blocked.
decreases to shift the columns of holes diagonally. After two pattern repeats (eight rows) the diagonal rhythm becomes easy to follow without counting every stitch.

items.name: Fingering weight yarn
items.substitutions: A wool or wool-silk fingering weight blocks well and holds the chevron angles sharply.

content.text: 16 dc (UK) x 10 rows = 10 x 10 cm in fingering weight with a 3.5 mm hook, blocked. The chevron lace fabric tends to be looser than plain double crochet; use a tighter tension gauge swatch in the actual pattern stitch if your yarn relaxes significantly.
Ch 5. Work (1 tr, ch 2, 1 tr) into the 5th ch from hook (one corner made). Turn. Row 1 (increase row): Ch 4 (counts as 1 tr, ch 1). 1 tr into same base stitch. Ch 2. (1 tr, ch 2, 1 tr) into the ch-2
space. Ch 2. (1 tr, ch 1, 1 tr) into the last tr. Turn. You now have 3 sections either side of the centre spine.

Row A (right side): Ch 3, 1 tr into first ch-1 space. *Ch 2, skip, dc2tog over next 2 sts, ch 2, 1 tr into next space*. Work across to spine, work (2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr) into spine space (spine increase). Work back to match the other side. Turn.
Row B (wrong side): Ch 3, 1 tr into ch-1 space. *Ch 2, 1 dc into ch-2 space, ch 2, 1 tr into next tr*. Repeat to spine, work (2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr) into spine. Mirror to end. Turn.
Row C (right side): Ch 3, *ch 2, dc2tog, ch 2, 1 tr*. Repeat to spine, increase at spine. Mirror. Turn.
Row D (wrong side): As Row B. Turn.
Repeat rows A-D until the shawl is 50 cm deep from the neck edge when held flat and unblocked. Work a plain treble border row, then fasten off.

Soak the shawl, press out water in a towel, then pin. Pin the two tip ends of the crescent first to the wingspan markers at 155 cm apart on the blocking mats, then pin the centre back point downward to 50 cm. Fill in with pins along each curved edge every 5 cm. Leave until fully dry.
makes the chevron diagonals sharp and the holes round.

attrs.intro: Waterfall shawls have a few common tension and shaping errors.

items.fix: Mark the dc2tog positions on Row A with stitch markers and check they shift one stitch to the right on Row C. The diagonal angle comes from this one-stitch shift.
items.cause: dc2tog worked in wrong position
items.symptom: Chevron diagonals not aligning between rows

items.fix: The spine increase is always (2 tr, ch 2, 2 tr), not more. Count the spine stitches after each row and confirm the total stitch count grows by 4 per full repeat.
items.cause: Too many increases at the spine

items.fix: Work the ch-3 turning chain loosely. If the edge still pulls, add a ch-4 turning chain and count it as the first treble plus one chain space.
items.cause: Turning chain too short

title: Wine bottle cosy
subtitle: A fitted bottle holder in ribbed double crochet
excerpt: A fitted wine bottle holder in ribbed double crochet in aran cotton: worked in the round from the base, with ribbed sides that grip the bottle and keep it insulated. Makes a good gift wrap too. Beginner skill.
sourceNotes: Original pattern. Crocheted bottle cosies are a domestic convention.

content.text: A wine bottle cosy is a 26 cm circumference fitted bottle holder in aran cotton: worked in

from a circular base, sized for a standard 750 ml wine bottle. The back-loop rib is slightly stretchy and grips the bottle. Works equally well as a gift wrap for a bottle of wine or as everyday insulation in a drinks cooler.
80 m aran cotton. One 100 m ball makes one cosy with yarn left over.
14 dc × 18 rows = 10 × 10 cm in aran cotton with a 5 mm hook. Circumference: 36 dc = approx. 26 cm.
Double crochet (dc). UK term; US equivalent is single crochet (sc)
BLO dc: double crochet worked through the back loop only
Round 2: 2 dc in each st (12 dc).
Round 3: *1 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (18 dc).
Round 4: *2 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (24 dc).
Round 5: *3 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (30 dc).
Round 6: *5 dc, 2 dc in next; repeat (36 dc). Sl st.
Round 7: ch 1, BLO dc in each st (36 dc). Sl st. Working BLO now and on every subsequent round creates the rib.
Rounds 8, 46: ch 1, BLO dc in each st (36 dc). Sl st each round. 40 rounds = approx. 22 cm of ribbed sides.
Round 47 (top border): ch 1, 1 dc in both loops of each st (36 dc). Sl st. Fasten off.
Weave in both ends. The rib stretches enough to slip over the bottle base easily and springs back around the body.
Remove bottle before washing. Machine-wash on 30°C gentle cycle. Lay flat to dry.
